Ad litteram quoque populus Israel, quando Deo fideliter deservivit, habitavit in terra promissionis ; sed quando ad idololatriam corruit, expellebatur de ea, vel in servitutem redigebatur in ea : quod erat quasi ea privari. Et simplices columbina simplicitate, permanebunt in ea : sicut de rectis jam dictum est. Impii vero de terra perdentur : quia desinunt esse membra Christi filiique Ecclesiæ, per inobedientiam, et incorporantur diabolo, atque de terra hujus exilii ad inferos pertrahuntur ; et interdum propter sua interficiuntur facinora, terraque hereditatis cœlestis privantur. Et qui inique agunt, auferentur ex ea : sicut de impiis expositum est.
paras.en: [[2:21|For they that are upright|Qui enim recti sunt]] in heart, namely the just, whose hearts are raised straight and directly to God and who shun the crookedness of vices, [[2:21|shall dwell in the earth|habitabunt in terra]]: for already, through grace, faith and charity, they rest in the Church militant, which is a pilgrim on earth; and afterwards, through glory and the beatific enjoyment, they will dwell eternally in the Church triumphant, in the land and country of the living and the Blessed. Now too they dwell well in the land of their own body, because they hold it subject to reason and brought into subjection to the spirit[[1 Cor 9:27||]]: in which sense the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:4|Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the land|Beati mites, quoniam ipsi hereditabunt terram]] [Denis reads *hereditabunt*, "shall inherit", for the Vulgate's *possidebunt*]. According to the letter also, the people of Israel, while they served God faithfully, dwelt in the land of promise; but when they fell into idolatry they were driven out of it, or reduced to servitude in it, which was as good as being deprived of it. [[2:21|and the simple|Et simplices]], with dovelike simplicity, [[2:21|shall continue in it|permanebunt in ea]]: as has already been said of the upright. [[2:22|But the wicked shall be destroyed from the earth|Impii vero de terra perdentur]], because through disobedience they cease to be members of Christ and sons of the Church, and are incorporated into the devil, and are dragged from the land of this exile down to hell; and sometimes they are put to death for their crimes, and are deprived of the land of the heavenly inheritance. [[2:22|and they that do unjustly, shall be taken away from it|Et qui inique agunt, auferentur ex ea]]: as has been expounded of the wicked.

paras.t: Itaque ex isto docemur capitulo, quam ferventer et indesinenter debeamus quærere, desiderare, amplecti, et custodire increatam Sapientiam Dei Patris, Unigenitum Dei, et dona ipsius. Nemo enim, ut ait Ambrosius, cum desidia quærit Christum, et pretiosissima Dei dona cum affectu condigno sunt exquirenda ac postulanda : imo cum tepore et negligentia pro eis rogare, est datorem illum altissimum in suis donis tam caris inhonorare, ac parvi pendere munera ejus. Ipse certe in suo obsequio respuit indevotum, evomit tepidum, negligentem frigidumque abhorret, sicut de hoc Eusebius Emisenus pulchre in suis loquitur Homiliis. Et utique si perpendamus, quam infatigabiliter multi philosophi pro naturali sapientia ac scientia laboraverunt, quam laboriose quoque et incessanter multi mercatores et alii pro terrena opulentia enituntur, merito intra nos de nostra confundemur ignavia, […] quia pro spiritualibus, supernaturalibus, ac præstantissimis Dei donis, pro sapientia infusa, pro salute æterna adipiscendis, tam modice laboramus, tam frigide deprecamur, tam parum accendimur.
paras.en: So from this chapter we are taught how fervently and unceasingly we ought to seek, desire, embrace and keep the uncreated Wisdom of God the Father, the Only-begotten of God, and his gifts. For no one, as Ambrose says, seeks Christ with sloth; and the most precious gifts of God are to be sought out and asked for with a worthy affection: nay, to pray for them with lukewarmness and negligence is to dishonour that most high Giver in his gifts so dear, and to set little store by his bounty. He certainly rejects the undevout in his service, vomits out the lukewarm, and abhors the negligent and cold, as Eusebius of Emesa speaks finely of this in his *Homilies*. And indeed, if we consider how tirelessly many philosophers have laboured for natural wisdom and knowledge, and how laboriously and unceasingly many merchants and others strive for earthly wealth, we shall rightly be confounded within ourselves at our own sloth, […] because for the spiritual, supernatural and most excellent gifts of God, for infused wisdom, for the gaining of eternal salvation, we labour so little, pray so coldly, and are so little kindled.

3.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI TERTII : FILI MI, NE OBLIVISCARIS LEGIS MEÆ.
3.title_en: Exposition of the third chapter: My son, forget not my law.

paras.t: Ad diversas virtutes actionesque virtuosas in isto admonemur capitulo; et ne acediosi simus ad obtemperandum, adjiciuntur fructus præclari et præmia gloriosa.
paras.en: In this chapter we are admonished to various virtues and virtuous actions; and lest we be slothful [*acediosi*: afflicted with *acedia*, the spiritual sloth that finds the things of God wearisome] in obeying, glorious fruits and rewards are added.

paras.t: Fili mi, ne obliviscaris legis meæ, id est legis divinæ. Denique minus dicit, et majus prætendit: quia non solum debemus legis divinæ non oblivisci, sed et jugiter recordari, imo eam opere adimplere, quemadmodum in primo habetur psalmo de homine justo: In lege Domini voluntas ejus, et in lege ejus meditabitur die ac nocte. Dupliciter quoque dicitur homo oblivisci legis Dei: primo, eam oblivioni omnino tradendo; secundo, eam non adimplendo in factis, sicque multi obliviscuntur ejus, qui tamen docent aut prædicant eam. Insuper multiplex est lex Dei, quam recordari ac adimplere debemus. Est etenim lex divina, lex naturalis, lex positiva. Et lex divina, in legem Mosaicam evangelicamque dividitur. Similiter lex positiva, in Jus canonicum, et Jus civile. Lex autem seu jus naturale, variam habet divisionem, prout de ista materia in prima parte Decreti, ex verbis Isidori ac aliorum diffuse tractatur. Hinc Dominus ait: Scribam ei multiplices leges meas, quæ quasi alienæ computatæ sunt. Unde et in Job dicitur: Utinam Deus ostenderet tibi secreta sapientiæ suæ, et intelligeres quod multiplex est lex ejus. Est etiam lex æterna et increata, quæ est exemplar, fons, causa, et regula omnis legis creatæ et rectæ. Et præcepta mea cor tuum custodiat tenaci memoria, et exsecutione idonea; et quæ opere adimplere non vales, devota voluntate adimple, ac citius quo poteris, adimplere propone: sicut de bonis fertur in Psalmo, Memores sunt mandatorum ipsius ad faciendum ea.
paras.en: [[3:1|My son, forget not my law|Fili mi, ne obliviscaris legis meæ]], that is, the divine law. Here he says less and means more: for we must not only not forget the divine law, but also call it to mind continually, and indeed fulfil it in deed, as is said of the just man in the first psalm: [[Ps 1:2|his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he shall meditate day and night|In lege Domini voluntas ejus, et in lege ejus meditabitur die ac nocte]]. A man is also said to forget the law of God in two ways: first, by consigning it wholly to oblivion; secondly, by not fulfilling it in deeds; and in this way many forget it who nevertheless teach or preach it. Moreover the law of God, which we must call to mind and fulfil, is manifold. For there is the divine law, the natural law, and the positive law. The divine law is divided into the Mosaic law and the law of the Gospel. Likewise the positive law into canon law and civil law. The law or right of nature has various divisions, as is treated at length on this matter in the first part of the Decretum, from the words of Isidore and others [the opening Distinctions of Gratian's *Decretum*, which begin from Isidore's *Etymologies* on the kinds of law]. Hence the Lord says: [[Osee 8:12|I shall write to him my manifold laws, which have been accounted as foreign|Scribam ei multiplices leges meas, quæ quasi alienæ computatæ sunt]]. And so it is said also in Job: [[Job 11:5|I wish that God|Utinam Deus]] would [[Job 11:6|shew thee the secrets of wisdom, and that his law is manifold|ostenderet tibi secreta sapientiæ suæ, et intelligeres quod multiplex est lex ejus]]. There is also the eternal and uncreated law, which is the exemplar, fount, cause and rule of every created and right law. [[3:1|And let thy heart keep my commandments|Et præcepta mea cor tuum custodiat]] with a tenacious memory and a fitting execution; and what thou canst not fulfil in deed, fulfil with devout will, and resolve to fulfil as soon as thou canst: as is said of the good in the Psalm, [[Ps 102:18|mindful of his commandments to do them|Memores sunt mandatorum ipsius ad faciendum ea]].

paras.t: Consequenter pollicitatione mercedis ad istud inducit. Longitudinem enim dierum, et annos vitæ, et pacem apponent tibi: id est, pro observantia præceptorum consequeris hæc bona pro præmio: quod primo intelligi potest de longa, prospera, atque pacifica vita in sæculo isto, quæ in veteri lege promittebatur sæpissime observatoribus legis Mosaicæ. Verumtamen bona illa terrena ac transitoria, non erant principale aut sufficiens præmium obedientiæ Deo exhibitæ ex caritate in actibus virtuosis, qui sunt spiritualia bona. Multi quoque Prophetæ et Sancti ac justi fuerunt in veteri Testamento, qui præfata bona consecuti non sunt in hac vita, imo adversa multa et mortem pro lege ac justitia sunt perpessi, sicut in libro Machabæorum ostenditur. Et per Ezechielem Dominus ad Jerusalem dixit: Occidam in te justum et impium. Ideo per longitudinem dierum, æterna duratio felicitatis in cœlo, et per annos vitæ, diuturnitas gloriæ, et per pacem, pax æternitatis omnem sensum exsuperans, principaliter designantur. Unde in Psalmo Dominus pollicetur: Longitudine dierum implebo eum, et ostendam illi salutare meum; et in Isaia habetur, Erit mensis ex mense, et sabbatum ex sabbato: per quæ verba æternitas designatur. Et rursus ibidem: Ecce ego declino in eos ut flumen pacis.
paras.en: Next he leads us to this by the promise of a reward. [[3:2|For they shall add to thee length of days, and years of life, and peace|Longitudinem enim dierum, et annos vitæ, et pacem apponent tibi]]: that is, for keeping the commandments thou shalt obtain these goods as a reward. This can first be understood of a long, prosperous and peaceful life in this world, which in the old law was very often promised to those who kept the law of Moses[[Ex 20:12||]][[Deut 4:40||]][[Deut 5:16||]][[Deut 6:3||]][[Deut 7:13||]][[Deut 8:1||]][[Deut 11:8||]][[Deut 25:15||]][[Deut 28:1||]][[Deut 30:16||]] [the margin gives Exod. xx, 12; Deut. iv, 40; v, 16; vi, 3; vii, 13–16; viii, 1; xi, 8, 9; xxv, 15; xxviii, 1–13; xxx, 16]. Yet those earthly and passing goods were not the chief or sufficient reward of obedience shown to God out of charity in virtuous acts, which are spiritual goods. Many Prophets, too, and saints and just men in the Old Testament did not obtain those goods in this life; on the contrary, they suffered many adversities and death for the law and for justice, as is shown in the book of Machabees[[2 Mach 6:10||]][[2 Mach 6:18||]][[2 Mach 7:1||]] [the margin gives II Mach. vi, 10, 11, 18–31; vii]. And through Ezechiel the Lord said to Jerusalem: I [[Ezech 21:3|will cut off in thee the just, and the wicked|Occidam in te justum et impium]]. Therefore by *length of days* is chiefly signified the eternal duration of happiness in heaven; by *years of life*, the long continuance of glory; and by *peace*, the peace of eternity, [[Phil 4:7|which surpasseth all understanding|omnem sensum exsuperans]]. Hence in the Psalm the Lord promises: [[Ps 90:16|I will fill him with length of days; and I will shew him my salvation|Longitudine dierum implebo eum, et ostendam illi salutare meum]]; and in Isaias we have, [[Is 66:23|there shall be month after month, and sabbath after sabbath|Erit mensis ex mense, et sabbatum ex sabbato]]: by which words eternity is signified. And again in the same place: [[Is 66:12|Behold I will bring upon her as it were a river of peace|Ecce ego declino in eos ut flumen pacis]] [Denis has "I will turn aside upon them like a river of peace"].

paras.t: Misericordia et veritas, id est justitia, non te deserant: id est, indesinenter habe in te misericordiam atque justitiam, ita ut opera misericordiæ, tam spiritualia quam corporalia, pro posse exerceas, et justitiam non omittas: quia et sic interdum ignoscendum est animæ peccatoris, ut nihilo minus juxta censuram justitiæ puniatur, aut etiam occidatur in corpore. Imo hoc ipsum misericordiæ est, quod in præsenti punitur, ne æternaliter condemnetur. Nam et pœnæ præsentis vitæ sunt medicinales. Præterea, triplicem veritatem habere et conservare debemus, videlicet, veritatem vitæ, veritatem doctrinæ, veritatem justitiæ, et esse veraces in verbis, fidelesque proximis. Hinc in Osee scriptum est: Misericordiam et judicium custodi; et in Zacharia, Veritatem tantum et pacem diligite. Clarius quoque paulo anterius in Zacharia habetur: Judicium verum judicate, et misericordiam et miserationes facite, unusquisque cum fratre suo.
paras.en: [[3:3|Let not mercy aud truth|Misericordia et veritas]], that is, justice, [[3:3|leave thee|non te deserant]]: that is, have mercy and justice in thee unceasingly, so that thou practise the works of mercy, spiritual as well as corporal, as far as thou canst, and dost not neglect justice: for sometimes the soul of a sinner is to be pardoned in such a way that he is nonetheless punished according to the sentence of justice, or even put to death in the body. Indeed this very thing is a mercy, that he is punished in the present, lest he be condemned eternally. For the penalties of the present life are medicinal. Moreover, we must have and keep a threefold truth, namely truth of life, truth of doctrine, and truth of justice, and be truthful in our words and faithful to our neighbours. Hence it is written in Osee: [[Osee 12:6|keep mercy and judgment|Misericordiam et judicium custodi]]; and in Zacharias, [[Zach 8:19|only love ye truth and peace|Veritatem tantum et pacem diligite]]. And a little earlier in Zacharias it is put more clearly: [[Zach 7:9|Judge ye true judgment, and shew ye mercy and compassion every man to his brother|Judicium verum judicate, et misericordiam et miserationes facite, unusquisque cum fratre suo]].

paras.t: Circumda eas gutturi tuo, id est, aliis quoque prædica eas, ut et ipsi nequaquam misericordiam et veritatem relinquant: et quantum ad hoc, quasi tuba exalta vocem tuam. Et sicut in Osee habetur, In gutture tuo sit tuba, ut cum sancto Job dicere queas: Non dedi ad peccandum guttur meum. Et describe eas in tabulis cordis tui, id est in capacitate et latitudine mentis atque memoriæ tuæ. De his tabulis ait Apostolus: Epistola estis Christi, scripta non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei vivi; non in tabulis lapideis, sed in tabulis cordis carnalibus. Unde per Ezechielem Dominus dixit: Dabo vobis cor carneum, id est molle, flexibile, et faciliter receptivum gratiæ ac virtutum. Ideo tabulæ cordis sunt essentialiter spirituales, quamvis per proprietatem et similitudinem carnales vocentur, sicut et cor nominatur carnale. Nam et juxta Philosophum, intellectus seu anima in principio sui, est velut tabula rasa.
paras.en: [[3:3|put them about thy neck|Circumda eas gutturi tuo]] [*gutturi*, literally "throat", which links the quotations that follow], that is, preach them to others also, so that they too may by no means forsake mercy and truth: and as to this, [[Is 58:1|lift up thy voice like a trumpet|quasi tuba exalta vocem tuam]]. And as we have in Osee, [[Osee 8:1|Let there be a trumpet in thy throat|In gutture tuo sit tuba]], so that thou mayest say with holy Job: [[Job 31:30|I have not been given my mouth to sin|Non dedi ad peccandum guttur meum]] [Latin "I have not given my throat to sin"]. [[3:3|and write them in the tables of thy heart|Et describe eas in tabulis cordis tui]], that is, in the capacity and breadth of thy mind and memory. Of these tables the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 3:3|you are the epistle of Christ, ministered by us, and written: not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God: not in tables of stone but in the fleshly tables of the heart|Epistola estis Christi, scripta non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei vivi; non in tabulis lapideis, sed in tabulis cordis carnalibus]]. Hence the Lord said through Ezechiel: I [[Ezech 36:26|will give you a heart of flesh|Dabo vobis cor carneum]], that is, soft, pliant and readily receptive of grace and the virtues. So the tables of the heart are in their essence spiritual, though by a property and likeness they are called fleshly, just as the heart too is called fleshly. For according to the Philosopher [Aristotle, *De anima* III], the intellect or soul at its beginning is like a blank tablet.

paras.t: Et invenies gratiam et disciplinam bonam coram Deo et hominibus: id est, per hæc acceptus et placens eris Deo ac proximis; incrementumque gratiæ et profectum virtutum consequeris divinitus, et proximis disciplinatus videberis. Imo et bona instructio efficaciaque docendi ac disciplinandi alios, conferentur tibi a Domino. Qui enim dona desuper sibi concessa communicat aliis, meretur majora, et spiritualem opulentiam a Deo sortitur. Unde et Seneca in suis Proverbiis: Eleemosyna, inquit, plus prodest danti, quam accipienti.
paras.en: [[3:4|And thou shalt find grace, and good understanding before God and men|Et invenies gratiam et disciplinam bonam coram Deo et hominibus]] [*disciplinam*: "discipline", "training"]: that is, by these things thou shalt be acceptable and pleasing to God and to thy neighbours; thou shalt obtain from God an increase of grace and progress in the virtues, and to thy neighbours thou shalt appear well disciplined. Indeed good instruction, and skill in teaching and training others, will be bestowed on thee by the Lord. For he who shares with others the gifts granted him from above merits greater ones, and obtains spiritual wealth from God. Hence Seneca too says in his Proverbs: Alms, he says, profit the giver more than the receiver.

paras.t: Habe fiduciam in Domino ex toto corde tuo: quoniam ipse est infinitæ pietatis ad succurrendum, invariabilis veritatis ad faciendum quod sperantibus in se promisit, atque omnipotens ad exsequendum. Qui ait per Isaiam: Ego Dominus, super quo non confundentur omnes qui exspectant me. Cui ait Psalmista: Sperent in te, qui noverunt nomen tuum, quoniam non dereliquisti quærentes te, Domine. Denique, quamvis spes ista in Deo habeat firmitatem ac certitudinem, quantum est ex parte Dei, ex qua parte nequaquam erit defectus optatæ salutis et gratiæ: tamen ex parte nostri, hoc est ex propriæ fragilitatis, defectuositatis ac culpæ consideratione, debet timor esse admixtus: ne forte indigni simus exaudiri, adjuvari atque salvari a Domino propter nostra demerita, prout in tractatu de Spe Thomas declarat. Imo nec certi sumus de hoc, quod habeamus spem formatam et efficacem in Deo, quum ignoremus an simus in caritate. Hinc inter spem et timorem semper spiritualiter moli debemus, ut spes sit mola superior, sublevans in sublime, et desperationem ac pusillanimitatem excludens; timor vero sit mola inferior, præsumptionem et immoderatam securitatem repellens: sicut in tertia parte Summæ suæ Antisiodorensis inducit.
paras.en: [[3:5|Have confidence in the Lord with all thy heart|Habe fiduciam in Domino ex toto corde tuo]]: for he is of infinite goodness to succour, of unchanging truth to do what he has promised to those who hope in him, and almighty to carry it out. He says through Isaias: [[Is 49:23|I am the Lord, for they shall not be confounded that wait for him|Ego Dominus, super quo non confundentur omnes qui exspectant me]] [Denis has "I the Lord, upon whom all shall not be confounded that wait for me"]. To him the Psalmist says: [[Ps 9:11|let them trust in thee who know thy name: for thou hast not forsaken them that seek thee, O Lord|Sperent in te, qui noverunt nomen tuum, quoniam non dereliquisti quærentes te, Domine]]. Further, although this hope in God has firmness and certainty as far as God's side is concerned (on which side the salvation and grace we long for will never fail), yet on our side, that is, from the consideration of our own frailty, deficiency and guilt, fear ought to be mixed with it: lest perhaps we be unworthy to be heard, helped and saved by the Lord because of our demerits, as Thomas declares in the treatise on Hope [*Summa theologiae* II-II, qq. 17–22]. Indeed we are not even certain whether we have a hope formed [that is, quickened by charity] and effective in God, since we do not know whether we are in charity[[Eccles 9:1||]]. Hence we must always be ground spiritually between hope and fear, so that hope is the upper millstone, raising us on high and shutting out despair and faintheartedness, and fear the lower millstone, driving back presumption and immoderate security: as the Auxerrois [William of Auxerre] puts it in the third part of his *Summa*.

paras.t: Et ne innitaris prudentiæ tuæ, id est, propriæ prudentiæ aut naturali industriæ non inhæreas, tanquam tibi sufficiant pro tuæ conversationis directione, atque ad evadendum tuæ salutis pericula, dæmonum, carnis ac mundi tentamenta: ne impleatur in te quod dicitur in Isaia, Sapientia tua et scientia tua decepit te. Innitendum est ergo divino auxilio atque angelicæ directioni, et meritis precibusque Sanctorum: pro quibus impetrandis, devote ac jugiter est orandum. Etenim, qui habitat in adjutorio Altissimi, in protectione Dei cœli commorabitur. Ideo per Prophetam scriptum est: Quis ambulat in tenebris, et non est lumen ei? Speret in nomine Domini, et innitatur super Deum suum. Item protestatur Dominus: Perditio tua ex te; in me tantummodo auxilium tuum. Nempe ad bene agendum, indigemus in omni actu meritorio, actuali motione Spiritus Sancti. Et ut ait Apostolus: Non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid ex nobis quasi ex nobis; sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est, qui operatur in nobis velle atque perficere. Itaque habitus acquisiti et infusi non nobis sufficiunt, sed actualibus motionibus, influxionibus, directionibus, auxiliis Dei jugiter indigemus, sicut de hoc Thomas in Summa contra gentiles, catholice atque subtiliter scribit.
paras.en: [[3:5|and lean not upon thy own prudence|Et ne innitaris prudentiæ tuæ]], that is, do not cling to thy own prudence or natural skill as if they were enough for thee to direct thy way of life and to escape the dangers to thy salvation, the temptations of the demons, the flesh and the world: lest there be fulfilled in thee what is said in Isaias, [[Is 47:10|Thy wisdom, and, thy knowledge, this hath deceived thee|Sapientia tua et scientia tua decepit te]]. We must lean, then, on the divine help, on the guidance of the angels, and on the merits and prayers of the saints: to obtain which we must pray devoutly and continually. For [[Ps 90:1|He that dwelleth in the aid of the most High, shall abide under the protection of the God of Jacob|qui habitat in adjutorio Altissimi, in protectione Dei cœli commorabitur]] [Denis has "of the God of heaven"]. Therefore it is written by the Prophet: Who [[Is 50:10|hath walked in darkness, and hath no light? let him hope in the name of the Lord, and lean upon his God|ambulat in tenebris, et non est lumen ei? Speret in nomine Domini, et innitatur super Deum suum]]. Again the Lord declares: [[Osee 13:9|Destruction is thy own, O Israel: thy help is only in me|Perditio tua ex te; in me tantummodo auxilium tuum]] [Denis has "Thy destruction is from thee"]. For in order to act well we need, in every meritorious act, an actual movement of the Holy Ghost. And as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 3:5|Not that we are sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves: but our sufficiency is from God|Non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid ex nobis quasi ex nobis; sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est]], [[Phil 2:13|who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish|qui operatur in nobis velle atque perficere]]. So acquired and infused habits [that is, the virtues as settled dispositions, whether gained by practice or given by God] are not enough for us; we continually need God's actual movements, influences, directions and helps, as Thomas writes of this, in a Catholic and subtle way, in the *Summa contra gentiles* [book III].

paras.t: In omnibus viis, id est actionibus tuis interioribus et exterioribus, cogita illum, id est, divinæ majestatis præsentiam pensa, et ad Deum intentionem tuam refer ac dirige, ejusque directionem et opem implora: quod in omni actione faciendum est actualiter aut habitualiter, sæpeque actualiter; imo quo sæpius, tanto et melius. Tales fuerunt magni illi illuminatissimi viri Elias et Eliseus, dicentes: Vivit Dominus ante cujus vultum sto hodie. Ista assidua consideratio divinæ præsentiæ, maxime confert ad stabiliendum mentem in Deo. Talis fuit Psalmista, qui loquitur, Providebam Dominum in conspectu meo semper; et sanctus Job, dicens, Nonne Deus considerat viam meam, et omnes gressus meos dinumerat? Et ipse diriget gressus tuos, id est affectiones tuas et actus, ad finem beatum, dando tibi lumen veræ discretionis, et gratiam spiritualis profectus, ac super semitas justitiæ te ducendo. Pro qua directione piissima oravit Propheta: Gressus meos dirige secundum eloquium tuum. Quem Deus sic dirigit, nisi cujus mentem illustrat et movet in omnibus ad intuendum et exsequendum quidquid sibi complacitum est? Hanc certe directionem meretur percipere, qui tam reverenter in cunctis attendit Dei præsentiam.
paras.en: [[3:6|In all thy ways|In omnibus viis]], that is, in all thy actions, inward and outward, [[3:6|think on him|cogita illum]], that is, ponder the presence of the divine majesty, refer and direct thy intention to God, and implore his guidance and help: which is to be done in every action, actually or habitually [that is, by a present act of the mind, or by an intention once made that still governs the act], and often actually; indeed, the oftener the better. Such were those great and most enlightened men Elias and Eliseus, who said: [[3 Kings 18:15|As the Lord of hosts liveth, before whose face I stand|Vivit Dominus ante cujus vultum sto]] this day[[3 Kings 17:1||]][[4 Kings 3:14||]] [the margin gives III Reg. xvii, 1 and IV Reg. iii, 14; Denis's wording is closest to Elias's words at 3 Kings 18:15]. This constant consideration of the divine presence does most to make the mind steadfast in God. Such was the Psalmist, who says, [[Ps 15:8|I set the Lord always in my sight|Providebam Dominum in conspectu meo semper]]; and holy Job, saying, [[Job 31:4|Doth not he consider my ways, and number all my steps?|Nonne Deus considerat viam meam, et omnes gressus meos dinumerat?]]? [[3:6|and he will direct thy steps|Et ipse diriget gressus tuos]], that is, thy affections and acts, to the blessed end, giving thee the light of true discernment and the grace of spiritual progress, and leading thee on the paths of justice[[Ps 22:3||]]. For this most loving direction the Prophet prayed: [[Ps 118:133|Direct my steps according to thy word|Gressus meos dirige secundum eloquium tuum]]. Whom does God direct in this way, but him whose mind he enlightens and moves in all things to see and carry out whatever is pleasing to him? This direction he certainly deserves to receive who in all things so reverently attends to God's presence.

paras.t: Ne sis sapiens apud temetipsum, id est propria reputatione. Sed quomodo intelligendum est istud? quum dicat Apostolus, Ut sapiens architectus fundamentum posui; itemque, Spiritum non hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis. Ergo qui sapientiam a Deo accepit, et in Scripturis est eruditus, potest sapientem se reputare. Et respondendum, quod non debet se in se sapientem putare, sed solum in Deo; nec sibi, sed Deo sapientiam suam adscribere; magis quoque insistere considerationi insipientiæ suæ, et defectuositatis ac culpæ, quam magnificationi sapientiæ suæ: potissime quum ignoret an habeat sapientiam quæ est donum, sine qua vitio puerilitatis impletur homo, et potius stultus quam sapiens est censendus. Et juxta hunc sensum apud Isaiam inducitur: Væ qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris, et coram vobismetipsis prudentes. Unde et Paulus Romanis: Nolite, inquit, esse prudentes apud vosmetipsos.
paras.en: [[3:7|Be not wise in thy own conceit|Ne sis sapiens apud temetipsum]], that is, in thy own estimation. But how is this to be understood, since the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 3:10|as a wise architect, I have laid the foundation|Ut sapiens architectus fundamentum posui]]; and again, [[1 Cor 2:12|we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is of God: that we may know the things that are given us from God|Spiritum non hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis]]? Therefore he who has received wisdom from God and is learned in the Scriptures may consider himself wise. The answer is that he must not think himself wise in himself, but only in God; and ascribe his wisdom not to himself but to God; and dwell rather on the consideration of his own foolishness, deficiency and guilt than on extolling his wisdom: above all since he does not know whether he has the wisdom which is a gift [of the Holy Ghost], without which a man is filled with the vice of childishness and is to be judged a fool rather than wise. And in this sense it is put in Isaias: [[Is 5:21|Woe to you that are wise in your own eyes, and prudent in your own conceits|Væ qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris, et coram vobismetipsis prudentes]]. Hence Paul too says to the Romans: [[Rom 12:16|Be not|Nolite]], he says, [[Rom 12:16|wise in your own conceits|esse prudentes apud vosmetipsos]].

paras.t: Time Deum casto et filiali timore. Ecce qui paulo ante locutus est, Habe fiduciam in Domino; hic subjungit, Time Deum: quasi dicat, Non ita confidas in misericordia Dei, quin expavescas ejus justitiam, quoniam hæc est sapientia vera. Et recede a malo, id est, malum culpæ ex corde abhorre et fuge: quia ex hoc apparet quod timeas Deum, et sapiens sis in eo. Juxta quod in Job dicitur: Ecce timor Domini ipsa est sapientia; et recedere a malo, intelligentia. Hoc est quod Vas electionis hortatur: Noli altum sapere, id est magna de te ex elatione sentire; sed time. Unde et sanctus ait Bernardus: In veritate didici, nihil coram Deo ita prodesse ad gratiam obtinendam, ad culpam vitandam, ad proficiendum in bonis, quam ut semper inveniaris non altum sapere, sed timere.
paras.en: [[3:7|fear God|Time Deum]] with a chaste and filial fear [that is, the fear of offending a beloved Father, as opposed to servile fear of punishment]. See: he who said a little before, [[3:5|Have confidence in the Lord|Habe fiduciam in Domino]], here adds, [[3:7|fear God|Time Deum]]: as if to say, Do not so trust in God's mercy as not to dread his justice, for this is true wisdom. [[3:7|and depart from evil|Et recede a malo]], that is, abhor and flee from the evil of sin with thy heart: for by this it is plain that thou fearest God and art wise in him. According to what is said in Job: [[Job 28:28|Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom: and to depart from evil, is understanding|Ecce timor Domini ipsa est sapientia; et recedere a malo, intelligentia]]. This is what the Vessel of election [Paul, Acts 9:15] exhorts: [[Rom 11:20|Be not highminded|Noli altum sapere]], that is, do not think great things of thyself out of pride, [[Rom 11:20|but fear|sed time]]. Hence St. Bernard too says: I have learned in truth that nothing so profits before God for obtaining grace, for avoiding sin, for advancing in good, as that thou be found always not highminded, but fearing.

paras.t: Sanitas quippe erit umbilico tuo, et irrigatio ossium tuorum. Posset hoc superficialiter sic exponi, juxta veteris legis promissa: Quod si præhabita feceris bona, corporaliter eris sanus et bene dispositus intus in umbilico et ossibus. Sed quoniam multæ sunt tribulationes ægritudinesque justorum in vita hac, spiritualiter interpretandum est istud, intelligendo per umbilicum, qui mollis et tener est, bona opera adhuc imperfecta: per ossa vero, quæ solida sunt, opera virtuosa perfecta. Sicque, Sanitas erit umbilico tuo, id est, opera tua imperfecta, a culpis venialibus ac reliquiis vitiorum purgabuntur per confidentiam Dei, humiliationem, ceterasque virtutes et actiones earum prætactas, atque in melius omni die proficient, et opera tua perfecta, erunt pura, inviolata, illæsa. Possunt quoque per umbilicum intelligi affectiones, motus et actus partis sensitivæ, videlicet appetitus concupiscibilis et irascibilis, in quibus sunt animæ passiones: in quibus est sanitas, dum per virtutes reformantur morales; per ossa autem, actus partis intellectivæ.
paras.en: [[3:8|For it shall be health to thy navel, and moistening to thy bones|Sanitas quippe erit umbilico tuo, et irrigatio ossium tuorum]]. This could be expounded superficially thus, according to the promises of the old law: that if thou doest the good things spoken of above, thou shalt be bodily healthy and well disposed within, in navel and bones. But since [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just|multæ sunt tribulationes ægritudinesque justorum]] in this life, and their sicknesses, this is to be interpreted spiritually, understanding by the navel, which is soft and tender, good works still imperfect, and by the bones, which are solid, perfect virtuous works. And so, [[3:8|it shall be health to thy navel|Sanitas erit umbilico tuo]]: that is, thy imperfect works will be purged of venial faults and the remnants of vices by trust in God, humility, and the other virtues and their acts touched on above, and will grow better every day; and thy perfect works will be pure, unviolated, unharmed. By the navel may also be understood the affections, movements and acts of the sensitive part, namely of the concupiscible and irascible appetites [the faculties of desire and of resistance], in which are the passions of the soul: in these there is health when they are reformed by the moral virtues; and by the bones, the acts of the intellective part.

paras.t: Consequenter fit admonitio ad sacrificia Deo placentia. Honora Dominum de tua substantia, id est, de rebus et opibus tibi concessis offer Deo sacrificia in lege præcepta, hostiasque spontaneas ex devotione, pro pace, pro gratiarum actione, pro spiritualibus charismatibus obtinendis, et eorum profectibus. De quibus oblationibus in Levitico, in libro Numerorum, ac Deuteronomio copiosa est mentio: quæ omnia offerebantur Deo in recognitionem universalis dominii sui, et quod ipse sit omnis boni collator. Et de primitiis omnium frugum tuarum, id est de melioribus fructibus terræ tuæ potiora, non viliora, offerendo Creatori dignitatis ac excellentiæ infinitæ. Unde et Abel obtulit Deo de primogenitis gregis sui, et adipibus eorum, et placuit Deo; Cain vero de fructibus terræ, utique de deterioribus, ut legitur in Genesi. Hinc scriptum est: Si offeratis claudum aut languidum, nonne malum est? Offer illud duci tuo, si placuerit ei: hoc est, si talia viliora offerretis seu exhiberetis principi vestro terreno, non ei placeret, sed indignaretur quod talia vilia sibi darentur. Hinc rursus in eodem fertur Propheta: Maledictus dolosus, qui habet in grege suo masculum, et votum faciens, immolat debile Domino. Spiritualiter autem de omnibus bonis nobis concessis, debemus Deo sacrificium laudis, gratiarum actionem, reverentiamque offerre: imo nos ipsos totaliter et quidquid habemus in ejus cultum obsequiumque convertere. Oblationes quoque et decimas corporales ab Ecclesia institutas, fideliter et libenter persolvere et offerre, nec in Dei conspectu vacui apparere, et quidquid præcipue bonum habemus aut agimus, debemus specialiter Deo adscribere; nec aliquid nobis ipsis, nisi peccata nostra et vitia, deputare. Da pauperibus: id est, non solum præfato modo de bonis tuis Deum honora, sed et pauperibus, qui sunt fratres et proximi tui, membraque Dei, communica et succurre.
paras.en: Next comes an admonition to sacrifices pleasing to God. [[3:9|Honour the Lord with thy substance|Honora Dominum de tua substantia]], that is, from the goods and riches granted thee offer God the sacrifices commanded in the law, and freewill victims out of devotion: for peace, for thanksgiving, for obtaining spiritual gifts and for progress in them. Of these offerings there is abundant mention in Leviticus, in the book of Numbers and in Deuteronomy: all of which were offered to God in acknowledgement of his universal dominion, and that he is the giver of every good. [[3:9|and give him of the first of all thy fruits|Et de primitiis omnium frugum tuarum]], that is, of the better fruits of thy land, the choicer, not the meaner, offering them to the Creator of infinite dignity and excellence. So Abel too [[Gen 4:4|offered of the firstlings of his flock, and of their fat|obtulit Deo de primogenitis gregis sui, et adipibus eorum]] to God, and pleased God; but Cain offered [[Gen 4:3|of the fruits of the earth|de fructibus terræ]], and of the worse, to be sure, as we read in Genesis. Hence it is written: [[Mal 1:8|if you offer the lame and the sick, is it not evil? offer it to thy prince, if he will be pleased with it|Si offeratis claudum aut languidum, nonne malum est? Offer illud duci tuo, si placuerit ei]]: that is, if you offered or presented such mean things to your earthly prince, it would not please him; he would be indignant that such mean things were given him. Hence again it is said in the same Prophet: [[Mal 1:14|Cursed is the deceitful man that hath in his flock a male, and making a vow offereth in sacrifice that which is feeble to the Lord|Maledictus dolosus, qui habet in grege suo masculum, et votum faciens, immolat debile Domino]]. Spiritually, however, from all the goods granted us we must offer God a sacrifice of praise, thanksgiving and reverence: indeed, turn ourselves wholly, and whatever we have, to his worship and service. We must also pay and offer faithfully and willingly the bodily offerings and tithes instituted by the Church, and not appear empty in God's sight[[Ex 23:15||]][[Ex 34:20||]][[Deut 16:16||]]; and whatever good we chiefly have or do, we must ascribe especially to God, and count nothing as ours but our sins and vices. *Give to the poor*[[3:9||]] [Denis reads *da pauperibus*, "give to the poor", where the Vulgate has *da ei*, "give him"]: that is, not only honour God with thy goods in the way just said, but also share with and succour the poor, who are thy brethren and neighbours and members of God.

paras.t: Et implebuntur horrea tua saturitate, id est fructibus terræ copiosis, qui tibi et tuis domesticis ad refectionem plene sufficient; et vino torcularia tua redundabunt, id est, vineæ tuæ tot proferent uvas, quod in torcularibus exprimetur de eis vinum abundans: quod in Deuteronomio quoque promittitur. Spiritualiter autem, qui opera pietatis exercet, et verbo cœlestis doctrinæ reficit audientes, ac poculo spiritualis consolationis recreat eos, meretur ut horrea sua impleantur saturitate, id est, potentiæ animæ suæ, quæ sunt subjecta gratiæ ac virtutum, præsertim intellectus atque voluntas, impleantur a Deo interna refectione; et torcularia ejus vino redundent, id est, vires præfatæ, in quibus ex littera trahitur spiritualis intelligentia, sicut ex uva per pressuram educitur vinum, repleantur spirituali ac sobria ebrietate, ex divinorum contemplatione et caritatis fervore.
paras.en: [[3:10|And thy barns shall be filled with abundance|Et implebuntur horrea tua saturitate]], that is, with plentiful fruits of the earth, which will fully suffice to feed thee and thy household; [[3:10|and thy presses shall run over with wine|et vino torcularia tua redundabunt]], that is, thy vineyards will bear so many grapes that abundant wine will be pressed from them in the winepresses: which is also promised in Deuteronomy[[Deut 11:14||]] [the margin gives Deut. xi, 13, 14]. Spiritually, however, he who practises works of piety, and refreshes his hearers with the word of heavenly doctrine, and revives them with the cup of spiritual consolation, deserves that his barns be filled with abundance: that is, that the powers of his soul, which are the subjects of grace and the virtues, above all the intellect and will, be filled by God with inward refreshment; and that his presses run over with wine: that is, that those same powers, in which the spiritual understanding is drawn out of the letter as wine is drawn from the grape by pressing, be filled with a spiritual and sober inebriation, from the contemplation of divine things and the fervour of charity.

paras.t: Insuper, juxta Glossam, quemadmodum electi habent thesauros in cœlo (secundum quod ait Salvator, Thesaurizate vobis thesauros in cœlo), sic et horrea ac torcularia habent ibidem: in quibus taliter reficientur ac potabuntur, quod ultra non esuriunt nec sitient. De quibus Filius Dei disseruit: Facite vobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis, ut, quum defecerit, recipiant vos in æterna tabernacula; itemque, in domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt, hoc est diversi gradus præmiorum, secundum varietatem ac differentiam meritorum.
paras.en: Moreover, according to the Gloss, just as the elect have treasures in heaven (according to the Saviour's saying, [[Matt 6:20|lay up to yourselves treasures in heaven|Thesaurizate vobis thesauros in cœlo]]), so they have barns and presses there too: in which they will be so fed and given drink that [[Apoc 7:16|They shall no more hunger nor thirst|ultra non esuriunt nec sitient]][[Is 49:10||]]. Of these the Son of God spoke: [[Luke 16:9|Make unto you friends of the mammon of iniquity: that when you shall fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings|Facite vobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis, ut, quum defecerit, recipiant vos in æterna tabernacula]] [Denis has "when it shall fail"]; and again, [[John 14:2|In my Father's house there are many mansions|in domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt]], that is, different degrees of rewards, according to the variety and difference of merits.

paras.t: Amplius, sicut ex verbis sanctorum Patrum Hieronymi et Augustini, imo ex Scripturis colligitur, fidelis persolutio decimarum, primitiarum et oblationum ab Ecclesia statutarum, constructio ecclesiarum, fundatio monasteriorum, exhibitio operum misericordiæ, quatuor mercedes a Domino sortiuntur. Prima est, abundantia opum, ex copiosa fertilitate agrorum et vinearum. Hinc loquitur Deus per Malachiam: Inferte omnem decimam in horreum meum, ut sit cibus in domo mea; et probate me super hoc, si non aperuero vobis cataractas cœli, et effudero vobis benedictionem meam usque ad abundantiam, et non erit sterilis vinea. Et per Aggæum: Quia domus mea deserta est, et vos festinastis unusquisque in domum suam; propter hoc super vos prohibiti sunt cœli, ne darent rorem, et terra prohibita est, ne daret germen suum. Et de hoc plenius alibi. Secunda merces, est prolongatio ac sanitas vitæ. Tertia vero, affluentia gratiæ in præsenti. Quarta autem, copia gloriæ in futuro. Denique in oblationibus quæ Deo fiunt, ipse qui cordium est inspector, magis respicit ad mentis sinceritatem, caritatem ac devotionem, quam ad munerum quantitatem. Ideo scriptum est in Genesi: Respexit Dominus ad Abel, et ad munera ejus. Primo enim attendit et approbavit ipsius sancti et innocentis Abel sincerissimam devotionem, et ita deinceps acceptavit sacrificia ejus. Hinc etiam Seneca in suis hortatur Proverbiis: Non adspicias quam plenas, sed quam puras manus quisque Deo admoveat. Nihilo minus Hostia altaris, videlicet sacrificium novæ legis, per se complacet Deo.
paras.en: Further, as is gathered from the words of the holy Fathers Jerome and Augustine, and indeed from the Scriptures, the faithful payment of tithes, first-fruits and offerings laid down by the Church, the building of churches, the founding of monasteries and the doing of works of mercy obtain four rewards from the Lord. The first is abundance of wealth, from the plentiful fertility of fields and vineyards. Hence God speaks through Malachias: [[Mal 3:10|Bring all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in my house, and try me in this, saith the Lord: if I open not unto you the flood-gates of heaven, and pour you out a blessing even to abundance|Inferte omnem decimam in horreum meum, ut sit cibus in domo mea; et probate me super hoc, si non aperuero vobis cataractas cœli, et effudero vobis benedictionem meam usque ad abundantiam]], and [[Mal 3:11|neither shall the vine in the field be barren|non erit sterilis vinea]]. And through Aggeus: [[Agg 1:9|because my house is desolate, and you make haste every man to his own house|Quia domus mea deserta est, et vos festinastis unusquisque in domum suam]]; [[Agg 1:10|Therefore the heavens over you were stayed from giving dew, and the earth was hindered from yielding her fruits|propter hoc super vos prohibiti sunt cœli, ne darent rorem, et terra prohibita est, ne daret germen suum]]. And of this more fully elsewhere. The second reward is length and health of life. The third, abundance of grace in the present. The fourth, a wealth of glory in the future. Lastly, in the offerings made to God, he who is the searcher of hearts[[1 Kings 16:7||]][[Prov 24:12||]][[Ecclus 23:28||]] [the margin is partly cut off; it reads (I) Reg. xvi, (7); Prov. (xx)iv, 12; Eccli. xxiii, (28)] looks more to sincerity of mind, charity and devotion than to the size of the gifts. Therefore it is written in Genesis: [[Gen 4:4|the Lord had respect to Abel, and to his offerings|Respexit Dominus ad Abel, et ad munera ejus]]. For first he regarded and approved the most sincere devotion of the holy and innocent Abel himself, and so afterwards accepted his sacrifices. Hence Seneca too exhorts in his Proverbs: Look not how full, but how pure are the hands each man raises to God. Nevertheless the Victim of the altar, namely the sacrifice of the new law, is pleasing to God of itself [that is, *ex opere operato*, by its own worth and not by the devotion of the offerer].

paras.t: Sed quia nonnulli in prosperis Deo obsequuntur, adhærent ac gratias agunt, in adversis autem deficiunt et labuntur (de quibus disseruit Christus, quod ad tempus credunt, et tempore tentationis recedunt: unde et in Psalmo dicitur, Confitebitur tibi quum benefeceris ei); ideo nunc hortatur Sapientia, ne adversis frangamur. Disciplinam Domini, fili mi, ne abjicias, neque deficias quum ab eo corriperis. Disciplina Dei est omnis adversitas, tribulatio, castigatio, increpatio: quæ ex divina providentia accidit nobis, a quocumque infligatur. Et sicut legitur, Deus increpat quandoque per dolorem in lectulo, et omnia ossa hominis marcescere facit. Per prælatos quoque vicarios suos, et per principes ac judices corripit et castigat: qui teste Apostolo ad Romanos, ministri Dei sunt, in hoc ipsum constituti. Omnia igitur ista æquanimiter ferre debemus, tanquam virgam fidelissimi patris: primo, quia per ista purgamur a vitiis; secundo, quia per hæc crescimus in virtutibus; tertio, quoniam per hæc a futuris gravissimis eripimur pœnis; quarto, quia per ista capiti nostro Christo propter nos passo, aliqualiter conformamur; quinto, quia per hæc corona æternæ felicitatis nobis augetur; sexto, quia per hæc efficimur in spirituali conversatione exercitati (Qui enim non est tentatus, quid scit?); septimo, quia ex horum eventu cognoscimus caritatem Patris cœlestis ad nos, qui ob tam multiplicem fructum et commodum nostrum, per præfata nos disciplinat.
paras.en: But since some serve God, cleave to him and give thanks in prosperity, but in adversity fail and fall away (of whom Christ said that [[Luke 8:13|they believe for a while and in time of temptation they fall away|ad tempus credunt, et tempore tentationis recedunt]]; whence it is said in the Psalm too, [[Ps 48:19|he will praise thee when thou shalt do well to him|Confitebitur tibi quum benefeceris ei]]), Wisdom now exhorts us not to be broken by adversity. [[3:11|My son, reject not the correction of the Lord: and do not faint when thou art chastised by him|Disciplinam Domini, fili mi, ne abjicias, neque deficias quum ab eo corriperis]]. The correction [*disciplina*] of God is every adversity, tribulation, chastisement and rebuke that befalls us by divine providence, by whomever it is inflicted. And as we read, God [[Job 33:19|rebuketh also by sorrow in the bed, and he maketh all his bones to wither|increpat quandoque per dolorem in lectulo, et omnia ossa hominis marcescere facit]]. He also corrects and chastises through prelates, his vicars, and through princes and judges, who, as the Apostle witnesses to the Romans, [[Rom 13:6|they are the ministers of God|ministri Dei sunt]], appointed for this very thing. All these things, then, we must bear with an even mind, as the rod of a most faithful father: first, because by them we are purged of vices; secondly, because by them we grow in virtues; thirdly, because by them we are snatched from the most grievous punishments to come; fourthly, because by them we are in some measure conformed to Christ our head, who suffered for us; fifthly, because by them the crown of eternal happiness is increased for us; sixthly, because by them we are made practised in the spiritual life ([[Ecclus 34:9|What doth he know, that hath not been tried?|Qui enim non est tentatus, quid scit?]]); seventhly, because from their coming we know the charity of the heavenly Father towards us, who for such manifold fruit and profit of ours corrects us by these things.

paras.t: Hinc subditur: Quem enim diligit Dominus, corripit, et quasi pater in filio complacet sibi, id est, beneplacitum est ei in his, sicut pater complacentiam habet in filio suo dilecto et bono. Ideo ait Glossa: Tanto minus de flagello quo castigamur, murmurare debemus, quanto certius in eo pignus paternæ dilectionis tenemus. Unde et ipse in Apocalypsi fatetur: Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo. Hinc de reprobis ait: Non visitabo super filias vestras quum fuerint fornicatæ. Per Ezechielem quoque ait de reprobo indurato: Auferetur zelus meus a te, non irascar tibi amplius. Et in Psalmo de impiis: Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordium eorum. Hæc est metuendissima et gravissima Dei plaga ac ira, dum justo judicio hominem sic relinquit. Desideremus ergo in vita præsenti paternæ castigari a Domino, et superiorum nostrorum correptiones atque correctiones hilariter amplectamur, quum et Apostolus jubeat: In disciplina perseverate; tanquam filiis vobis se offert Deus. Quis enim filius quem non corripit pater? Quod si extra disciplinam estis, ergo adulteri, et non filii estis. Hinc etiam in Job habetur: Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino. Increpationem ergo Domini ne reprobes: quoniam ipse vulnerat, et medetur; percutit, et manus ejus sanabunt.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[3:12|For whom the Lord loveth, he chastiseth: and as a father in the son he pleaseth himself|Quem enim diligit Dominus, corripit, et quasi pater in filio complacet sibi]], that is, he is well pleased in them, as a father takes pleasure in his beloved and good son. Therefore the Gloss says: The more surely we hold in the scourge with which we are chastised a pledge of fatherly love, the less we ought to murmur at it. Hence he himself declares in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:19|Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise|Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo]]. Hence he says of the reprobate: [[Osee 4:14|I will not visit upon your daughters, when they shall commit fornication|Non visitabo super filias vestras quum fuerint fornicatæ]]. Through Ezechiel too he says of the hardened reprobate: [[Ezech 16:42|my jealousy shall depart from thee|Auferetur zelus meus a te]], I will [[Ezech 16:42|be angry no more|non irascar tibi amplius]]. And in the Psalm, of the wicked: [[Ps 80:13|So I let them go according to the desires of their heart|Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordium eorum]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxx (for lxxx), 13]. This is the most dreadful and grievous stroke and wrath of God, when by a just judgment he abandons a man so. Let us desire, then, to be chastised by the Lord in a fatherly way in this present life, and let us cheerfully embrace the reproofs and corrections of our superiors, since the Apostle too bids us: [[Heb 12:7|Persevere under discipline. God dealeth with you as with his sons. For what son is there whom the father doth not correct?|In disciplina perseverate; tanquam filiis vobis se offert Deus. Quis enim filius quem non corripit pater?]]? [[Heb 12:8|But if you be without chastisement|Quod si extra disciplinam estis]], [[Heb 12:8|then are you bastards and not sons|ergo adulteri, et non filii estis]]. Hence we have also in Job: [[Job 5:17|Blessed is the man whom God correcteth: refuse not, therefore, the chastising of the Lord|Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino. Increpationem ergo Domini ne reprobes]]: [[Job 5:18|For he woundeth, and cureth: he striketh, and his hands shall heal|quoniam ipse vulnerat, et medetur; percutit, et manus ejus sanabunt]].

paras.t: Beatus homo qui invenit sapientiam, id est, qui a Deo suscipit ac retinet eam, præsertim illam quæ est donum Spiritus Sancti: in qua potissime crescit, disciplinam Domini modo prætacto gratanter ferendo, et in omni adversitate patientiam conservando; et qui affluit prudentia, quæ est virtus moralis dignissima, virtutum auriga, docens modum in cunctis tenere, ac ordinate ad finem intentum procedere: in qua qui affluit seu abundat, aptus est et alios gubernare.
paras.en: [[3:13|Blessed is the man that findeth wisdom|Beatus homo qui invenit sapientiam]], that is, who receives it from God and keeps it, above all that wisdom which is a gift of the Holy Ghost: in which he grows most by bearing the correction of the Lord gladly in the way just described and keeping patience in every adversity; [[3:13|and is rich in prudence|et qui affluit prudentia]], which is the most worthy moral virtue, the charioteer of the virtues, teaching us to keep the measure in all things and to proceed in order to the end intended: he who is rich or abounds in it is fit to govern others also.

paras.t: Melior est acquisitio ejus negotiatione auri et argenti: quia incomparabiliter est præstantior corporalibus ac transitoriis opibus. Primi et purissimi fructus ejus. Fructus sapientiæ hujus, sunt actiones, delectationes et cetera bona quæ oriuntur ex ea: qui fructus sunt primi, id est principales atque præcipui, sicut et ipsa sapientia inter virtutes et dona tenet primatum; et item purissimi ex sua natura, quia versantur circa supermundissimum illud objectum, quod Deus est, et circa spiritualia ac divina. Contemplatio quoque, quæ est actus et fructus sapientiæ hujus, est affectuosa ac limpida Dei cognitio. Circa hoc scribit quidam: Purissimi sunt fructus sapientiæ, quia spiritualia bona non habent aliquod malum admixtum, sicut frequenter habent corporalia, ut aurum, argentum, et consimilia habent annexam sollicitudinem, impedientem mentis elevationem in Deum. Quod non videtur congrue dictum, præsertim quum Isaias affirmet: Quasi pannus menstruatæ universæ justitiæ nostræ. Gregorius quoque in Moralibus super Job, frequenter effatur, quod mens nostra in divinorum contemplatione diu non figitur: quoniam carnis infirmitas et instabilitas cordis trahunt deorsum. Nonne indesinenter ac miserabiliter experimur, quantæ distractiones, venialesque culpæ orationibus ac meditationibus nostris assidue misceantur, et in divino obsequio negligentiæ, pigritiæ, ac somnolentiæ multæ contingant?
paras.en: [[3:14|The purchasing thereof is better than the merchandise of silver|Melior est acquisitio ejus negotiatione auri et argenti]] [Denis reads "of gold and silver"]: for it is incomparably more excellent than bodily and passing riches. [[3:14|the chief and purest|Primi et purissimi]] are [[3:14|her fruit|fructus ejus]] [Denis takes "first and purest" with "her fruits"; the Douay-Rheims, with the usual reading, joins them to gold: "and her fruit than the chief and purest gold"]. The fruits of this wisdom are the actions, delights and other goods that spring from it: and these fruits are *first*, that is, principal and foremost, just as wisdom itself holds the first place among the virtues and gifts; and also *purest* by their nature, because they are concerned with that supremely pure object which is God, and with spiritual and divine things. Contemplation too, which is the act and fruit of this wisdom, is an affectionate and limpid knowledge of God. On this a certain writer says: The fruits of wisdom are purest, because spiritual goods have no evil mixed with them, as bodily goods often have: gold, silver and the like have anxiety attached, which hinders the raising of the mind to God. This does not seem fittingly said, especially since Isaias affirms: [[Is 64:6|all our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman|Quasi pannus menstruatæ universæ justitiæ nostræ]]. Gregory too often says in the *Morals on Job* that our mind is not long fixed in the contemplation of divine things, because the weakness of the flesh and the instability of the heart drag it down. Do we not experience unceasingly and miserably how many distractions and venial faults are constantly mingled with our prayers and meditations, and how many negligences, sluggishnesses and drowsinesses befall us in the service of God?

paras.t: Pretiosior est sapientia cunctis opibus transitoriis ac terrenis: et omnia quæ desiderantur, ex universitate corporalium rerum, huic non valent comparari. Si autem prædicta exponantur de Sapientia increata, quæ in hac vita per fidem, caritatem et contemplationem aliquo modo invenitur et habetur, certum est quod illa incomparabiliter cunctis præmineat rebus creatis. De hac pretiositate et dignitate sapientiæ, in libro Sapientiæ multa dicuntur. De qua et in Job asseritur: Nescit homo pretium ejus. Non dabitur aurum obrizum pro ea, nec conferetur lapidi sardonycho pretiosissimo vel sapphiro.
paras.en: [[3:15|She is more precious|Pretiosior est]], wisdom is, [[3:15|than all riches|cunctis opibus]] that are passing and earthly: [[3:15|and all the things that are desired|et omnia quæ desiderantur]] out of the whole range of bodily things [[3:15|are not to be compared to her|huic non valent comparari]]. But if these words are expounded of the uncreated Wisdom, which in this life is in some way found and possessed by faith, charity and contemplation, it is certain that it surpasses all created things beyond compare. Of this preciousness and dignity of wisdom many things are said in the book of Wisdom[[Wis 7:1||]] [the margin gives Sap. vii–x]. Of it Job also affirms: [[Job 28:13|Man knoweth not the price thereof|Nescit homo pretium ejus]]. [[Job 28:15|The finest gold shall not purchase it|Non dabitur aurum obrizum pro ea]], [[Job 28:16|It shall not be compared|nec conferetur]] [[Job 28:16|with the most precious stone sardonyx, or the sapphire|lapidi sardonycho pretiosissimo vel sapphiro]].

paras.t: Longitudo dierum in dextera ejus, et in sinistra illius divitiæ et gloria. Dextera et sinistra metaphorice adscribitur sapientiæ, intelligendo per dexteram ejus, potiora et præclariora sapientiæ bona; per sinistram vero, secundaria ejus bona. Itaque in dextera sapientiæ, est longitudo dierum, id est dies æternitatis, et beatifica visio increatæ et incommutabilis veritatis: ad quæ sapientia habet primum ac principalem respectum. In sinistra vero ipsius, sunt divitiæ exteriores, et gloria, id est claritas famæ: quia ad sapientiam duo hæc consequi solent, sicut in Salomone. Vel per divitias et gloriam designantur accidentalia præmia Beatorum, ad quæ sapientia ista perducit.
paras.en: [[3:16|Length of days is in her right hand, and in her left hand riches and glory|Longitudo dierum in dextera ejus, et in sinistra illius divitiæ et gloria]]. A right hand and a left are ascribed to wisdom metaphorically: by her right hand are understood the better and more excellent goods of wisdom, and by her left her secondary goods. So in the right hand of wisdom is *length of days*, that is, the day of eternity, and the beatific vision of the uncreated and unchangeable truth: to which wisdom looks first and chiefly. In her left hand are outward *riches*, and *glory*, that is, brightness of fame: for these two usually follow on wisdom, as in Solomon. Or by riches and glory are signified the accidental rewards of the blessed [that is, joys added to the essential reward, the vision of God], to which this wisdom leads.

paras.t: Viæ ejus, viæ pulchræ. Viæ sapientiæ, sunt actiones et processus, seu doctrinæ ac merita ejus : quæ omnia bene dicuntur viæ, quoniam sicut via est medium inter duo extrema, et inter terminos duos; sic actiones et merita vitæ præsentis, sunt media quædam inter istud exsilium sæculumque futurum, seu inter mansionem istam terrenam et patriam Beatorum. Itaque viæ, id est actiones, contemplationes, delectationes, et merita sapientiæ, sunt viæ pulchræ : quia in ipsis est splendor veritatis, lux gratiæ ac virtutis sinceritas; immunditiam etiam peccati depellunt. Et sicut in corporalibus dicitur pulchrum, quod oblectat corporeum visum; sic spiritualiter pulchrum censetur, quod interiorem visum, scilicet intellectum, delectat : quod actibus sapientiæ competit valde, quum et Philosophus dicat quod philosophia, id est naturalis sapientia, admirabiles delectationes habet admixtas. De qua re in libro Sapientiæ plurima continentur. Et omnes semitæ illius pacificæ. Nam contemplationes et actiones, gustus et profectus sapientiæ hujus, in semetipsis tranquilla sunt, et mentem quietant, perturbationem excludunt, atque ad pacem æternitatis perducunt.
paras.en: [[3:17|Her ways are beautiful ways|Viæ ejus, viæ pulchræ]]. The ways of wisdom are its actions and proceedings, or its teachings and merits: all of which are well called ways, since, as a way is a middle between two extremes and between two end-points, so the actions and merits of the present life are a kind of middle between this exile and the world to come, or between this earthly dwelling and the fatherland of the Blessed. And so the ways, that is, the actions, contemplations, delights and merits of wisdom, are beautiful ways: for in them is the splendour of truth, the light of grace and the purity of virtue; they also drive out the uncleanness of sin. And as in bodily things that is called beautiful which delights the bodily sight, so spiritually that is reckoned beautiful which delights the inward sight, namely the intellect: and this belongs in a high degree to the acts of wisdom, since the Philosopher too says that philosophy, that is, natural wisdom, has wonderful delights mingled with it. On this matter a great deal is contained in the book of Wisdom[[Wis 7:1||]] [the margin gives Sap. vii–ix]. [[3:17|And all her paths are peaceable|Et omnes semitæ illius pacificæ]]. For the contemplations and actions, the relish and the progress of this wisdom, are tranquil in themselves, and quiet the mind, shut out disturbance, and lead to the peace of eternity.

paras.t: Insuper viæ increatæ Sapientiæ prorsus pulcherrimæ sunt, utpote Christi præcepta, documenta, et exempla seu opera, omnem turpitudinem culpæ deformitatemque falsitatis excludentia ex se et prohibentia aliis; et semitæ ejus pacificæ, id est evangelica ejus consilia ad pacem pectoris ac tranquillissimam vitam disponentia ac perducentia. Docent enim, inquietudinem passionum, sollicitudinem temporalium, occupationem terrenorum, concupiscentias carnis omnino vitare, atque in solo Deo recolligere ac figere mentem. Rursus, semitæ Christi pacificæ, quia per ejus mysteria ac opera reconciliati exsistimus Deo.
paras.en: Moreover, the ways of the uncreated Wisdom are altogether most beautiful, namely Christ's precepts, teachings, and examples or works, which shut out of themselves and forbid to others all foulness of guilt and deformity of falsehood; and [[3:17|her paths are peaceable|semitæ ejus pacificæ]], that is, his gospel counsels, which dispose and lead to peace of heart and a most tranquil life. For they teach us to shun altogether the restlessness of the passions, anxiety over temporal things, busyness with earthly things and the desires of the flesh, and to gather and fix the mind on God alone. Again, the paths of Christ are peaceable because through his mysteries and works we have been reconciled to God.

paras.t: Lignum vitæ est his qui apprehenderint eam : id est, sapientia instar ligni vitæ, quod est in paradiso, spiritualiter reficit, et in vita gratiæ conservat, ac roborat sapientem. Quemadmodum lignum illud vitæ situm in medio paradisi, conservativum fuit et est vitæ corporalis in suo vigore; sic Christus quoque, qui etiam, dum iret ut crucifigeretur, nuncupavit se viride lignum, recte dicitur lignum vitæ credentibus in se : quia multiplici alimonia reficit ac sustentat fideles, quousque de vita gratiæ ad vitam gloriæ elevantur, videlicet pane lacrimarum, vigore operationum bonarum, donis gratiæ ac virtutum, consolatione et spe futurorum, imo se ipso, suique corporis ac sanguinis Sacramento. Nam ait : Ego sum panis vitæ; et, Hic est panis vivus de cœlo descendens, ut si quis manducaverit ex ipso, non moriatur in æternum. Et qui tenuerit eam, id est, qui vitaverit omne peccatum mortale, quo donum sapientiæ perditur, et gratiosa Christi præsentia tollitur, beatus est jam in spe et merito, ac prælibatione et dispositione propinqua.
paras.en: [[3:18|She is a tree of life to them that lay hold on her|Lignum vitæ est his qui apprehenderint eam]]: that is, wisdom, like the tree of life which is in paradise, spiritually refreshes the wise man, keeps him in the life of grace and strengthens him. As that tree of life set in the midst of paradise[[Gen 2:9||]] served and serves to keep bodily life in its vigour, so Christ too, who, as he was going to be crucified, called himself the green wood[[Luke 23:31||]], is rightly called the tree of life to those who believe in him: for he refreshes and sustains the faithful with manifold nourishment until they are raised from the life of grace to the life of glory, namely with [[Ps 79:6|the bread of tears|pane lacrimarum]], with the vigour of good works, with the gifts of grace and of the virtues, with the consolation and hope of things to come, nay, with himself and with the Sacrament of his Body and Blood. For he says: [[John 6:48|I am the bread of life|Ego sum panis vitæ]]; and, [[John 6:50|This is the bread which cometh down from heaven: that if any man eat of it, he may not die|Hic est panis vivus de cœlo descendens, ut si quis manducaverit ex ipso, non moriatur in æternum]] [Denis's wording, "the living bread … may not die for ever", draws also on John 6:51–52]. [[3:18|And he that shall retain her|Et qui tenuerit eam]], that is, he who shuns every mortal sin, by which the gift of wisdom is lost and the gracious presence of Christ taken away, [[3:18|is blessed|beatus est]] even now in hope and merit, and by a foretaste and a near disposition.

paras.t: Dominus sapientia fundavit terram, stabilivit cœlos prudentia. Sapientia quandoque dicitur in Deo absolute, et est ipsa divina essentia; et toti superbeatissimæ Trinitati communis est, et una in tribus supersanctis Personis. Attamen Filio appropriatur, sicut et bonitas Spiritui Sancto. Filius enim est verbum et emanatio intellectus Dei Patris; sapientia vero ad intellectum est pertinens. Quandoque autem sapientia dicitur in divinis notionaliter, personaliter seu relative de Filio, qui, ut ait Apostolus, est virtus et sapientia Patris. Et utroque modo potest hic accipi. Nam Deus Trinitas sapientia sua, id est per sapientiam suam, tanquam per exemplar et artem operis sui, universa creavit, juxta illud Psalmi : Omnia in sapientia fecisti. Pater quoque per unigenitum Filium suum condidit cuncta, secundum quod ait Scriptura : Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Dominus ergo sapientia sua fundavit, id est, in medio mundi firmiter et immobiliter fecit ac posuit, terram, sicut cantatur : Etenim firmavit orbem, qui non commovebitur. Constituit enim eam in medio universi pro centro. Et de hoc loquitur Deus Job subtiliter : Ubi, inquiens, eras quando ponebam fundamenta terræ ? Quis posuit mensuras ejus ? vel quis tetendit super eam lineam ? Super quo bases ejus solidatæ sunt ? Præterea, in Deo idem sunt sapientia et prudentia ; sed in quantum sapientia Dei, respectu creaturarum, est practica, vocatur prudentia : sicque per suam prudentiam stabilivit orbes cœlestes, quoniam esse incorruptibile atque perpetuum tribuit illis, quamvis alibi scriptum sit, Ipsi peribunt : quod non est de corruptione substantialis esse, sed de variatione cujusdam accidentalis esse intelligendum.
paras.en: [[3:19|The Lord by wisdom hath founded the earth, hath established the heavens by prudence.|Dominus sapientia fundavit terram, stabilivit cœlos prudentia]] Wisdom is sometimes said of God absolutely, and is the divine essence itself; and it is common to the whole most superblessed Trinity, and one in the three supersanctified Persons. Yet it is appropriated to the Son [that is, attributed to one Person in particular, though common to all three], as goodness is to the Holy Ghost. For the Son is the Word and the emanation of the intellect of God the Father, and wisdom belongs to the intellect. But sometimes wisdom is said in divine things notionally [that is, of what distinguishes one Person from another], personally or relatively, of the Son, who, as the Apostle says, is the power and wisdom of the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]]. And it can be taken here in either way. For God the Trinity created all things by his wisdom, that is, through his wisdom, as through the exemplar and the art of his work, according to that saying of the Psalm: [[Ps 103:24|thou hast made all things in wisdom|Omnia in sapientia fecisti]]. The Father too founded all things through his only-begotten Son, as Scripture says: [[John 1:3|All things were made by him|Omnia per ipsum facta sunt]]. The Lord therefore by his wisdom founded the earth, that is, made it and set it firmly and immovably in the midst of the world, as is sung: [[Ps 92:1|For he hath established the world which shall not be moved|Etenim firmavit orbem, qui non commovebitur]] For he set it in the middle of the universe as its centre. And of this God speaks subtly to Job: [[Job 38:4|Where|Ubi]], he says, [[Job 38:4|wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?|eras quando ponebam fundamenta terræ]] [[Job 38:5|Who hath laid the measures thereof|Quis posuit mensuras ejus]]? [[Job 38:5|or who hath stretched the line upon it|vel quis tetendit super eam lineam]]? [[Job 38:6|Upon what are its bases grounded|Super quo bases ejus solidatæ sunt]]? Besides, in God wisdom and prudence are the same; but inasmuch as the wisdom of God, with respect to creatures, is practical, it is called prudence: and so by his prudence he established the heavenly spheres, since he gave them an incorruptible and everlasting being, although it is written elsewhere, [[Ps 101:27|They shall perish|Ipsi peribunt]]: which is to be understood not of the corruption of their substantial being, but of the change of a certain accidental being.

paras.t: Sapientia illius eruperunt abyssi, id est venæ ventriculique aquarum exsistentes sub terra, vel particularia maria, seu congregationes aquarum Oceani. Hoc namque est opus infinitæ sapientiæ omnipotentis Opificis, quod in ventriculis terræ aqua sic continetur, et erumpit in fontes ac puteos, atque in flumina magna per terram fluentia, et omnes hæ aquæ ex Oceano originaliter derivantur ac manant : ex quo etiam fons paradisi habet originem, qui in quatuor magna flumina erumpit, partitur, ac funditur, ut in Genesi habetur. Tempore quoque diluvii rupti sunt omnes fontes abyssi magnæ, ut rursus scriptum est in Genesi. Hinc ait Altissimus : Quis conclusit ostiis mare, quando erumpebat quasi de vulva procedens ? Et nubes rore concrescunt, id est densantur ; quia sapientia Dei sic ordinante, pro terræ irrigatione et fructificatione, ex solis calore vapores et exhalationes ex aquis elevantur, ac inspissantur in aere, fiuntque nubes : ex quarum resolutione descendunt imber et ros, quamvis diversimode. Ros namque, secundum Philosophum, est effectus temperati caloris, et ex subtiliori nube descendens, et frequentius generatur in vere. In his ergo sapientia Dei relucet. Propter quod in Scripturis hæc multoties continentur, ut omnipotentiam ac providentiam Creatoris in suis contemplemur, miremur, ac veneremur effectibus. Hinc scriptum est : Si voluerit extendere nubes quasi tentorium suum, et fulgurare lumine suo desuper, cardines quoque maris operiet : per hæc enim judicat populos, et dat escam multis mortalibus. Et rursus ait Scriptura : Frumentum desiderat nubes, et nubes spargunt lumen suum : quæ lustrant cuncta per circuitum, quocumque eas voluntas gubernantis duxerit.
paras.en: [[3:20|By his wisdom the depths have broken out|Sapientia illius eruperunt abyssi]], that is, the veins and hollows of the waters that lie under the earth, or the particular seas, or the gatherings of the waters of the Ocean. For this is the work of the infinite wisdom of the almighty Maker: that water is so held in the hollows of the earth, and breaks out into springs and wells, and into great rivers flowing through the land, and all these waters are derived and flow in their origin from the Ocean: from which the fountain of paradise also has its origin, which breaks out, divides and pours itself into four great rivers, as we have it in Genesis[[Gen 2:6||]] [the margin gives Gen. ii, 6; the four rivers are in Gen 2:10]. At the time of the flood, too, [[Gen 7:11|all the fountains of the great deep were broken up|rupti sunt omnes fontes abyssi magnæ]], as again is written in Genesis. Hence the Most High says: [[Job 38:8|Who shut up the sea with doors, when it broke forth as issuing out of the womb:|Quis conclusit ostiis mare, quando erumpebat quasi de vulva procedens]] [the margin reads "Ibid. 10"; the words are Job 38:8] [[3:20|And the clouds grow thick with dew|Et nubes rore concrescunt]], that is, become dense; for by the ordering of God's wisdom, for the watering and fruitfulness of the earth, vapours and exhalations are raised from the waters by the heat of the sun and thickened in the air, and become clouds: from whose dissolving come down rain and dew, though in different ways. For dew, according to the Philosopher, is the effect of a moderate heat, comes down from a finer cloud, and is formed more often in spring. In these things, then, the wisdom of God shines out. For this reason these things are contained many times in the Scriptures, that we may contemplate, wonder at and revere the almighty power and providence of the Creator in his effects. Hence it is written: [[Job 36:29|If he will spread out clouds as his tent,|Si voluerit extendere nubes quasi tentorium suum]] [[Job 36:30|And lighten with his light from above, he shall cover also the ends of the sea.|et fulgurare lumine suo desuper, cardines quoque maris operiet]] [[Job 36:31|For by these he judgeth people, and giveth food to many mortals|per hæc enim judicat populos, et dat escam multis mortalibus]] [the margin gives Job xxxviii, 29–31; the words are Job 36:29–31] And again Scripture says: [[Job 37:11|Corn desireth clouds, and the clouds spread their light:|Frumentum desiderat nubes, et nubes spargunt lumen suum]] [[Job 37:12|Which go round about, whithersoever the will of him that governeth them shall lead them|quæ lustrant cuncta per circuitum, quocumque eas voluntas gubernantis duxerit]].

paras.t: Spiritualiter, Dominus sapientia fundavit terram, id est, Pater per unicum Filium suum instituit et firmavit militantem Ecclesiam in terra peregrinantem, quam in fidei soliditate, spe et caritate fundavit. Stabilivit quoque cœlos, id est sanctos Apostolos et prædicatores ac contemplativos, quorum conversatio est in cœlis, prudentia, in qua et ipsos perficit ad regimen aliorum ; vel, Cœlos, id est triumphantem Ecclesiam, cujus perpetua et secura mansio est in cœlo empyreo. Sapientia illius eruperunt abyssi, id est, fluenta gratiæ et doctrinæ, ex fontibus sacramentorum et sacrorum voluminum profluxerunt. Et nubes, id est aliorum prælati et doctores, qui instar nubium elevantur de terra, et stillicidia influunt doctrinarum, rore concrescunt, id est, superna irrigatione sapientiæ irrigantur, ac torrente voluptatis divinæ inundantur. Unde Isaias loquitur Deo : Ros tuus, ros dulcis.
paras.en: Spiritually, [[3:19|The Lord by wisdom hath founded the earth|Dominus sapientia fundavit terram]], that is, the Father through his only Son established and made firm the Church militant, a pilgrim on earth, which he founded in the solidity of faith, in hope and in charity. He also [[3:19|hath established the heavens|Stabilivit quoque cœlos]], that is, the holy Apostles and preachers and contemplatives, whose conversation is in heaven, [[3:19|by prudence|prudentia]], in which he also perfects them for the governing of others; or, the heavens, that is, the Church triumphant, whose everlasting and secure dwelling is in the empyrean heaven. [[3:20|By his wisdom the depths have broken out|Sapientia illius eruperunt abyssi]], that is, the streams of grace and doctrine have flowed forth from the fountains of the sacraments and of the sacred books. [[3:20|And the clouds|Et nubes]], that is, the prelates and teachers of others, who like clouds are raised above the earth and pour down the drops of doctrine, [[3:20|grow thick with dew|rore concrescunt]], that is, are watered by the heavenly watering of wisdom and flooded with the torrent of divine delight. Hence Isaias says to God: Thy dew, sweet dew[[Is 26:19||]] [the margin gives Is. xxvi, 19, where the Vulgate reads ros lucis ros tuus, "thy dew is the dew of the light"; the print marks Denis's words with an asterisk].

paras.t: Fili mi, ne effluant hæc ab oculis tuis, id est, præfatæ saluberrimæ instructiones et exhortationes nequaquam recedant ab intuitu et memoria interiorum oculorum tuorum. Custodi legem, eam recolendo ac implendo, et consilium, acquiescendo bonis consiliis ; et erit vita animæ tuæ : id est, hæc faciendo, habebis vitam gratiæ in præsenti, et vitam gloriæ in futuro. Unde Salvator : Si vis, inquit, intrare ad vitam, serva mandata. Ideo scriptum est : Hic liber mandatorum Dei, et lex quæ est in æternum : omnes qui tenent eam, pervenient ad vitam ; qui autem derelinquunt eam, ad mortem. Et gratia faucibus tuis : id est, gratia discretionis ad loquendum, instruendum, et corripiendum opportune et fructuose præstabit tibi ; eruntque verba legis divinæ interiori tuo palato suavia : juxta illud, Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua ! Vel, Gratia erit faucibus tuis, id est, temperantiæ virtus donabitur gustui tuo, ad reficiendum te moderate. De quibus fauces fertur in Job : Nonne auris verba dijudicat, et fauces comedentis, saporem ? Hanc enim temperantiam sapientia confert, quoniam facit in spiritualibus delectari, et carnalia aspernari oblectamenta. Prudentia quoque præfigit mensuram in cibo et potu.
paras.en: [[3:21|My son, let not these things depart from thy eyes|Fili mi, ne effluant hæc ab oculis tuis]], that is, let the most wholesome instructions and exhortations given above never depart from the gaze and memory of thy inward eyes.
