[[3:21|keep the law|Custodi legem]], by recalling it and fulfilling it, [[3:21|and counsel|et consilium]], by assenting to good counsels; [[3:22|And there shall be life to thy soul|et erit vita animæ tuæ]]: that is, by doing these things thou shalt have the life of grace in the present and the life of glory in the future. Hence the Saviour: [[Matt 19:17|if thou wilt|Si vis]], he says, [[Matt 19:17|enter into life, keep the commandments|intrare ad vitam, serva mandata]]. Therefore it is written: [[Bar 4:1|This is the book of the commandments of God, and the law, that is for ever: all they that keep it, shall come to life: but they that have forsaken it, to death|Hic liber mandatorum Dei, et lex quæ est in æternum : omnes qui tenent eam, pervenient ad vitam ; qui autem derelinquunt eam, ad mortem]] [[3:22|and grace to thy mouth|Et gratia faucibus tuis]] [fauces is properly "throat" or "palate"; Denis's two readings play on this]: that is, he will give thee the grace of discretion to speak, instruct and reprove in season and with fruit; and the words of the divine law shall be sweet to thy inward palate, according to that saying: [[Ps 118:103|How sweet are thy words to my palate|Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua]]! [the margin gives Ps. cxviii, 3; the verse is Ps 118:103] Or, Grace shall be to thy palate, that is, the virtue of temperance shall be given to thy taste, so that thou mayest feed thyself in moderation. Of which palate it is said in Job: [[Job 12:11|Doth not the ear discern words, and the palate of him that eateth, the taste?|Nonne auris verba dijudicat, et fauces comedentis, saporem]] For wisdom confers this temperance, since it makes a man delight in spiritual things and spurn carnal pleasures. Prudence too fixes the measure in food and drink.

paras.t: Tunc ambulabis fiducialiter in via tua : id est, bona conversatione proficies confidenter, et proficiendo confides in Domino; conscientiam quoque bonam habendo, eris vir bonæ spei. Nam et Philosophus protestatur, quod hi qui in divinis bene se habent, melioris sunt spei. Et pes tuus non impinget, id est, affectus tuus seu operatio, qua tendis ad finem, non cespitabit recedendo a via virtutum ac medio rationis. Prudentia etenim diriget te, ut cum Propheta dicere queas, Pes meus stetit in directo ; et cum sancto Job, Vestigia ejus secutus est pes meus.
paras.en: [[3:23|Then shalt thou walk confidently in thy way|Tunc ambulabis fiducialiter in via tua]]: that is, by a good life thou shalt go forward confidently, and in going forward thou shalt trust in the Lord; and having a good conscience, thou shalt be a man of good hope. For the Philosopher too declares that those who stand well in divine things are of better hope. [[3:23|and thy foot shall not stumble|Et pes tuus non impinget]], that is, thy affection or working, by which thou tendest to the end, shall not trip by departing from the way of the virtues and the mean of reason. For prudence will direct thee, so that thou canst say with the Prophet, [[Ps 25:12|My foot hath stood in the direct way|Pes meus stetit in directo]]; and with holy Job, [[Job 23:11|My foot hath followed his steps|Vestigia ejus secutus est pes meus]].

paras.t: Si dormieris, non timebis ; quiesces, et suavis erit somnus tuus. Hoc ad litteram ita est, quod virtuosus et sapiens, prudens et innocens, justus et perfectus, securior atque tranquillior est in cunctis ; nec in somno terretur, sed dulciter dormit. Nam sicut animus inordinatus sibi ipsi pœnalis ac gravis est, sic animus ordinatus est jucundus, quietus et dulcis ; et per sapientiam consolari se potest, per patientiam quoque completam manet in adversitatibus etiam magnis imperturbatus. Propter quod dicitur in Ethicis, quod studiosi habent phantasmata meliora, dum a vigilia ad somnum pertranseunt. Nam quod homo in vigilia tractat, hoc sibi in somno solet occurrere. Ideo, sicut iniqui in vigilia frequenter de insidiis et terribilibus eis imminentibus cogitant, sic in somno terribilia et molesta sæpe somnia habent. Nihilo minus ex tentatione diaboli et corporali indispositione, potest et justis in somno terror occurrere, et inquietudo absque malitia generari, prout beatus Job de se ipso testatur : Si dormiero, dicam, Quando consurgam ? Et : Terrebis me per somnia. Loquitur autem Salomon conformando se legi, quæ observatoribus suis securum et quietum somnum in Deuteronomii libro promisit, transgressoribus vero prædixit contrarium. Unde ibidem inducitur de iniquo : Erit vita tua quasi pendens ante te; timebis die ac nocte, et non credes vitæ tuæ. Mane dices, Quis mihi det vesperam ? et vespere, Quis mihi det mane? propter cordis tui formidinem, qua terreberis. Insuper justus et innocens, quum dormierit somno mortis, aut non timebit, aut a suo timore cito eripietur, et erit securus. Quidam vero ita divini sunt, quod etiam in somno orant, psallunt, meditantur, et multa intelligunt, quæ vigilando intelligere non valebant. Quibus dicere licet : Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat.
paras.en: [[3:24|If thou sleep, thou shalt not fear: thou shalt rest, and thy sleep shall be sweet.|Si dormieris, non timebis ; quiesces, et suavis erit somnus tuus]] This is so according to the letter: the virtuous and wise man, prudent and innocent, just and perfect, is more secure and more tranquil in all things; nor is he frightened in sleep, but sleeps sweetly. For as a disordered mind is a punishment and a burden to itself, so an ordered mind is cheerful, quiet and sweet; and it can comfort itself by wisdom, and by complete patience it remains undisturbed even in great adversities. For this reason it is said in the Ethics that the virtuous have better images in the fancy as they pass from waking to sleep. For what a man deals with when awake usually comes back to him in sleep. And so, as the wicked often think when awake of plots and terrors hanging over them, so in sleep they often have terrible and troublesome dreams. Nevertheless, through the temptation of the devil and an ill disposition of the body, terror can befall the just too in sleep, and restlessness arise without any malice, as blessed Job testifies of himself: [[Job 7:4|If I lie down to sleep, I shall say: When shall I rise?|Si dormiero, dicam, Quando consurgam]] And: [[Job 7:14|Thou wilt frighten me with dreams|Terrebis me per somnia]]. Now Solomon speaks in keeping with the law, which in the book of Deuteronomy promised secure and quiet sleep to those who keep it, but foretold the contrary to transgressors. So there it is said of the wicked man: [[Deut 28:66|And thy life shall be as it were hanging before thee. Thou shalt fear night and day, neither shalt thou trust thy life|Erit vita tua quasi pendens ante te; timebis die ac nocte, et non credes vitæ tuæ]] [[Deut 28:67|In the morning thou shalt say: Who will grant me evening? and at evening: Who will grant me morning? for the fearfulness of thy heart, wherewith thou shalt be terrified|Mane dices, Quis mihi det vesperam ? et vespere, Quis mihi det mane? propter cordis tui formidinem, qua terreberis]]. Moreover, the just and innocent man, when he sleeps the sleep of death, will either not fear, or will quickly be rescued from his fear and be secure. And some are so godly that even in sleep they pray, sing psalms, meditate, and understand many things which they could not understand awake. Such may say: [[Cant 5:2|I sleep, and my heart watcheth|Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat]].

paras.t: Ne paveas repentino terrore, id est, non concutiaris timore, qui inopinate ac subito solet oriri ex aliquo sensibili strepitu, clamore, phantasia, aut simili quod solet timeri.
paras.en: [[3:25|Be not afraid of sudden fear|Ne paveas repentino terrore]], that is, be not shaken by the fear that is wont to arise unexpectedly and suddenly from some noise heard, a cry, an apparition, or the like that is wont to be feared.

paras.t: Verumtamen primi motus naturalium passionum non bene sunt in nostra potestate; sed quo magis in virtutibus crescimus, eo facilius eos refrenamus ac moderamur. Idcirco quod ait, Ne paveas repentino terrore, sic accipi potest, ut non immoremur tali formidini, sed ex consideratione divinæ præsentiæ, et confidentia protectionis supernæ eam abjiciamus, ac animemur in Deo. Ideo subditur : et irruentes tibi potentias impiorum non metuas : quod tam de invisibilibus, quam visibilibus hostibus potest exponi. Nam de visibilibus ait Salvator : Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt. Non enim timendi sunt immoderato seu carnali aut mundano timore, quamvis naturalis timor non exstet illicitus. Perfectius vero et melius est, ut sit homo paratus pati quidquid adversi voluerit aut permiserit Deus ei accidere : et hoc, amore Dei, et pro suis peccatis, et pro exercitatione virtutis, ac incremento salutis. Invisibiles quoque hostes non sunt timendi timore inordinato et immoderato, qui rationem et actum virtutum impediat et conturbet ; sed ex consideratione divinæ præsentiæ, et confidentia protectionis supernæ, atque subventionis angelicæ sunt vilipendendi. Ideo subditur :
paras.en: Yet the first movements of the natural passions [that is, the stirrings that come before reason can consent or refuse] are not fully in our power; but the more we grow in the virtues, the more easily we rein them in and moderate them. Therefore what he says, [[3:25|Be not afraid of sudden fear|Ne paveas repentino terrore]], can be taken thus: that we should not dwell on such fear, but cast it off by considering the divine presence and trusting in heavenly protection, and take heart in God. Hence it is added: [[3:25|nor of the power of the wicked falling upon thee|et irruentes tibi potentias impiorum]], that is, fear them not: which can be expounded of invisible as well as visible enemies. For of visible ones the Saviour says: [[Matt 10:28|fear ye not them that kill the body|Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt]]. For they are not to be feared with an immoderate, carnal or worldly fear, though natural fear is not unlawful. But it is more perfect and better that a man be ready to suffer whatever adversity God wills or permits to befall him: and this for the love of God, for his own sins, for the exercise of virtue and for the increase of his salvation. The invisible enemies too are not to be feared with a disordered and immoderate fear, which hinders and disturbs reason and the act of the virtues; rather, by considering the divine presence and trusting in heavenly protection and angelic help, they are to be held cheap. Therefore it is added:

paras.t: Dominus enim erit in latere tuo, id est, gratiose adsistet, si confidas in eo, et ad ipsum sincere confugias, et custodiet pedem tuum, ne capiaris ab hostibus, id est, ne vel corporaliter vel spiritualiter noceant tibi. Quod si Dominus permiserit te corporaliter lædi ab eis, hoc erit pro tuo meliori, dummodo patienter sustineas : sicut permisit S. Antonium a dæmonibus flagellari, sanctosque martyres a tyrannis occidi ; quotidie quoque permittit justos a pravis infestari hominibus. Ideo viri perfecti excludunt omnem carnalem, mundanum et inordinatum timorem. Unde sanctus Job : Si expavi, inquit, ad multitudinem nimiam. Et Psalmista : Dominus illuminatio mea, et salus mea : quem timebo? Dominus protector vitæ meæ : a quo trepidabo? etc. Itemque : Providebam Dominum in conspectu meo semper, quoniam a dextris est mihi, ne commovear.
paras.en: [[3:26|For the Lord will be at thy side|Dominus enim erit in latere tuo]], that is, he will graciously stand by thee, if thou trust in him and flee to him sincerely, [[3:26|and will keep thy foot that thou be not taken|et custodiet pedem tuum, ne capiaris]] by thy enemies, that is, lest they harm thee either in body or in spirit. And if the Lord permits thee to be hurt in body by them, this will be for thy good, provided thou bear it patiently: as he permitted St. Antony to be scourged by the demons, and the holy martyrs to be slain by tyrants; and daily too he permits the just to be harassed by wicked men. Therefore perfect men shut out all carnal, worldly and disordered fear. Hence holy Job: [[Job 31:34|If I have been afraid|Si expavi]], he says, [[Job 31:34|at a very great multitude|ad multitudinem nimiam]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 26:1|The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?|Dominus illuminatio mea, et salus mea : quem timebo? Dominus protector vitæ meæ : a quo trepidabo?]] etc. And again: [[Ps 15:8|I set the Lord always in my sight: for he is at my right hand, that I be not moved.|Providebam Dominum in conspectu meo semper, quoniam a dextris est mihi, ne commovear]]

paras.t: Præterea, aliqui sunt ita perfecti, quod nec primos motus repentinæ formidinis sentiant. Unde, ut in Vitis Patrum habetur, quum quidam interrogasset abbatem Theodorum, Si fiat strepitus improvise, aut sonitus magnus, timesne? Qui respondit : Si cœlum terræ adhæreat, Theodorus non formidat. Sanctus quoque abbas Macarius, quum in templo quodam idolorum se posuisset ad dormiendum, et calvariam suo capiti quasi pro pulvinari supposuisset, cœpit diabolus clamare ex illa calvaria. Macarius vero nil metuens, cum capite suo tundebat super calvariam, dicens diabolo : Si aliquid potes, fac. Econtra, quidam sunt tam imperfecti, quod facile immoderanterque timeant, præsertim nocturno tempore, dum fuerint soli, non pensantes Omnipotentis et sanctorum angelorum præsentiam ; nec attendentes pulcherrimum sensum præclarissimi psalmi, qui incipit, Qui habitat in adjutorio Altissimi. Est autem timor immoderatus valde pœnalis, miser, et detestandus. Propter quod etiam Seneca dixit : Heu, quam miserum est, metuendo fieri senem !
paras.en: Moreover, some are so perfect that they do not feel even the first movements of sudden fear. Hence, as we read in the Lives of the Fathers, when someone asked abbot Theodore, "If a noise is made unexpectedly, or a loud sound, art thou afraid?", he answered: "If heaven were to cleave to the earth, Theodore would not be afraid." The holy abbot Macarius too, when he had lain down to sleep in a temple of idols and had put a skull under his head for a pillow, the devil began to cry out from that skull. But Macarius, fearing nothing, struck the skull with his head, saying to the devil: "If thou canst do anything, do it." On the other hand, some are so imperfect that they are easily and immoderately afraid, especially at night when they are alone, not weighing the presence of the Almighty and of the holy angels, nor heeding the most beautiful sense of the most excellent psalm that begins, [[Ps 90:1|He that dwelleth in the aid of the most High|Qui habitat in adjutorio Altissimi]]. Now immoderate fear is very painful, wretched and detestable. For this reason Seneca too said: "Alas, how wretched it is to grow old in fear!"

paras.t: Noli prohibere benefacere eum qui potest, id est, neminem a bono actu impedias, aut retardes, quin scilicet tempore opportuno faciat illum : alioqui omissio boni illius imputabitur tibi. Si vales, et ipse fac bonum, alteri succurrendo, seu opus virtutum quodcumque exercendo.
paras.en: [[3:27|Do not withhold him from doing good, who is able|Noli prohibere benefacere eum qui potest]], that is, hinder or delay no one from a good act, so that he do it not at the fitting time: otherwise the omission of that good will be laid to thy account. [[3:27|if thou art able, do good thyself also|Si vales, et ipse fac bonum]], by helping another, or by practising any work of the virtues.

paras.t: Ne dicas amico, id est proximo tuo, aliquid a te rationabiliter postulanti : Vade, et revertere, et cras dabo tibi ; quum statim possis dare : nisi rationabile impedimentum mox dandi occurrat. In tali etenim casu, dilatio nec liberalitati, nec misericordiæ, nec caritati concordat. Imo sicut, teste Apostolo, hilarem, sic et celerem, datorem diligit Deus. Nec nobilis animi est, ut faciat vel permittat proximum suum a se tristem recedere ; sed sicut volumus exaudiri a Deo, exaudiamus et proximos. Etenim, juxta versiculum, Qui cito dat, bis dat ; nescit dare, qui dare tardat. Hinc Seneca in suis scribit Proverbiis : Inopi beneficium bis dat, qui dat celeriter. Et rursus notabiliter protestatur : Beneficiis humana vita constat, et concordia ; non terrore, sed mutuo amore in fœdus auxiliumque commune constringitur.
paras.en: [[3:28|Say not to thy friend|Ne dicas amico]], that is, to thy neighbour, who asks something of thee reasonably: [[3:28|Go, and come again: and to morrow I will give to thee|Vade, et revertere, et cras dabo tibi]]; [[3:28|when thou canst give at present|quum statim possis dare]]: unless some reasonable hindrance to giving at once arises. For in such a case delay agrees neither with liberality, nor with mercy, nor with charity. Nay, as by the Apostle's witness God loveth a cheerful giver[[2 Cor 9:7||]], so also a prompt one. Nor is it the mark of a noble mind to make or let one's neighbour go away from one sad; but as we wish to be heard by God, let us also hear our neighbours[[Matt 6:12||]][[Tob 4:16||]] [the margin gives Matth. vi, 12 and Tob. iv, 16: Denis is alluding, not quoting]. For, as the verse has it, "He who gives quickly gives twice; he knows not how to give, who is slow to give." Hence Seneca writes in his Proverbs: "He gives a kindness twice to the needy, who gives quickly." And again he declares notably: "Human life stands by kindnesses and concord; it is bound into a league and common help not by terror, but by mutual love."

paras.t: Ne moliaris amico tuo malum, id est, damnum, aut infestationem non excogites, nec inferre coneris proximo tuo, quum ille in te habeat fiduciam. Hoc namque impiissimum esset, et contra legem naturalem, divinam, ac positivam. Imo econtrario opta et procura ei bonum, sicut confidit de te. Gravissimus certe est inimicus occultus et familiaris, qui putatur amicus. Hinc Seneca Tulliusque testantur : Pejora sunt tecta odia, quam aperta. Et iterum Seneca fassus est : Gravior est inimicus qui latet sub pectore. De hoc Cyrillus in suis Proverbiis plenius docet, prout suis locis tangetur.
paras.en: [[3:29|Practise not evil against thy friend|Ne moliaris amico tuo malum]], that is, do not devise harm or molestation, nor try to bring it on thy neighbour, [[3:29|when he hath confidence in thee|quum ille in te habeat fiduciam]]. For this would be most impious, and against the natural, divine and positive law. Nay, on the contrary, wish and procure his good, as he trusts in thee. Truly the most grievous enemy is the hidden and familiar one, who is thought a friend. Hence Seneca and Tully bear witness: "Hidden hatreds are worse than open ones." And again Seneca owns: "The worse enemy is he who lurks in the breast." Of this Cyril teaches more fully in his Proverbs, as will be touched on in its places.

paras.t: Ne contendas adversus hominem frustra, id est inaniter et sine causa idonea, quum ipse tibi nihil mali fecerit. Verumtamen judex, qui est publica persona, arguere debet non solum eos qui peccant in ipsum, sed et injuriosos in alios. Contentio autem proprie sumpta, ab Apostolo inter mortalia computatur peccata : quæ, ut ait Ambrosius, est impugnatio agnitæ veritatis, cum confidentia clamoris. Unde rursus ait Apostolus : Noli verbis contendere; ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium. Hinc Seneca in Proverbiis suis disseruit : Cum pari contendere, anceps est; cum superiore, furiosum; cum inferiore, sordidum.
paras.en: [[3:30|Strive not against a man without cause|Ne contendas adversus hominem frustra]], that is, idly and without fitting cause, [[3:30|when he hath done thee no evil|quum ipse tibi nihil mali fecerit]]. Yet a judge, who is a public person, must rebuke not only those who sin against him, but also those who wrong others. Now contention, taken properly, is counted by the Apostle among mortal sins[[Gal 5:20||]] [the margin gives Gal. v, 21; contentions are named in v. 20, the sentence on such sins is in v. 21]: which, as Ambrose says, is the attacking of acknowledged truth with the boldness of clamour. Hence again the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 2:14|Contend not in words: for it is to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers|Noli verbis contendere; ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium]] [the margin gives Tim. ii; the verse is 2 Tim 2:14]. Hence Seneca discoursed in his Proverbs: "To contend with an equal is hazardous; with a superior, mad; with an inferior, mean."

paras.t: Ne æmuleris hominem injustum, id est, eum non ames, in quantum talis est, sed in quantum homo viator : nec eum sequaris in vitiis, nec invidentiam contra eum concipias, de ejus prosperitate dolendo; sed committe hoc occulto judicio Dei, nisi forsan periculosum sit bono communi. Ideo scriptum est : Noli æmulari in malignantibus. Nec imiteris vias ejus : Quia abominatio Domini est omnis illusor, id est injustus, qui ipso facto illusor est, et Dei præcepta irridet, ac spernit in opere. Ideo est abominabilis Deo, qui justus est, et justitias dilexit, oditque omnes qui operantur iniquitatem. Et cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus. Hoc dupliciter potest exponi. Primo, quod sermocinatio illusoris est cum simplicibus, quoniam tales facilius potest decipere. Innocens enim credit omni verbo, quum sit humanarum astutiarum fraudumque ignarus. Secundo, quod sermocinatio Dei sit cum simplicibus, qui quum sint sinceri ac innocentes, specialiter sunt capaces illuminationis divinæ. Ideo in ipsis loquitur Deus, et secreta sapientiæ suæ eis revelat.
paras.en: [[3:31|Envy not the unjust man|Ne æmuleris hominem injustum]] [æmulari means both "to envy" and "to emulate"; Denis's gloss takes in both], that is, love him not inasmuch as he is such, but inasmuch as he is a man and a wayfarer: neither follow him in his vices, nor conceive envy against him by grieving at his prosperity; but commit this to the hidden judgement of God, unless perhaps it be dangerous to the common good. Therefore it is written: [[Ps 36:1|Be not emulous of evildoers|Noli æmulari in malignantibus]]. [[3:31|and do not follow his ways|Nec imiteris vias ejus]]: [[3:32|For every mocker is an abomination to the Lord|Quia abominatio Domini est omnis illusor]], that is, the unjust man, who by that very fact is a mocker, and derides the precepts of God and spurns them in deed. Therefore he is abominable to God, who is just, and [[Ps 10:8|hath loved justice|justitias dilexit]], and hateth [[Ps 5:7|all the workers of iniquity|omnes qui operantur iniquitatem]]. [[3:32|and his communication is with the simple|Et cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus]]. This can be expounded in two ways. First, that the mocker's talk is with the simple, since he can deceive such more easily. For [[Prov 14:15|The innocent|Innocens]], indeed, [[Prov 14:15|believeth every word|credit omni verbo]], being ignorant of human cunning and frauds. Secondly, that God's communication is with the simple, who, being sincere and innocent, are especially capable of divine illumination. Therefore God speaks in them, and reveals to them the secrets of his wisdom[[Ps 50:8||]] [the margin reads Ps. i, 8; the words recall Ps 50:8].

paras.t: Egestas a Domino in domo impii. Certum est, quod spiritualium divitiarum seu virtutum inopia sit in corde iniqui et in domesticis ejus, qui ei in vitiis sunt conformes; quandoque etiam temporalibus rebus propter suos excessus privantur. Habitacula autem justorum benedicentur, id est, congregationes seu personæ virtuosæ abundabunt bonis gratiæ in hac vita, et bonis gloriæ æternalis in patria. Benedicuntur quoque, id est laudantur, a multis, et frequenter etiam in temporalibus satis abundant.
paras.en: [[3:33|Want is from the Lord in the house of the wicked|Egestas a Domino in domo impii]]. It is certain that a want of spiritual riches, or virtues, is in the heart of the wicked man and in those of his household who are like him in vices; and sometimes they are also deprived of temporal things because of their excesses. [[3:33|but the habitations of the just shall be blessed|Habitacula autem justorum benedicentur]], that is, virtuous communities or persons shall abound with the goods of grace in this life, and with the goods of eternal glory in the fatherland. They are also blessed, that is, praised [benedicere, "to bless", is literally "to speak well of"], by many, and often they abound well enough in temporal things too.

paras.t: Ipse Deus deludet illusores : in quorum interitu ridet; et quum debitas incurrerint pœnas, eos subsannat, ut dictum est. Permittet quoque eos a dæmonibus decipi, laqueosque incidere, quos aliis parant; et in die judicii eorumdem, ostendet eos delusos. Ideo in Isaia præcipitur : Nolite illudere, ut non constringantur vincula vestra. Denique Judæos incredulos, qui Christum illuserunt, permittet ab Antichristo illudi. Atque, ut asserit Glossa, illusor est, qui verba Dei, quæ novit, implere contemnit; vel ea perverse intelligendo, ac male docendo corrumpit. Et mansuetis dabit gratiam, id est virtutum et gratiæ incrementa. Quemadmodum enim ira, sua inquietudine mentem a gratia impedit; sic mansuetudo, sua quiete efficit eam spiritualium charismatum susceptivam, ejusque precem Deo acceptam, sicut in libro Judith habetur : Mansuetorum et humilium semper tibi placuit oratio. Hinc divinus Dionysius in epistola ad Demophilum monachum protestatur, quod Moyses, David, et Joseph præcipuam apud Dominum gratiam invenerunt, quoniam mites erant. At vero, pro eo quod hic habetur, Ipse deludet illusores, mansuetis autem dabit gratiam, Septuaginta transtulerunt : Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Et juxta hanc litteram beatissimi apostoli Petrus et Jacobus in suis epistolis istam introducunt scripturam, ut tangit Glossa.
paras.en: [[3:34|He shall scorn the scorners|Ipse Deus deludet illusores]]: he laughs at their destruction; and when they have incurred their due punishments, he mocks them, as has been said[[Prov 1:26||]]. He will also let them be deceived by the demons and fall into the snares they lay for others[[Ps 7:16||]]; and in their day of judgement he will show them up as deluded. Therefore the command is given in Isaias: [[Is 28:22|do not mock, lest your bonds be tied strait|Nolite illudere, ut non constringantur vincula vestra]]. Lastly, he will let the unbelieving Jews, who mocked Christ, be deluded by Antichrist. And, as the Gloss asserts, a mocker is one who scorns to fulfil the words of God which he knows, or corrupts them by understanding them perversely and teaching them wrongly. [[3:34|and to the meek he will give grace|Et mansuetis dabit gratiam]], that is, increase of virtues and of grace. For as anger by its restlessness keeps the mind from grace, so meekness by its quiet makes it receptive of spiritual gifts, and makes its prayer acceptable to God, as we have it in the book of Judith: [[Jdt 9:16|the prayer of the humble and the meek hath always pleased thee|Mansuetorum et humilium semper tibi placuit oratio]]. Hence the divine Dionysius, in his letter to the monk Demophilus, declares that Moses[[Num 12:3||]], David[[Ps 131:1||]] and Joseph[[Gen 45:4||]] found special grace with the Lord because they were meek [the margin gives Gen. xlv, 4–15 for Joseph]. But for what is here, [[3:34|He shall scorn the scorners|Ipse deludet illusores]], [[3:34|to the meek he will give grace|mansuetis autem dabit gratiam]], the Septuagint translated: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. And according to this reading the most blessed apostles Peter[[1 Pet 5:5||]] and James[[Jas 4:6||]] bring this scripture into their epistles, as the Gloss notes.

paras.t: Gloriam sapientes possidebunt : quia sempiternam in cœlis gloriam consequentur, et spirituali jucunditate contemplando divina replentur, sicut in Ethicis ait Philosophus : Homo contemplativus plenus est jucundis theorematibus, in quorum consideratione lætatur. Sapientes etiam in vita sua, et post obitum habent famam laudabilem. Nam et sapientiæ honor debetur. Unde in Ecclesiastico fertur : Collaudabunt multi sapientiam ejus : non recedet memoria ejus. Et in Daniele legitur : Qui docti fuerint, fulgebunt quasi splendor firmamenti. Stultorum exsultatio, ignominia, id est detestanda et fatua, quia eorum lætitia est inanis, et lætantur in rebus vanis, stultis, illicitis, sicut præhabitum est : Lætantur quum male fecerint. Porro in Hebræo (ut fertur) habetur : Stultorum exaltatio, ignominia. Sunt enim exaltatione, honore, prælatione indigni; et quanto plus promoventur ac sublimantur, tanto eorum stoliditas magis ostenditur : sicut et nuditas simiæ retro tanto plus ridenda monstratur, quanto amplius ascendendo levatur. Ideo Seneca dixit : Superbi gloria cito fit ignominia.
paras.en: [[3:35|The wise shall possess glory|Gloriam sapientes possidebunt]]: for they shall attain everlasting glory in heaven, and are filled with spiritual joy in contemplating divine things, as the Philosopher says in the Ethics: "The contemplative man is full of delightful truths, in the consideration of which he rejoices." The wise also have a praiseworthy fame in their life and after their death. For honour too is due to wisdom. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 39:12|Many shall praise his wisdom|Collaudabunt multi sapientiam ejus]]: [[Ecclus 39:13|The memory of him shall not depart away|non recedet memoria ejus]]. And in Daniel we read: [[Dan 12:3|they that are learned, shall shine as the brightness of the firmament|Qui docti fuerint, fulgebunt quasi splendor firmamenti]]. [[3:35|the promotion of fools is disgrace|Stultorum exsultatio, ignominia]] [Denis reads exsultatio, "rejoicing", where the Vulgate has exaltatio, "promotion"; he gives that reading next as the Hebrew's], that is, a detestable and foolish rejoicing, for their gladness is empty, and they rejoice in vain, foolish and unlawful things, as was said before: [[Prov 2:14|Who are glad when they have done evil|Lætantur quum male fecerint]]. Moreover, in the Hebrew (as is said) we have: [[3:35|the promotion of fools is disgrace|Stultorum exaltatio, ignominia]]. For they are unworthy of promotion, honour and prelacy; and the more they are advanced and raised up, the more their dullness is shown: as the bareness of an ape's hind parts is shown the more laughable, the higher it climbs. Hence Seneca said: "The glory of the proud quickly becomes disgrace."

4.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI QUARTI : AUDITE, FILII, DISCIPLINAM PATRIS.
4.title_en: Elucidation of the fourth chapter: Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father.

paras.t: Rursus hortatur Salomon ad sapientiæ desiderium ac amorem, et in hoc ponit se in exemplum. Audite, fili, disciplinam patris cœlestis, Dei omnipotentis; vel mei, qui sum pater vester per sapientiæ excellentiam. Atque ad litteram, auctoritate regiæ dignitatis potuit se patrem appellare, præsertim subditorum suorum. Et attendite, id est, diligenter advertite verba mea, ut sciatis prudentiam : quia primo oportet scire, deinde operari. Et quamvis prudentia, quæ est virtus infusa, sit immediate et tota a Deo, tamen ad ejus infusionem ac profectum potest se homo disponere, et per studium ac experientiam proficit in eadem. Donum bonum tribuam vobis, utpote sapientiam, ad quam homo hominem potest disponere, excitare, inducere.
paras.en: Again Solomon exhorts to the desire and love of wisdom, and in this he sets himself forth as an example. [[4:1|Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father|Audite, fili, disciplinam patris]]: of the heavenly Father, almighty God; or mine, who am your father by excellence of wisdom. And literally, by the authority of his royal dignity he could call himself a father, especially of his subjects. [[4:1|and attend|Et attendite]], that is, diligently heed my words, [[4:1|that you may know prudence|ut sciatis prudentiam]]: for first one must know, and then act. And although prudence, which is an infused virtue [that is, one given by God, not acquired by practice], is immediately and wholly from God, yet a man can dispose himself to its infusion and growth, and by study and experience he makes progress in it. [[4:2|I will give you a good gift|Donum bonum tribuam vobis]], namely wisdom, to which one man can dispose, arouse and lead another.

paras.t: Nam et ego Salomon filius patris mei, David regis, fui tenellus, id est valde tener et delicatus. Unde David dixit ad populum Israel : Salomonem filium meum elegit Dominus adhuc puerum et tenellum. Et unigenitus coram matre mea Bethsabee. Contra hoc est duplex objectio : prima, quia, ut secundo Regum narratur, David genuit ex Bethsabee filium unum ante Salomonis nativitatem ; secunda, quoniam primo Paralipomenon scriptum est, In Jerusalem nati sunt ei, scilicet David regi, filii Sammaa et Sobab, Nathan et Salomon, quatuor de Bethsabee. Ad horum primum respondet Hieronymus, quod primus ille filius ex David et Bethsabee genitus, sine nomine, id est ante circumcisionem, in qua nomen imponebatur, discessit quasi numquam fuisset. Et etiam, quia in circumcisione fiebat ab originali peccato purgatio, quæ fuit spiritualis regeneratio, sicut ut modo Baptismus ; sicque puer ille ante hujusmodi nativitatem videtur obiisse. Unde de sacratissimo Joanne Baptista legitur angelus patri illius prænuntiasse : Pro eo quod non credidisti verbis meis, non poteris loqui usque in diem nativitatis ejus. Nam usque in octavum diem, quo S. Joannes fuit circumcisus, pater ipsius permansit mutus, ut patet in Luca. Ad secundum communiter respondetur, quod tres alii jam præfati, fuerunt carnales filii Uriæ ex Bethsabee, et adoptivi filii David, qui ipsam Bethsabee ducendo uxorem, filios ejus adoptavit in suos.
paras.en: [[4:3|For I also|Nam et ego]], Solomon, [[4:3|was my father's son|filius patris mei]], King David's, [[4:3|tender|fui tenellus]], that is, very tender and delicate. Hence David said to the people of Israel: [[1 Par 29:1|Solomon my son, whom alone God hath chosen, is as yet young and tender|Salomonem filium meum elegit Dominus adhuc puerum et tenellum]]. [[4:3|and as an only son in the sight of my mother|Et unigenitus coram matre mea]] Bethsabee. Against this there is a twofold objection. The first, that, as is related in the second book of Kings, David begot one son of Bethsabee before the birth of Solomon[[2 Kings 11:27||]]. The second, that in the first book of Paralipomenon it is written: [[1 Par 3:5|And these sons were born to him in Jerusalem|In Jerusalem nati sunt ei]], that is, to King David, [[1 Par 3:5|Simmaa, and Sobab, and Nathan, and Solomon, four of Bethsabee|filii Sammaa et Sobab, Nathan et Salomon, quatuor de Bethsabee]]. To the first of these Jerome answers that that first son begotten of David and Bethsabee departed without a name, that is, before circumcision, in which the name was given, as though he had never been. And also, since in circumcision there was a cleansing from original sin, which was a spiritual regeneration, as Baptism is now, that child seems to have died before a birth of this kind. Hence we read of the most holy John the Baptist that the angel foretold to his father: [[Luke 1:20|because thou hast not believed my words|Pro eo quod non credidisti verbis meis]], thou [[Luke 1:20|shalt not be able to speak until the day|non poteris loqui usque in diem]] of his birth [that is, his spiritual birth in circumcision; the Gospel has 'until the day wherein these things shall come to pass']. For until the eighth day, on which St. John was circumcised[[Luke 1:59||]], his father remained dumb, as appears in Luke[[Luke 1:64||]]. To the second it is commonly answered that the three others already named were the sons of Urias by Bethsabee according to the flesh, and the adoptive sons of David, who, in taking Bethsabee herself to wife, adopted her sons as his own.

paras.t: Et docebat me pater meus, videlicet David, atque dicebat : Suscipiat verba mea cor tuum, custodi præcepta mea, quæ tibi propono de observanda justitia, de divino obsequio, de templo ædificando. Qualiter enim de his David Salomonem instruxerit, in primo Paralipomenon libro partim habetur. Vel Salomon per patrem suum intelligit Deum, qui per Nathan dixit de ipso, Ego ero illi in patrem ; et per matrem, Synagogam, cujus exstitit filius, et quasi unigenitus ab ea dilectus, sicut nunc unusquisque fidelis vocatur Ecclesiæ filius. Vel Salomon in persona Christi hæc loquitur, qui fuit unicus naturalisque Filius Patris æterni, et unigenitus Filius Virginis : quem secundum naturam assumptam Pater ab incarnationis instanti instruxit plenissime in momento ; et fuit tenerrimus corpore, tanquam ex purissimis sanctæ Virginis natus sanguinibus, et nobilissimæ prorsus complexionis, atque in omni caritate ac pietate in visceribus misericordiæ omnino tenellus, et tenerrimus mente.
paras.en: [[4:4|And he taught me|Et docebat me]], my father, namely David, [[4:4|and said: Let thy heart receive my words, keep my commandments|atque dicebat : Suscipiat verba mea cor tuum, custodi præcepta mea]], which I set before thee concerning the keeping of justice, the service of God, and the building of the temple. For how David instructed Solomon about these things is found in part in the first book of Paralipomenon[[1 Par 28:9||]][[1 Par 28:10||]] [the margin reads I Par. viii, 9, 10, evidently for xxviii, 9, 10]. Or Solomon means by his father God, who said of him through Nathan: [[2 Kings 7:14|I will be to him a father|Ego ero illi in patrem]] [the margin gives I Reg. vii; Nathan's prophecy is 2 Kings 7:14, and Denis's wording is that of 1 Par 22:10]; and by his mother the Synagogue, whose son he was, and loved by her as an only son, just as now every one of the faithful is called a son of the Church. Or Solomon says these things in the person of Christ, who was the only and natural Son of the eternal Father, and the only-begotten Son of the Virgin: whom, according to the nature He assumed, the Father instructed most fully in an instant from the moment of the incarnation; and He was most tender in body, as being born of the most pure blood of the holy Virgin, and of an altogether most noble complexion [that is, bodily constitution]; and in all charity and pity, in the bowels of mercy, wholly tender, and most tender in mind.

paras.t: Posside sapientiam ; posside prudentiam. Ne obliviscaris, neque declines a verbis oris mei. Ne dimittas eam, et custodiet te; dilige eam, et conservabit te. Principium sapientiæ, posside sapientiam : id est, admonitio ista, qua te exhortor, dicens, Posside, id est, acquire, conserva, custodi sapientiam, est principium sapientiæ tibi, quia hanc exhortationem suscipiendo, incipis ad sapientiam ascendere seu disponi. Juxta quem modum Seneca asserit : Magna pars boni est, velle fieri bonum. Et in omni possessione tua acquire prudentiam : id est, de nulla opulentia acquisita seu tibi donata sis contentus, nisi prudentiam quoque possideas, sine qua ceteræ virtutes mox degenerarent in vitia.
paras.en: [[4:5|Get wisdom, get prudence: forget not, neither decline from the words of my mouth|Posside sapientiam ; posside prudentiam. Ne obliviscaris, neque declines a verbis oris mei]]. [[4:6|Forsake her not, and she shall keep thee: love her, and she shall preserve thee|Ne dimittas eam, et custodiet te; dilige eam, et conservabit te]]. [[4:7|The beginning of wisdom, get wisdom|Principium sapientiæ, posside sapientiam]]: that is, this admonition with which I exhort thee, saying, Get, that is, acquire, keep, guard wisdom, is for thee the beginning of wisdom; for in receiving this exhortation thou beginnest to rise to wisdom, or to be disposed for it. In this sense Seneca asserts: It is a great part of goodness to wish to become good. [[4:7|and with all thy possession purchase prudence|Et in omni possessione tua acquire prudentiam]]: that is, be content with no wealth acquired or given thee unless thou possess prudence also, without which the other virtues would soon degenerate into vices.

paras.t: Arripe illam, puta prudentiam seu sapientiam, et exaltabit te, id est, spiritualiter magnum efficiet, atque idoneum alios gubernare ; et glorificaberis ab ea, quum eam fueris amplexatus in corde, ut sponsam carissimam. Nempe in dono sapientiæ proficiendo, fit homo tandem quasi consiliarius ac secretarius Dei, et in regno cœlesti glorificari meretur. In præsenti quoque multipliciter honoratur, sicut de hoc Sapientiæ octavo multa habentur. Hinc ait Philosophus, quod sapientia est divina possessio. Dabit capiti tuo augmenta gratiarum : id est, per sapientiam cor tuum proficiet in omni gratia, virtute, dono et fructu Spiritus Sancti ; et corona inclyta proteget te, id est, aurea illa, quæ est præmium essentiale in patria, faciet te securum in sempiternum. De qua in Psalmo dicitur Deo : Posuisti in capite ejus coronam de lapide pretioso ; et in libro Sapientiæ, Accipient regnum decoris, et diadema speciei de manu Domini ; et iterum, Ut darem lugentibus Sion coronam pro cinere.
paras.en: [[4:8|Take hold on her|Arripe illam]], namely prudence or wisdom, [[4:8|and she shall exalt thee|et exaltabit te]], that is, she shall make thee great in spirit, and fit to govern others; [[4:8|thou shalt be glorified by her, when thou shalt embrace her|et glorificaberis ab ea, quum eam fueris amplexatus]] in thy heart, as a most dear bride. For by advancing in the gift of wisdom a man at length becomes, as it were, a counsellor and confidant of God, and merits to be glorified in the heavenly kingdom. In the present life too he is honoured in many ways, as is said at length on this in the eighth chapter of Wisdom[[Wis 8:3||]] [the margin gives Wis. viii, 3–18]. Hence the Philosopher says that wisdom is a divine possession. [[4:9|She shall give to thy head increase of graces|Dabit capiti tuo augmenta gratiarum]]: that is, through wisdom thy heart shall advance in every grace, virtue, gift and fruit of the Holy Ghost; [[4:9|and protect thee with a noble crown|et corona inclyta proteget te]], that is, that golden crown which is the essential reward in our fatherland [that is, heaven] shall make thee secure for ever. Of which it is said to God in the Psalm: [[Ps 20:4|thou hast set on his head a crown of precious stones|Posuisti in capite ejus coronam de lapide pretioso]]; and in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:17|shall they receive a kingdom of glory, and a crown of beauty at the hand of the Lord|Accipient regnum decoris, et diadema speciei de manu Domini]]; and again: [[Is 61:3|To appoint to the mourners of Sion, and to give them a crown for ashes|Ut darem lugentibus Sion coronam pro cinere]] [Denis's wording is shortened: 'that I might give to the mourners of Sion a crown for ashes'].

paras.t: Audi, fili mi, et suscipe verba mea, ut multiplicentur tibi anni vitæ : id est, quatenus in præsenti vivas, quamdiu hic fueris, per gratiam, atque in die æternitatis per gloriam. Viam sapientiæ demonstrabo tibi, id est, docebo te qualiter ad sapientiam veram queas pertingere, et in ea proficere, et qui sint actus ipsius ; ducam te per semitas æquitatis, id est per præcepta justitiæ ;
paras.en: [[4:10|Hear, O my son, and receive my words, that years of life may be multiplied to thee|Audi, fili mi, et suscipe verba mea, ut multiplicentur tibi anni vitæ]]: that is, so that in the present thou mayest live by grace as long as thou art here, and in the day of eternity by glory. [[4:11|I will shew thee the way of wisdom|Viam sapientiæ demonstrabo tibi]], that is, I will teach thee how thou mayest attain to true wisdom and advance in it, and what its acts are; [[4:11|I will lead thee by the paths of equity|ducam te per semitas æquitatis]], that is, by the precepts of justice;

paras.t: quas quum ingressus fueris, exsequendo divina mandata, non arctabuntur gressus tui : id est, libere et jucunde servies Deo, et actiones tuæ atque affectiones erunt in latitudine caritatis. Et quanto plus in via Dei profeceris, tanto facilius ac delectabilius erit tibi Deo servire : quia caritas fervens instigabit te ad agendum omne bonum alacriter, ut grata mente Domino psallas : Viam mandatorum tuorum cucurri, quum dilatasti, id est, per caritatem extendisti, cor meum, ad diligendum te ferventer ac proximos, et ad considerandum pertinentia ad salutem. Hinc ait Salvator : Jugum meum suave est. Apostolus quoque : Dilatatum est, inquit, cor nostrum. Nihilo minus arcta est via salutis, habendo respectum ad humanæ fragilitatis conditionem; attamen per caritatem dulcescit. Et currens, id est ea quæ Dei sunt, fervide exsequens, non habebis offendiculum, id est, non impinges cadendo per culpam, sed recto perges itinere ad beatitudinem æternalem.
paras.en: [[4:12|Which when thou shalt have entered|quas quum ingressus fueris]], by carrying out the divine commandments, [[4:12|thy steps shall not be straitened|non arctabuntur gressus tui]]: that is, thou shalt serve God freely and gladly, and thy actions and affections shall be in the breadth of charity. And the more thou advancest in the way of God, the easier and more delightful it will be for thee to serve God; for fervent charity will spur thee to do every good thing eagerly, so that with a grateful mind thou singest to the Lord: [[Ps 118:32|I have run the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge|Viam mandatorum tuorum cucurri, quum dilatasti]], that is, didst extend through charity, [[Ps 118:32|my heart|cor meum]], to love Thee and my neighbours fervently, and to consider the things that belong to salvation. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 11:30|For my yoke is sweet|Jugum meum suave est]]. The Apostle too says: [[2 Cor 6:11|our heart is enlarged|Dilatatum est, inquit, cor nostrum]]. Nevertheless the way of salvation is strait, having regard to the condition of human frailty; yet through charity it grows sweet. [[4:12|and when thou runnest|Et currens]], that is, carrying out fervently the things that are God's, [[4:12|thou shalt not meet a stumblingblock|non habebis offendiculum]], that is, thou shalt not stumble and fall through sin, but shalt go on by a straight road to everlasting beatitude.

paras.t: Tene disciplinam, id est correptionem, correctionem et salutarem doctrinam, quia ipsa est vita tua : id est, per eam vives in gratia, et deinceps beatus eris in gloria.
paras.en: [[4:13|Take hold on instruction|Tene disciplinam]], that is, reproof, correction and wholesome teaching, [[4:13|because it is thy life|quia ipsa est vita tua]]: that is, by it thou shalt live in grace, and afterwards be blessed in glory.

paras.t: Ne delecteris in semitis impiorum, id est, in actibus vitiosis nullatenus glorieris, nec aliorum impietati aut vanitati consentias. In spectaculis, torneamentis, hastiludiis, choreis et consimilibus vanitatibus non habeas complacentiam aut consensum, nec alienis peccatis communices : quibus plane communicas, si eorum impietati aut vanitati consentias aut læteris. Condolendum igitur aliis, dum eos talibus occupari et delectari videmus aut scimus. Nec corrideamus eis in vanitatibus et insaniis falsis. Ideo quippe hortatur Apostolus : Nolite communicare infructuosis operibus tenebrarum, magis autem redarguite. Hinc subditur : nec tibi placeat via malorum, id est actio iniquorum. Fuge ab ea, nec transeas per illam ; declina, et desere eam, id est, ut etiam vites occasionem omnem peccandi, incautum adspectum, contactum, amplexum et oscula, confabulationes furtivas, munuscula. Qui enim non vitat occasiones peccandi, cito incidit in laqueum inimici, et Dei offensam.
paras.en: [[4:14|Be not delighted in the paths of the wicked|Ne delecteris in semitis impiorum]], that is, glory in no way in vicious acts, and do not consent to the impiety or vanity of others. Take no pleasure in, and give no consent to, spectacles, tournaments, jousts, dances and like vanities, and do not share in the sins of others: which thou plainly sharest if thou consentest to or rejoicest in their impiety or vanity. We ought therefore to grieve for others when we see or know them to be busied with and delighted by such things. Nor let us smile with them as they turn [[Ps 39:5|to vanities, and lying follies|in vanitatibus et insaniis falsis]]. For this is why the Apostle exhorts: [[Eph 5:11|have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness: but rather reprove them|Nolite communicare infructuosis operibus tenebrarum, magis autem redarguite]]. Hence it is added: [[4:14|neither let the way of evil men please thee|nec tibi placeat via malorum]], that is, the doing of the wicked. [[4:15|Flee from it, pass not by it: go aside, and forsake it|Fuge ab ea, nec transeas per illam ; declina, et desere eam]]: that is, so that thou avoid also every occasion of sinning: the unguarded look, touching, embraces and kisses, stolen conversations, little gifts. For he who does not avoid the occasions of sin soon falls into the snare of the enemy, and into the offence of God.

paras.t: Non enim dormiunt nisi malefecerint, id est, iniqui in vitiis assueti, non quiescunt nisi procedant in actus illicitos, ad quos habitus pravus, consuetudoque pessima (quæ est altera quædam natura ligni) eos inclinant. Nam et Philosophus protestatur : Qualis quisque est, talia cupit, loquitur, operatur. Hinc Christus in Evangelio talibus ait : Hypocritæ, quomodo potestis bona loqui cum sitis mali? Et in Jeremia dicitur vitiosis : Si mutare potest Æthiops pellem suam, et pardus varietates suas, et vos poteritis benefacere, quum didiceritis malum. Hinc disseruit Augustinus : Moles imposita monumento, ipsa est dura vis consuetudinis, qua premitur anima, ut nec resurgere nec respirare permittatur. Verumtamen, sicut ad consuetudinem paulatim pertingitur, sic ipsa paulatim Deo auxiliante eradicatur, quamvis difficulter id fiat. Attamen quibusdam repente tanta infunditur gratiæ copia, ut celeriter atque faciliter vincant, abhorreant, vitent quidquid paulo ante ex prava consuetudine placuit, prout in libro Confessionum electissimus Augustinus sibi contigisse fatetur. Nec capitur somnus ab eis, id est, somnum non capiunt, nisi supplantaverint infirmiores ac simplices. Comedunt panem impietatis, et vinum iniquitatis bibunt, id est, cibis ac potibus injuste acquisitis reficiuntur, in pravisque actibus et affectibus, quasi in esculento et poculento, delectantur.
paras.en: [[4:16|For they sleep not, except they have done evil|Non enim dormiunt nisi malefecerint]], that is, the wicked who are accustomed to vices do not rest unless they go on to unlawful acts, to which an evil habit and a most wicked custom (which is a kind of second nature) incline them. For the Philosopher too declares: As each man is, such things he desires, speaks and does. Hence Christ says to such men in the Gospel: Hypocrites, [[Matt 12:34|how can you speak good things, whereas you are evil?|quomodo potestis bona loqui cum sitis mali?]] [Denis has 'Hypocrites' where the Gospel has 'O generation of vipers']. And in Jeremias it is said to the vicious: [[Jer 13:23|If the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots: you also may do well, when you have learned evil|Si mutare potest Æthiops pellem suam, et pardus varietates suas, et vos poteritis benefacere, quum didiceritis malum]]. Hence Augustine discoursed: The stone laid on the tomb is the hard force of custom, by which the soul is pressed down so that it is allowed neither to rise again nor to breathe. Nevertheless, as custom is reached little by little, so little by little, with God's help, it is rooted out, though this is done with difficulty. Yet to some so great an abundance of grace is suddenly poured in that they quickly and easily overcome, abhor and shun whatever pleased them a little before out of evil custom, as the most choice Augustine confesses happened to him, in the book of the Confessions. [[4:16|and their sleep is taken away|Nec capitur somnus ab eis]] [Denis reads *capitur*, 'is taken', for the Vulgate's *rapitur*, 'is snatched away'], that is, they take no sleep, [[4:16|unless they have made some to fall|nisi supplantaverint]], the weaker and the simple. [[4:17|They eat the bread of wickedness, and drink the wine of iniquity|Comedunt panem impietatis, et vinum iniquitatis bibunt]], that is, they refresh themselves with food and drink unjustly gotten, and take delight in evil acts and affections as in meat and drink.

paras.t: Justorum autem semita quasi lux splendens, procedit et crescit usque ad perfectam diem. Semita justorum est conversatio bonorum et contemplatio virtuosorum : in qua lux gratiæ, splendor sapientiæ, puritas cordis relucent. Hæc crescit spirituali profectu usque ad perfectam diem, id est, ad summum gradum doni sapientiæ ac virtutum, et usque ad diem æternitatis, de qua cantamus. Quia melior est dies una in atriis tuis super millia : hoc est, de fide transit ad speciem, de spe ad comprehensionem, de caritate ad beatificam fruitionem. De qua via loquitur Isaias : Hæc est via, ambulate in ea, et non declinetis neque ad dexteram, neque ad sinistram ; et iterum, Semita justi recta est. Et Psalmista : Psallam et intelligam in via immaculata.
paras.en: [[4:18|But the path of the just, as a shining light|Justorum autem semita quasi lux splendens]], [[4:18|goeth forwards, and increaseth even to perfect day|procedit et crescit usque ad perfectam diem]]. The path of the just is the conduct of the good and the contemplation of the virtuous, in which the light of grace, the splendour of wisdom and purity of heart shine forth. This grows by spiritual progress [[4:18|even to perfect day|usque ad perfectam diem]], that is, to the highest degree of the gift of wisdom and of the virtues, and even to the day of eternity, of which we sing: [[Ps 83:11|For better is one day in thy courts above thousands|Quia melior est dies una in atriis tuis super millia]]: that is, it passes from faith to sight, from hope to possession, from charity to the beatific enjoyment. Of which way Isaias speaks: [[Is 30:21|This is the way, walk ye in it: and go not aside neither to the right hand, nor to the left|Hæc est via, ambulate in ea, et non declinetis neque ad dexteram, neque ad sinistram]]; and again: [[Is 26:7|the path of the just is right|Semita justi recta est]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 100:1|I will sing,|Psallam]] [[Ps 100:2|And I will understand in the unspotted way|et intelligam in via immaculata]].

paras.t: Via autem impiorum tenebrosa : quia eorum vita tenebris ignorantiæ et errorum, caligine vitiorum, enormitate culparum, et immoderantiis passionum est plena, juxta illud in Psalmo : Fiat via illorum tenebræ et lubricum. Hinc de iniquis loquitur Paulus : Fuistis aliquando tenebræ. Et Joannes : Tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt ; itemque, Lux venit in mundum, et dilexerunt homines tenebras magis quam lucem. Nesciunt ubi corruunt, id est, proprium lapsum non advertunt, nec qualiter inferno propinquent, attendunt, nec pensant sua pericula. Et dato quod informi et nuda notitia hoc aliqualiter pensent, non tamen formata et efficaci notitia : quia excæcati sunt corde, et quasi insensibiles ad ea quæ Dei sunt ac suæ salutis.
paras.en: [[4:19|The way of the wicked is darksome|Via autem impiorum tenebrosa]]: for their life is full of the darkness of ignorance and errors, the gloom of vices, the enormity of sins and the excesses of the passions, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 34:6|Let their way become dark and slippery|Fiat via illorum tenebræ et lubricum]]. Hence Paul says of the wicked: [[Eph 5:8|you were heretofore darkness|Fuistis aliquando tenebræ]]. And John: [[John 1:5|the darkness did not comprehend it|Tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt]]; and likewise: [[John 3:19|the light is come into the world and men loved darkness rather than the light|Lux venit in mundum, et dilexerunt homines tenebras magis quam lucem]]. [[4:19|they know not where they fall|Nesciunt ubi corruunt]], that is, they do not notice their own fall, nor heed how near they draw to hell, nor weigh their dangers. And granted that they weigh this somewhat by an unformed and bare knowledge, yet not by a formed and effective knowledge [that is, knowledge not quickened by charity and so not moving them to act]: for they are blinded in heart, and as it were without feeling for the things that are God's and that belong to their salvation.

paras.t: Fili mi, ausculta sermones meos, et ad eloquia mea inclina aurem tuam. Qui enim ex Deo est, verba Dei audit. Ne recedant ab oculis tuis interioribus, custodi ea in medio cordis tui. Huic simile est illud Deuteronomii : Erunt verba Domini in corde tuo, et meditaberis sedens in domo tua, et ambulans in itinere, et dormiens atque consurgens ; eruntque et movebuntur inter oculos tuos. Vita enim sunt invenientibus, id est recolentibus, ac opere exercentibus ea. Ideo ait Salvator : Verba quæ ego locutus sum vobis, spiritus et vita sunt. Et universæ carni sanitas, id est, salus omnium hominum consistit in audientia et effectu verborum Dei.
paras.en: [[4:20|My son, hearken to my words, and incline thy ear to my sayings|Fili mi, ausculta sermones meos, et ad eloquia mea inclina aurem tuam]]. For [[John 8:47|He that is of God heareth the words of God|Qui enim ex Deo est, verba Dei audit]] [the margin reads Ibid. viii, 7, for John 8:47]. [[4:21|Let them not depart from thy eyes|Ne recedant ab oculis tuis]], thy inward eyes; [[4:21|keep them in the midst of thy heart|custodi ea in medio cordis tui]]. Like this is that of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 6:6|these words which I command thee this day, shall be in thy heart|Erunt verba Domini in corde tuo]] [Denis has 'The words of the Lord shall be in thy heart'], [[Deut 6:7|and thou shalt meditate upon them sitting in thy house, and walking on thy journey, sleeping and rising|et meditaberis sedens in domo tua, et ambulans in itinere, et dormiens atque consurgens]]; [[Deut 6:8|and they shall be and shall move between thy eyes|eruntque et movebuntur inter oculos tuos]]. [[4:22|For they are life to those that find them|Vita enim sunt invenientibus]], that is, to those who call them to mind and practise them in deed. Therefore the Saviour says: [[John 6:64|The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life|Verba quæ ego locutus sum vobis, spiritus et vita sunt]]. [[4:22|and health to all flesh|Et universæ carni sanitas]], that is, the salvation of all men consists in hearing the words of God and carrying them out.

paras.t: Omni custodia custodi cor tuum : id est, cum summa et jugi diligentia præserva mentem tuam ab omni cogitatione immunda, ab omni affectione iniqua, ab omni omissione culpabili ; et insuper exerce eam assidue in meditationibus et affectionibus sanctis, et verbis actibusque virtutum ; quia ex ipso vita procedit : id est, ex cordis puritate vita gratiæ derivatur in actu omni exteriori ; et nisi cor custodiatur, reliqua bona fiunt inaniter. Imo, quemadmodum ex corporeo corde dependet et oritur vita naturæ, ita a corde spirituali, quod est mens, pendet ac pullulat vita gratiæ, ac profectus in ea. Ideo ait Salvator : Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Et Deuteronomii quarto : Custodi temetipsum et animam tuam sollicite. Invisibiles namque hostes ipsum cor tanquam pretiosissimum obsident castrum. Idcirco intentissima custodia est necessaria homini evadere cupienti. Hinc ait Eusebius Emisenus : Quid est quod nos vigiliis laboribusque conficimus, et ea quæ Deus maxime in nobis esse desiderat ac requirit (hoc est cor mundum a quotidianis culpis ac negligentiis istis, quas qui non vitat, paulatim deficit, et ad graviora prolabitur), non habemus? Itemque : Hæc est, inquit, spiritualium bonorum ratio, ut quum ea summo labore constet acquiri, tam facile pereant, ut vix possit intelligi. Et inde est, quod interdum nos sanctos putamus, quoniam lucra de laboribus æstimamus, et detrimenta subsequentia non pensamus. Itaque, juxta doctrinam Climaci, ponamus in janua cordis portarium et custodem, ipsum Dei timorem, qui nihil illicitum permittat intrare, aut intus manere ; et sit cor nostrum semper in Domino. Nam quod amat, in eo se figere solet. Propter quod sanctus testatur Hieronymus : Gulosus cor habet in ventre, lascivus in lumbis, superbus in eminentia, avarus in pecunia. Hinc loquitur Isaias : Super custodiam meam ego sum stans totis noctibus ; Habacuc quoque, Super custodiam meam stabo, et contemplabor quid respondeam ad arguentem me.
paras.en: [[4:23|With all watchfulness keep thy heart|Omni custodia custodi cor tuum]]: that is, with the greatest and unceasing diligence preserve thy mind from every unclean thought, from every wicked affection, from every culpable omission; and moreover exercise it constantly in holy meditations and affections, and in words and acts of virtue; [[4:23|because life issueth out from it|quia ex ipso vita procedit]]: that is, from purity of heart the life of grace flows into every outward act; and unless the heart is guarded, the other good things are done in vain. Nay, just as the life of nature depends on and springs from the bodily heart, so the life of grace, and progress in it, depends on and springs from the spiritual heart, which is the mind. Therefore the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart: they shall see God|Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt]]. And Deuteronomy, chapter four: [[Deut 4:9|Keep thyself therefore, and thy soul carefully|Custodi temetipsum et animam tuam sollicite]]. For invisible enemies besiege the heart itself as a most precious castle. Therefore the most attentive watch is needed by a man who wishes to escape. Hence Eusebius of Emesa says: How is it that we wear ourselves out with vigils and labours, and do not have the things that God most desires and requires to be in us (that is, a heart clean of these daily faults and negligences; he who does not avoid them gradually fails and slips into graver ones)? And again: This, he says, is the way of spiritual goods: though it is certain that they are acquired with the greatest labour, they perish so easily that it can hardly be understood. And hence it is that we sometimes think ourselves holy, because we reckon the gains from our labours and do not weigh the losses that follow. Therefore, according to the teaching of Climacus, let us set at the door of the heart a porter and guard, the fear of God itself, which allows nothing unlawful to enter or to remain within; and let our heart be always in the Lord. For the heart is wont to fix itself in what it loves. For this reason St. Jerome testifies: The glutton has his heart in his belly, the lustful in his loins, the proud in high places, the covetous in money. Hence Isaias says: [[Is 21:8|I am upon my ward, standing whole nights|Super custodiam meam ego sum stans totis noctibus]]; Habacuc also: [[Hab 2:1|I will stand upon my watch|Super custodiam meam stabo]], and I will consider [[Hab 2:1|what I may answer to him that reproveth me|quid respondeam ad arguentem me]].

paras.t: Remove a te os pravum, ita ut tu nec prava loquaris, nec ora loquentium mala consentiendo advertas, sed fugias. Sic Salvator docet manum, pedem, oculum scandalizantem abscindere. Atque Apostolus : Mortificate, ait, membra vestra quæ sunt super terram. Simili modo detrahentia labia sint procul a te, ut nec detrahas, nec detrahenti communices. Detractio namque enorme est vitium, et gravius rapina ac furto : quoniam aufert nomen bonum, quod divitiis antefertur. De hoc vitio infra magis dicetur. Unde et Jacobus ait apostolus : Nolite alterutrum detrahere, fratres mei ; qui enim detrahit fratri, detrahit legi.
paras.en: [[4:24|Remove from thee a froward mouth|Remove a te os pravum]], so that thou neither speak froward things, nor heed with consent the mouths of those who speak evil, but flee them. So the Saviour teaches us to cut off the hand, the foot, the eye that scandalizes[[Matt 18:8||]][[Matt 18:9||]]. And the Apostle: [[Col 3:5|Mortify|Mortificate]], he says, [[Col 3:5|your members which are upon the earth|membra vestra quæ sunt super terram]]. In like manner [[4:24|let detracting lips be far from thee|detrahentia labia sint procul a te]], so that thou neither detract nor share with a detractor. For detraction is an enormous vice, and graver than robbery and theft, since it takes away a good name, which is preferred before riches[[Prov 22:1||]]. More will be said of this vice below. Hence James the apostle also says: [[Jas 4:11|Detract not one another, my brethren|Nolite alterutrum detrahere, fratres mei]]; for [[Jas 4:11|He that detracteth his brother|qui enim detrahit fratri]] [[Jas 4:11|detracteth the law|detrahit legi]].

paras.t: Oculi tui interiores recta videant, id est, justa ac salubria pensent ac approbent, inter vera et falsa, inter bona et mala discernant, et qualiter sit agendum, voluntate ostendant. Et palpebræ tuæ intellectuales, id est scientiæ et notitiæ tibi concessæ, præcedant gressus tuos, id est, opera tua præveniant, quatenus sicut per exteriorem visum consideras quo et qualiter sit eundum, ita per scientiam et Scripturam quam scis, perpendas qualiter sit tibi vivendum : sicque consideratio præveniat actum, et vitiorum obliquitatem ac viarum pericula fugiat ac devitet, prout in libro de Consideratione plenius docet Bernardus. Hinc Aggæus propheta ait : Ponite corda vestra super vias vestras. Et Apostolus monet : Videte quomodo caute ambuletis.
paras.en: [[4:25|Let thy eyes|Oculi tui]], the inward ones, [[4:25|look straight on|recta videant]], that is, let them weigh and approve what is just and wholesome, discern between true and false, between good and evil, and show the will how it must act. [[4:25|and let thy eyelids|Et palpebræ tuæ]] of the understanding, that is, the knowledge and learning granted thee, [[4:25|go before thy steps|præcedant gressus tuos]], that is, let them go before thy works; so that, as by outward sight thou considerest whither and how thou must go, so by the knowledge and the Scripture thou knowest thou mayest ponder how thou must live: and so let consideration go before action, and flee and avoid the crookedness of vices and the dangers of the ways, as Bernard teaches more fully in the book On Consideration. Hence the prophet Aggeus says: [[Agg 1:5|Set your hearts to consider your ways|Ponite corda vestra super vias vestras]] [literally, 'set your hearts upon your ways']. And the Apostle warns: [[Eph 5:15|See therefore, brethren, how you walk circumspectly|Videte quomodo caute ambuletis]].

paras.t: Dirige semitas pedibus tuis, id est, actiones tuas ordina bonis affectibus, ut procedant ex caritate et desiderio complacendi Deo : sicut hortatur Apostolus, Omnia autem decenter et secundum ordinem fiant in vobis. Et omnes viæ tuæ stabilientur, id est, opera tua fient stabiliter bona. Ordinatio namque prudentiæ et caritas, valde stabiliunt mentem in Deo, et opera ex se procedentia faciunt firma : sicut econtrario passiones, vitia ac imprudentia agitant hominem, et per diversa instar venti effundunt, juxta illud Psalmi : Deus meus, pone illos ut rotam, et sicut stipulam ante faciem venti. Propterea per Jeremiam loquitur Dominus : Si abstuleris offendicula tua a facie mea, non commoveberis. Hinc Seneca libro de quatuor Virtutibus, ait : Si prudentiam amplecteris, ubique idem eris ; et prout rerum ac temporis varietas exiget, ita te accommodabis et applicabis rebus atque temporibus ; nec te in eis mutabis, sed potius coaptabis, sicut manus est eadem quum in palmam extenditur, et dum in pugnum restringitur.
paras.en: [[4:26|Make straight the path for thy feet|Dirige semitas pedibus tuis]], that is, order thy actions by good affections, so that they proceed from charity and the desire of pleasing God, as the Apostle exhorts: [[1 Cor 14:40|But let all things be done decently and according to order|Omnia autem decenter et secundum ordinem fiant]] among you. [[4:26|and all thy ways shall be established|Et omnes viæ tuæ stabilientur]], that is, thy works shall be stably good. For the ordering of prudence, and charity, greatly establish the mind in God, and make firm the works that proceed from it: as, on the contrary, passions, vices and imprudence toss a man about and scatter him in different directions like the wind, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 82:14|O my God, make them like a wheel; and as stubble before the wind|Deus meus, pone illos ut rotam, et sicut stipulam ante faciem venti]]. Therefore the Lord says through Jeremias: [[Jer 4:1|if thou wilt take away thy stumblingblocks out of my sight, thou shalt not be moved|Si abstuleris offendicula tua a facie mea, non commoveberis]]. Hence Seneca says in the book On the Four Virtues: If thou embrace prudence, thou wilt everywhere be the same; and as the variety of things and of times shall require, so wilt thou accommodate and apply thyself to things and times; nor wilt thou change thyself in them, but rather adapt thyself, as the hand is the same when it is stretched out into an open palm and when it is closed into a fist.

paras.t: Ne declines ad dextram neque ad sinistram : id est, regia via incede, nec ad aliquod vitiosum extremum divertas, sed persevera in medio virtutis, prout recta determinat ratio. Virtus namque, secundum Philosophum, est quædam medietas inter duo extrema culpabilia : quorum unum est manifeste malum, ideo per sinistram significatur ; aliud bonum, imo valde bonum esse putatur, ideo per dextram designatur. Quemadmodum in virtute abstinentiæ, medium est abstinere prout vires queunt sufferre ; manifesteque malum est, omnino abstinere, et jejunare non velle. Sed ultra vires abstinere et jejunare, apparet quandoque valde laudabile, quamvis ex indiscreto fervore procedat. Porro, secundum Glossam, declinat ad dextram, qui de justitia sua præsumit ; ad sinistram, qui palam peccat. Declinat quoque ad dextram, qui prosperis vel promissis ab itinere recto allicitur ; ad sinistram vero, qui per adversitates aut comminationes dejicitur. Hinc scriptum est : Hæc est via, ambulate in ea, et non declinetis neque ad dextram, neque ad sinistram. Averte pedem tuum a malo, id est, affectum tuum compesce ab actu illicito, et omne quod agis, refrena a vitio.
paras.en: [[4:27|Decline not to the right hand, nor to the left|Ne declines ad dextram neque ad sinistram]]: that is, walk on the royal road, and turn aside to no vicious extreme, but persevere in the mean of virtue, as right reason determines. For virtue, according to the Philosopher, is a kind of mean between two blameworthy extremes: one of which is plainly evil, and so is signified by the left; the other is thought good, nay very good, and so is denoted by the right. Thus in the virtue of abstinence the mean is to abstain as far as one's strength can bear; and it is plainly evil not to abstain at all and to be unwilling to fast [the Latin, *omnino abstinere*, 'to abstain altogether', seems to lack a *non*; the sense requires 'not to abstain at all']. But to abstain and fast beyond one's strength sometimes appears very praiseworthy, although it proceeds from indiscreet fervour. Further, according to the Gloss, he declines to the right who presumes on his own justice; to the left, he who sins openly. He also declines to the right who is enticed from the straight road by prosperity or promises; to the left, he who is cast down by adversities or threats. Hence it is written: [[Is 30:21|This is the way, walk ye in it: and go not aside neither to the right hand, nor to the left|Hæc est via, ambulate in ea, et non declinetis neque ad dextram, neque ad sinistram]]. [[4:27|turn away thy foot from evil|Averte pedem tuum a malo]], that is, restrain thy affection from unlawful acts, and curb from vice all that thou doest.

paras.t: Totum autem quod subditur in isto capitulo (ut refert Lyra) non est in Hebræo, neque de textu ; sed per modum glossæ ab aliquo creditur fuisse adjunctum, ac postea ex scriptorum imperitia textui mixtum.
paras.en: Now all that follows in this chapter (as Lyra reports) is not in the Hebrew, nor part of the text; but it is believed to have been added by someone by way of a gloss, and afterwards, through the unskilfulness of copyists, mixed into the text.

paras.t: Vias enim quæ a dextris sunt, novit Dominus. Ea quæ virtuosa et bona sunt, Deus noscit per approbationem, sicut Dominus ad Moysen : Te ipsum, inquit, novi ex nomine. Vitiosa autem et reproba, scit nuda et simplici intelligentia, juxta illud : Cognovi multa scelera vestra. Si ergo per vias quæ a dextris sunt, intelligantur viæ veraciter bonæ, seu actus justitiæ, illas scit Dominus per approbationem ; si vero per eas intelligantur viæ quæ multum bonæ videntur, et tamen ex indiscretione procedunt, illas novit per intelligentiam simplicem et reprobationem. Sed primo modo videntur hic accipi, quum subdatur : perversæ vero sunt quæ a sinistris sunt, id est, ad extremum aperte malum declinant. Ipse autem Deus rectos faciet gressus tuos, dando tibi gratiam conversandi juxta suorum rectitudinem præceptorum : de quibus dicitur, Rectæ viæ Domini, et justi ambulabunt in eis. Non ergo præsumamus de viribus nostris, sed auxilio gratiæ jugiter innitamur, quoniam sine ipso nihil meritorium possumus facere. Ideo cum Psalmista precemur, Deduc me, Domine, in via tua; et, Gressus meos dirige secundum eloquium tuum. Nihilo minus Apostolus monet: Rectos gressus facite pedibus vestris. Oportet enim nos cooperari gratiæ Dei, atque per liberum arbitrium acceptare divinum instinctum, et consentire directioni divinæ. Itinera autem tua in pace producentur, id est, opera tua erunt pacifica, et actus tui paci pectoris erunt conjuncti, et ad pacem æternitatis perducent. Etenim pax multa diligentibus legem Dei. Et Job dicitur : Acquiesce Deo, et habeto pacem ; et per hoc habebis fructus optimos.
paras.en: [[4:27|For the Lord knoweth the ways that are on the right hand|Vias enim quæ a dextris sunt, novit Dominus]]. The things that are virtuous and good God knows by approval, as the Lord said to Moses: [[Ex 33:17|thee|Te ipsum]], He says, [[Ex 33:17|I have known by name|novi ex nomine]]. But the vicious and reprobate He knows by bare and simple understanding, according to that: [[Amos 5:12|I know your manifold crimes|Cognovi multa scelera vestra]] [the margin's verse number is partly unread: Amos v, 1…]. If then by the ways that are on the right hand are understood ways truly good, or acts of justice, the Lord knows them by approval; but if by them are understood ways that seem very good and yet proceed from indiscretion, He knows them by simple understanding and by reproving them. But they seem to be taken here in the first way, since there is added: [[4:27|but those are perverse which are on the left hand|perversæ vero sunt quæ a sinistris sunt]], that is, which turn aside to the extreme that is openly evil. [[4:27|But he will make thy courses straight|Ipse autem Deus rectos faciet gressus tuos]] [Denis reads *gressus*, 'steps', for *cursus*], by giving thee grace to live according to the rightness of His precepts, of which it is said: [[Osee 14:10|the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them|Rectæ viæ Domini, et justi ambulabunt in eis]]. Let us not therefore presume on our own strength, but lean continually on the help of grace, since without it we can do nothing meritorious. Therefore let us pray with the Psalmist: [[Ps 85:11|Conduct me, O Lord, in thy way|Deduc me, Domine, in via tua]]; and: [[Ps 118:133|Direct my steps according to thy word|Gressus meos dirige secundum eloquium tuum]] [the margin reads Ps. cxviii, 33, for verse 133]. Nonetheless the Apostle warns: [[Heb 12:13|make straight steps with your feet|Rectos gressus facite pedibus vestris]]. For we must co-operate with the grace of God, and by free will accept the divine prompting, and consent to the divine direction. [[4:27|he will bring forward thy ways in peace|Itinera autem tua in pace producentur]], that is, thy works shall be peaceable, and thy acts shall be joined with peace of heart, and shall lead to the peace of eternity. For [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|pax multa diligentibus legem Dei]]. And it is said to Job: [[Job 22:21|Submit thyself then to him, and be at peace: and thereby thou shalt have the best fruits|Acquiesce Deo, et habeto pacem ; et per hoc habebis fructus optimos]].

paras.t: Ecce in isto capitulo multipliciter, et per verba sæpius repetita, ad desiderium et amorem, ad studium et amplexum sapientiæ admonemur. Nec mirum, quoniam tanta est dignitas ejus, quod in actu ipsius, Unigenitus Dei beatitudinem nostram constituit : Hæc est, inquiens, vita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum. Denique, sicut in suis Proverbiis ait Cyrillus : Nihil est homo, si sit sapientia destitutus ; qui se ignorat, nihil est sibi. Et præsertim miser et pauper est, qui suum non novit Creatorem. Propter quod dixit Apostolus : Qui ignorat, ignorabitur. Atque in Osee asserit Dominus : Conticuit populus meus, eo quod non habuerit scientiam Dei. Quid prodest rutilantia cæco, eloquentia surdo, prudentia fatuo?
paras.en: See how in this chapter, in many ways and with words often repeated, we are admonished to the desire and love, to the pursuit and embrace, of wisdom. Nor is it any wonder, since its dignity is so great that the Only-begotten of God placed our beatitude in its act: [[John 17:3|Now this is|Hæc est]], He says, [[John 17:3|eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God|vita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum]]. Lastly, as Cyril says in his Proverbs: Man is nothing if he is destitute of wisdom; he who does not know himself is nothing to himself. And above all he is wretched and poor who does not know his Creator. For this reason the Apostle said: [[1 Cor 14:38|if any man know not, he shall not be known|Qui ignorat, ignorabitur]] [the margin reads Cor. xiv, 3, for 1 Cor 14:38]. And in Osee the Lord declares: [[Osee 4:6|My people have been silent, because they had no knowledge|Conticuit populus meus, eo quod non habuerit scientiam Dei]] [Denis adds 'of God']. What does brightness profit the blind, eloquence the deaf, prudence the fool?

paras.t: Præterea, ad vigilantissimam cordis custodiam hic monemur : quam exercere poterimus, si omnipotentis præsentiam Judicis sagaciter ponderemus. Si enim reverendo aliquo homine præsente ac intuente, erubesceremus nos turpiter, negligenter et inhoneste habere : cur super hoc in Dei vultu non verecundamur? Hinc S. Bernardus in epistola ad Fratres de Monte Dei, edocuit, quod ad habendum se honeste ac virtuose in solitudine et seorsum, plurimum valet ut homo imaginetur sibi quasi præsentem aliquem venerabilem virum, sub cujus adspectu agat omne quod agit: et quod illo intuente agere vereretur, coram Deo agere vereatur. Idcirco in epistolis suis ait et Seneca : Sic vive cum hominibus, tanquam Deus videat ; sic loquere cum Deo, tanquam homines audiant te. Accipe admonitionem salubrem, quam affigere animo tuo volo. Aliquis vir bonus nobis eligendus est, et ante oculos semper habendus, ut sic semper tanquam spectante eo vivamus, et omnia tanquam illo vidente faciamus. Magna pars tollitur vitiorum, si peccanti testis venerandus adsistat.
paras.en: Further, we are here admonished to the most watchful keeping of the heart: which we shall be able to practise if we shrewdly weigh the presence of the almighty Judge. For if, in the presence and sight of some man worthy of reverence, we should blush to behave basely, carelessly and unbecomingly, why are we not ashamed of this before the face of God? Hence St. Bernard taught, in the letter to the Brethren of Mont-Dieu, that for behaving honourably and virtuously in solitude and apart it avails very much that a man imagine some venerable man present, as it were, under whose eyes he does all that he does: and that what he would fear to do in that man's sight, he should fear to do before God. Therefore Seneca too says in his letters: So live with men as if God saw; so speak with God as if men heard thee. Take a wholesome admonition, which I wish thee to fix in thy mind.
