Some good man must be chosen by us and always kept before our eyes, so that we may always live as if he were looking on, and do all things as if he saw. A great part of sins is taken away if a witness to be revered stands by one who is about to sin.

paras.t: Præterea, in isto capitulo, ad evitandum sollicite omnem detractionem instruimur. Quocirca pensandum quia, ut ait Thomas in secunda secundæ, quæstione 73, Sicut quis nocet alteri facto dupliciter, scilicet manifeste, ut in violentia et rapina, et secrete, sicut in furto ; sic unus nocet alteri verbis duobus modis : primo occulte, ut in detractione ; secundo aperte, sicut in contumelia. Dicitur autem homo detrahere, non quia semper aliquid minuat de veritate, sed quoniam quantum in se est, intendit bonitatem famæ alterius minorare directe aut indirecte. Directe, quatuor modis : primo, dum alteri falsum imponit ; secundo, dum culpam ejus exaggerat seu adauget ; tertio, dum revelat occulta ; quarto, dum ea quæ bona sunt, affirmat prava intentione peracta. Indirecte quoque dupliciter : primo, dum negat bonum alterius ; secundo, dum malitiose reticet illud. At vero quam grave sit crimen detractio, constat ex hoc, quod Apostolus ad Romanos, detractores vocat odibiles Deo. Et item ex hoc, quod, ut refert S. Clemens, beatissimus princeps Apostolorum asseruit esse tria homicidii genera. Primum est homicidium corporale. Secundum est odium : nam in prima Canonica sua ait Joannes, Omnis qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est. Tertium, detractio : de qua testatur Bernardus, quod sit gladius ex utraque parte acutus, interficiens tam animam detrahentis, quam mentem audientis. Hinc de S. Pacomio legitur, quod quum audiret aliquem detrahentem, protinus fugit ab illo tanquam a basilisco.
paras.en: Further, in this chapter we are taught to avoid carefully all detraction. Wherefore we must consider that, as Thomas says in the Secunda Secundae, question 73: Just as one harms another by deed in two ways, namely openly, as in violence and robbery, and secretly, as in theft; so one harms another by words in two ways: first secretly, as in detraction; secondly openly, as in contumely [that is, insult to a man's face]. Now a man is said to detract, not because he always takes something from the truth, but because, as far as in him lies, he intends to lessen the good of another's reputation, directly or indirectly. Directly, in four ways: first, when he imputes something false to another; secondly, when he exaggerates or increases his fault; thirdly, when he reveals hidden things; fourthly, when he asserts that things which are good were done with an evil intention. Indirectly also in two ways: first, when he denies another's good; secondly, when he maliciously keeps silent about it. But how grave a crime detraction is appears from this, that the Apostle, writing to the Romans, calls detractors hateful to God[[Rom 1:30||]]. And also from this, that, as St. Clement relates, the most blessed prince of the Apostles declared that there are three kinds of homicide. The first is bodily homicide. The second is hatred: for John says in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 3:15|Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer|Omnis qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est]]. The third, detraction: of which Bernard testifies that it is a sword sharp on both sides, killing both the soul of the detractor and the mind of the hearer. Hence we read of St. Pachomius that when he heard anyone detracting, he at once fled from him as from a basilisk.

paras.t: Postremo hortatur nos scriptura hujus capituli, ut in omnibus simus considerati et circumspecti, et ex prudenti deliberatione procedamus in actum. Nempe, ut ait Bernardus, consideratio mentem purificat, regit affectus, dirigit actus, corrigitque excessus ; mores componit, vitam ordinat et honestat.
paras.en: Lastly, the text of this chapter exhorts us to be considerate and circumspect in all things, and to proceed to action from prudent deliberation. For, as Bernard says, consideration purifies the mind, rules the affections, directs the acts and corrects excesses; it composes the manners, orders the life and makes it honourable.

5.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI QUINTI : FILI MI, ATTENDE SAPIENTIAM.
5.title_en: Explanation of the fifth chapter: My son, attend to my wisdom.

paras.t: Hic rursus in exordio ad sapientiam amplectendam breviter exhortatur; et quia hanc potissime impedit venereorum voluptas, docet diffuse hanc esse vitandam.
paras.en: Here again, in the opening, he briefly exhorts us to embrace wisdom; and since the pleasure of the flesh hinders it most of all, he teaches at length that this pleasure is to be shunned.

paras.t: Fili mi, attende sapientiam meam, et prudentiæ meæ inclina aurem tuam, ut custodias cogitationes, et disciplinam labia tua conservent. Istud jam frequenter expositum est. Ne intenderis fallaciæ mulieris. Istud dicitur in Hebræo non haberi. Attamen sensus est, quod versutiis mulierum non sit insistendum ad imitandum, sed potius ad præcavendum.
paras.en: [[5:1|My son, attend to my wisdom, and incline thy ear to my prudence|Fili mi, attende sapientiam meam, et prudentiæ meæ inclina aurem tuam]], [[5:2|That thou mayst keep thoughts, and thy lips may preserve instruction|ut custodias cogitationes, et disciplinam labia tua conservent]]. This has already been explained often. [[5:2|Mind not the deceit of a woman|Ne intenderis fallaciæ mulieris]]. This is said not to be found in the Hebrew. Yet the sense is that the wiles of women are to be heeded, not in order to imitate them, but rather in order to guard against them.

paras.t: Favus enim distillans labia meretricis, id est, instar favi guttantis delectant; et nitidius oleo guttur ejus: quod sic polit et ornat, ut magis ametur. Novissima autem illius amara quasi absinthium: quoniam multa mala pœnæ et culpæ, in corpore et in anima, etiam in hac vita comitantur luxuriam, deinde æterna damnatio, juxta illud Apocalypsis: Quantum glorificavit se, et in deliciis fuit, tantum date illi tormentum et luctum. Et acuta quasi gladius biceps: quoniam corpus animamque affligunt, et pœnam damni ac pœnam sensus infligunt.
paras.en: [[5:3|For the lips of a harlot are like a honeycomb dropping|Favus enim distillans labia meretricis]]: that is, they delight like a dripping honeycomb; [[5:3|and her throat is smoother than oil|et nitidius oleo guttur ejus]]: which she so polishes and adorns that she may be loved the more. [[5:4|But her end is bitter as wormwood|Novissima autem illius amara quasi absinthium]]: since many evils of punishment and of guilt, in body and in soul, attend lust even in this life, and afterwards eternal damnation, according to that of the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 18:7|As much as she hath glorified herself and lived in delicacies, so much torment and sorrow give ye to her|Quantum glorificavit se, et in deliciis fuit, tantum date illi tormentum et luctum]]. [[5:4|and sharp as a two-edged sword|Et acuta quasi gladius biceps]]: since they afflict body and soul, and inflict the pain of loss and the pain of sense [that is, the two pains of the damned: the loss of the sight of God, and the torment that is felt].

paras.t: Pedes ejus descendunt in mortem, et ad inferos gressus ejus penetrant: quia affectiones ejus sunt libidinosæ, et opera ejus mortaliter vitiosa. Per semitam vitæ gratiæ, id est per observantiam legis divinæ, non ambulat, nec curat prolificare, sed deliciari: vitam quoque naturæ abbreviat. Vagi sunt gressus ejus et investigabiles: quoniam motibus passionum undique circumfertur, et concupiscentiarum inquietudine agitatur plus quam in particulari queat effari.
paras.en: [[5:5|Her feet go down into death, and her steps go in as far as hell|Pedes ejus descendunt in mortem, et ad inferos gressus ejus penetrant]]: for her affections are lustful, and her works mortally vicious. [[5:6|They walk not|non ambulat]] [[5:6|by the path of life|Per semitam vitæ]] of grace, that is, by the keeping of the divine law; nor does she care to bear offspring, but only to take her pleasure; she also shortens the life of nature. [[5:6|her steps are wandering, and unaccountable|Vagi sunt gressus ejus et investigabiles]]: since she is carried about on every side by the motions of the passions, and driven by the restlessness of her desires more than could be told in detail.

paras.t: Nunc autem, fili mi, audi me, et ne recedas a verbis oris mei. Longe fac ab ea viam tuam: quia ad vitandum vitia carnis, maxime confert occasiones eorum vitare, colloquia et adspectum, imo et imaginem venereorum statim repellere, seque ad meditandum salubria, et quæ compunctionem inducunt convertere, videlicet ad intentam dominicæ passionis memoriam, ad considerationem rigoris divini judicii, atque æterni supplicii, et in qualem putredinem et fœtorem caro hæc sordida cito sit resolvenda. Et ne appropinques foribus domus ejus, ne contra propositum tuum alliciaris.
paras.en: [[5:7|Now, therefore, my son, hear me, and depart not from the words of my mouth|Nunc autem, fili mi, audi me, et ne recedas a verbis oris mei]]. [[5:8|Remove thy way far from her|Longe fac ab ea viam tuam]]: for to shun the vices of the flesh it helps most of all to shun their occasions, conversation and looks; nay, to drive away at once even the image of sensual things, and to turn oneself to meditating on wholesome things and on those that bring compunction: namely, to an attentive remembrance of the Lord's passion, to the consideration of the rigour of the divine judgment and of eternal punishment, and of into what rottenness and stench this filthy flesh is soon to be dissolved. [[5:8|and come not nigh the doors of her house|Et ne appropinques foribus domus ejus]], lest thou be enticed against thy resolve.

paras.t: Ne des alienis honorem tuum: id est, ingenitam tuam libertatem ac honorabilem mentem atque imaginem, qua Creatori tuo assimilaris, non subdas jugo vitiorum, servituti diaboli, turpitudini carnalitatis, ne impleatur in te illud in Psalmo: Homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit; comparatus est jumentis insipientibus. Denique admirabilis est honor hominis, quod per Christi incarnationem, passionem, adoptionem et gratiam factus est filius Dei, membrum, miles ac frater Christi, heres vitæ æternæ, proles Ecclesiæ. Non igitur vilificet homo se ipsum in tantum, ut vitiis serviendo fiat servus diaboli, adversarius Christi, mancipium iniquitatis, filius perditionis. Anima quoque per fidem et caritatem sponsa est Salvatoris, sed per immunditiam culpæ fit adultera dæmonis. Et annos tuos crudeli: id est, actus vitæ temporis, quo hic vivis, non exhibeas juxta instigationem diaboli, qui adeo ferox est, ut nihil minus ei de nobis sufficiat, quam ut æterna felicitate nos privet, ac secum infernali damnationi involvat.
paras.en: [[5:9|Give not thy honour to strangers|Ne des alienis honorem tuum]]: that is, do not subject thy inborn freedom, and thy honourable mind, and the image by which thou art made like to thy Creator, to the yoke of vices, to the bondage of the devil, to the foulness of carnality; lest that in the Psalm be fulfilled in thee: [[Ps 48:21|Man when he was in honour did not understand: he hath been compared to senseless beasts|Homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit; comparatus est jumentis insipientibus]][[Ps 48:13||]]. Indeed, wonderful is the honour of man, in that through the incarnation, passion, adoption and grace of Christ he has been made a son of God[[Rom 8:16||]], a member, soldier and brother of Christ, an heir of eternal life[[Rom 8:17||]], an offspring of the Church. Let not man, then, so debase himself that by serving vices he become a slave of the devil, an adversary of Christ, a chattel of iniquity, a son of perdition. The soul too, through faith and charity, is the bride of the Saviour, but through the uncleanness of guilt she becomes the adulteress of the devil. [[5:9|and thy years to the cruel|Et annos tuos crudeli]]: that is, do not spend the acts of the lifetime in which thou livest here at the prompting of the devil, who is so savage that nothing less will satisfy him concerning us than to rob us of eternal happiness and drag us with him into infernal damnation.

paras.t: Tam crudelissimo igitur hosti nequaquam te subdas, nec unquam consentias, ne forte impleantur extranei viribus tuis, id est, ne vires naturæ roburque gratiæ auferant tibi invisibiles hostes, personæque lubricæ, et meretricum lenones; et labores tui sint in domo aliena, id est, facultates et opes tuæ a meretricibus consumantur, et opera meritoria, quibus aliquando Deo servisti, ab hostibus tuæ salutis annihilentur, id est, mercede priventur; et gemas in novissimis, sero pœnitendo, quando consumpseris carnes tuas et corpus tuum, per luxuriam enervando et exhauriendo. Hinc in Proverbiis suis ait Cyrillus libidinoso: Quid est quod coeundo effundis? Nonne digestissima medulla? nonne vitæ admirabiliter sementiva humanæ naturæ, radicalis carnis substantia? et divitiarum generativæ virtutis thesauraria vena? Quid ingratus in nihilum projicis?
paras.en: To so very cruel an enemy, then, never subject thyself, nor ever consent, [[5:10|Lest strangers be filled with thy strength|ne forte impleantur extranei viribus tuis]]: that is, lest invisible enemies, and wanton persons, and the pimps of harlots take from thee the strength of nature and the vigour of grace; [[5:10|and thy labours be in another man's house|et labores tui sint in domo aliena]]: that is, lest thy means and riches be consumed by harlots, and the meritorious works by which thou didst once serve God be brought to nothing by the enemies of thy salvation, that is, be robbed of their reward; [[5:11|And thou mourn at the last|et gemas in novissimis]], repenting too late, [[5:11|when thou shalt have spent thy flesh and thy body|quando consumpseris carnes tuas et corpus tuum]], unnerving and draining them by lust. Hence Cyril in his Proverbs [probably the medieval book of moral fables, also called *Speculum sapientiae*, ascribed to a St Cyril] says to the lustful man: What is it that thou pourest out in coition? Is it not the most refined marrow? Is it not the root-substance of the flesh, wonderfully seminal of the life of human nature, the treasure-vein of the riches of the power of generation? Why, ungrateful one, dost thou cast it away for nothing?

paras.t: Et dicas: Cur detestatus sum disciplinam, per quam carnales concupiscentiæ refrenantur, et increpationibus non acquievit cor meum, nec audivi vocem docentium me, et magistris non inclinavi aurem meam ad caste vivendum? Pene fui in omni malo, id est, fere pollutus sum omni peccato, in medio ecclesiæ, id est ecclesiasticorum, et synagogæ cæterorum sæculariumque credentium: et hoc damnabilius est, quod peccavi non ex ignorantia, sed ex certa scientia, et inter fideles et spirituales personas, quarum nec documentis nec exemplis correctus sum.
paras.en: [[5:11|and say|Et dicas]]: [[5:12|Why have I hated instruction|Cur detestatus sum disciplinam]], by which the desires of the flesh are curbed, [[5:12|and my heart consented not to reproof|et increpationibus non acquievit cor meum]], [[5:13|And have not heard the voice of them that taught me|nec audivi vocem docentium me]], [[5:13|and have not inclined my ear to masters|et magistris non inclinavi aurem meam]] to live chastely? [[5:14|I have almost been in all evil|Pene fui in omni malo]], that is, I have been defiled with almost every sin, [[5:14|in the midst of the church|in medio ecclesiæ]], that is, of churchmen, [[5:14|and of the congregation|et synagogæ]] of the other, secular believers [Denis takes *ecclesia* for the clergy and *synagoga*, the congregation, for the lay faithful]; and this is the more damnable, that I sinned not from ignorance but from sure knowledge, and among faithful and spiritual persons, by whose teachings and examples I was not corrected.

paras.t: Bibe aquam sapientiæ et doctrinæ, de cisterna tua, id est de sacra Scriptura, et voluminibus vere catholicis; vel de gratia habituali et sapientia infusa vel acquisita exsistente in te, ut ex habitu procedas in actum, et de sapientiæ dono in contemplationis exercitium; et fluenta putei tui, id est, meritis gratiæ tibi collatæ reficiaris. Hinc in Isaia dictum est: Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris. Et alio loco in eodem Propheta: Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas. In Apocalypsi quoque: Qui sitit, veniat; et qui vult, accipiat aquam vitæ gratis. Christus quoque in Evangelio: Aqua, inquit, quam ego dabo, fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam. Puteus etiam dici potest cor profundum, desuper illustratum, divinis charismatibus adimpletum.
paras.en: [[5:15|Drink water|Bibe aquam]] of wisdom and doctrine [[5:15|out of thy own cistern|de cisterna tua]], that is, from Holy Scripture and from truly catholic books; or from the habitual grace and the wisdom, infused or acquired, that exists in thee, so that thou mayest go forth from the habit into the act, and from the gift of wisdom into the exercise of contemplation; [[5:15|and the streams of thy own well|et fluenta putei tui]], that is, be refreshed by the merits of the grace bestowed on thee. Hence it is said in Isaias: [[Is 12:3|Thou shall draw waters with joy out of the saviour's fountains|Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris]]. And in another place in the same Prophet: [[Is 55:1|All you that thirst, come to the waters|Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas]]. In the Apocalypse also: [[Apoc 22:17|he that thirsteth, let him come. And he that will, let him take the water of life, freely|Qui sitit, veniat; et qui vult, accipiat aquam vitæ gratis]]. Christ too in the Gospel: [[John 4:14|the water|Aqua]], he says, [[John 4:14|that I will give him shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting|quam ego dabo, fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam]]. The well can also be called the deep heart, enlightened from above and filled with divine gifts.

paras.t: Deriventur fontes tui foras: id est, sapientiam, scientiam et doctrinam tibi concessas, quibus intus redundas, communica aliis prædicando, consulendo, docendo, corripiendo: sicut princeps Apostolorum hortatur, Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes; et sicut in Daniele legitur, Qui multos erudiunt ad justitiam, fulgebunt quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates. Et in plateis, id est in latitudine populi, et in locis patentibus, aquas tuas divide, et charismata tibi concessa aliis impertire, spiritualia misericordiæ opera exercendo, ac proximos ædificando.
paras.en: [[5:16|Let thy fountains be conveyed abroad|Deriventur fontes tui foras]]: that is, the wisdom, knowledge and doctrine granted thee, with which thou overflowest within, share with others by preaching, counselling, teaching, correcting; as the prince of the Apostles exhorts: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another|Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes]]; and as is read in Daniel: [[Dan 12:3|they that instruct many to justice|Qui multos erudiunt ad justitiam]] [[Dan 12:3|shall shine|fulgebunt]] [[Dan 12:3|as stars for all eternity|quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates]]. [[5:16|and in the streets|Et in plateis]], that is, in the breadth of the people and in open places, [[5:16|divide thy waters|aquas tuas divide]]: impart to others the gifts granted thee, by practising the spiritual works of mercy and edifying thy neighbours.

paras.t: Habeto eas solus, nec sint alieni participes tui. Hoc prima facie videtur jam dictis contrariari. Sic ergo est exponendum: Habeto eas solus, id est, in tua sint potestate, et in corde tuo, tanquam in subjecto, originaliter ac habitualiter solæ remaneant, nec in hoc sint alii participes tui, ut a tam salubri usu gratiarum istarum possint te impedire. Vel, Alieni, id est infideles atque hæretici, tecum societatem non habeant, nec suas doctrinas commisceant tuis. Quæ enim societas luci ad tenebras?
paras.en: [[5:17|Keep them to thyself alone, neither let strangers be partakers with thee|Habeto eas solus, nec sint alieni participes tui]]. At first sight this seems to contradict what has just been said. So it is to be explained thus: [[5:17|Keep them to thyself alone|Habeto eas solus]], that is, let them be in thy power, and let them remain in thy heart alone, as in their subject [that is, the one in whom they inhere], at their source and as a habit; and let others not be partakers with thee in this, so as to be able to hinder thee from so wholesome a use of these graces. Or: [[5:17|strangers|Alieni]], that is, unbelievers and heretics, let them have no fellowship with thee, nor mingle their doctrines with thine. For [[2 Cor 6:14|what fellowship hath light with darkness|Quæ enim societas luci ad tenebras]]?

paras.t: Sit vena tua, id est sapientia et doctrina, ex qua aliis potum animæ refectivum, et concupiscentiarum vitiorumque refrigerativum tribuis, benedicta a Domino, qui tanto plus eam in se ipsa augeat atque perficiat, quanto liberalius communicatur et aliis. Qui enim spiritualia sua charismata proximis impertitur, nequaquam ex hoc minorationem, sed spiritualem locupletationem sortitur; fitque particeps omnium bonorum quæ ex sua communicatione fiunt ab aliis.
paras.en: [[5:18|Let thy vein|Sit vena tua]], that is, the wisdom and doctrine from which thou givest others a drink that refreshes the soul and cools desires and vices, [[5:18|be blessed|benedicta]] by the Lord, who will increase and perfect it in itself the more, the more freely it is shared with others too. For he who imparts his spiritual gifts to his neighbours gains thereby no lessening but a spiritual enrichment, and becomes a partaker of all the good that others do as a result of his sharing.

paras.t: Et lætare legitime cum muliere adolescentiæ tuæ, id est uxore, quam in adolescentia accepisti. Cerva carissima, et gratissimus hinnulus, id est, hæc sit tibi dilecta ac socia, tanquam cerva gratissima et fecunda. Et quoniam vir caput est mulieris, et uxor sub potestate mariti est, sit tibi uxor tua subjecta et acquiescens ut hinnulus: qui cervæ est pullus. Ubera ejus inebrient te omni tempore opportuno. Magna enim est delectatio copulæ conjugali admixta. Et in amore ejus delectare jugiter, scilicet suo loco et tempore, in quantum delectatio illa est licita, nec limites matrimonii transcendens. Quemadmodum enim ille actus matrimonialis fieri potest sine peccato, dum fit desiderio prolis ad Dei obsequium educandæ, vel ad persolvendum debitum carnis, sive ad vitandum incontinentiæ malum in compare; sic et delectatio actui illi annexa, potest esse sine culpa et licita, prout super quartum Sententiarum doctores declarant.
paras.en: [[5:18|and rejoice|Et lætare]] lawfully [[5:18|with the wife of thy youth|cum muliere adolescentiæ tuæ]], that is, the wife whom thou didst take in thy youth. [[5:19|Let her be thy dearest hind, and most agreeable fawn|Cerva carissima, et gratissimus hinnulus]]: that is, let her be beloved by thee and thy companion, as a most agreeable and fruitful hind. And since [[Eph 5:23|the husband is the head of the wife|vir caput est mulieris]][[1 Cor 11:3||]], and the wife is under the power of her husband, let thy wife be subject to thee and yielding, like a fawn, which is the young of the hind. [[5:19|let her breasts inebriate thee at all times|Ubera ejus inebrient te omni tempore]] that are fitting. For great is the delight joined to conjugal union. [[5:19|be thou delighted continually with her love|Et in amore ejus delectare jugiter]], that is, in its own place and time, so far as that delight is lawful and does not pass the bounds of matrimony. For just as that act of matrimony can be done without sin, when it is done from desire of offspring to be brought up for the service of God, or to render the debt of the flesh [that is, the marriage debt, what each spouse owes the other], or to avert the evil of incontinence in one's partner; so too the delight joined to that act can be without fault and lawful, as the doctors declare on the fourth book of the Sentences [of Peter Lombard, which treats of marriage].

paras.t: Loquitur autem Salomon tam extense, non ut ad libidinem carnalitatemque provocet, sed ut pusillos ad vitia pronos, ab omni concubitu adulterino et illicito revocet. Ideo subditur: Quare seduceris, fili mi, id est, seduci te sinis, vel te ipsum seducis, ab aliena uxore aut fornicatrice, et foveris in sinu alterius? quasi dicat: Quum possis sine peccato cum propria uxore deliciari, cur cum tanto facinore delectaris cum aliis feminis?
paras.en: Now Solomon speaks at such length, not to provoke to lust and carnality, but to call back the little ones who are prone to vice from all adulterous and unlawful intercourse. Therefore it is added: [[5:20|Why art thou seduced, my son|Quare seduceris, fili mi]], that is, why dost thou let thyself be seduced, or seduce thyself, [[5:20|by a strange woman|ab aliena]], another man's wife or a fornicatress, [[5:20|and art cherished in the bosom of another|et foveris in sinu alterius]]? As if to say: Since thou canst take thy pleasure without sin with thy own wife, why dost thou take thy delight, with so great a crime, in other women?

paras.t: Respicit Dominus viam hominis, id est omne quod agit, sive in die, sive in nocte, et omnes gressus illius considerat. Ideo in Jeremia habetur: Si occultabitur vir in absconditis, et ego non videbo eum? Et sanctus Job loquitur Deo: Observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti. Ideo saltem timore altissimi ac metuendissimi Judicis omnia intuentis, debes a tanto scelere revocari, et verecundari de omni turpitudine vitiorum in præsentia supersanctissimi Dei, nec coram facie ejus tam fœde et viliter te habere. Ad quod te quoque debent inducere mala quæ ex peccato sequuntur. De quibus subjungitur:
paras.en: [[5:21|The Lord beholdeth the ways of man|Respicit Dominus viam hominis]], that is, all that he does, whether by day or by night, [[5:21|and considereth all his steps|et omnes gressus illius considerat]]. Hence it is found in Jeremias: [[Jer 23:24|Shall a man be hid in secret places, and I not see him|Si occultabitur vir in absconditis, et ego non videbo eum?]]? [the margin gives Jer. x; the words are Jer 23:24] And holy Job says to God: [[Job 13:27|hast observed all my paths, and hast considered the steps of my feet|Observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti]]. Therefore, at least for fear of the most high and most dreadful Judge who beholds all things, thou oughtest to be called back from so great a crime, and to be ashamed of all the foulness of vice in the presence of the all-holy God, and not to behave so foully and basely before his face. To this the evils that follow from sin ought also to lead thee; of which it is added:

paras.t: Iniquitates suæ capiunt impium, id est, faciunt eum diabolo subditum, et in captivitatem infelicem redactum, ita quod perdit gratiæ libertatem; et funibus peccatorum suorum quisque constringitur, id est, arctatur atque ligatur, ita ut nequeat se extendere ad Dei obsequium, nec egredi ad meritorie operandum, quum sit spiritualiter mortuus, et quasi diaboli equus. Peccata etenim rationem excæcant, vires debilitant, et bonum naturæ lædunt. Hinc gloriosissimus princeps Apostolorum in sua secunda ait Canonica: Iniqui sunt servi corruptionis; a quo enim quis superatus est, hujus et servus est. Vas quoque electionis, loquens de impiis: Resipiscant, inquit, a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem. Hoc sensit Propheta, qui pœnitens dixit: Iniquitates meæ supergressæ sunt caput meum, et sicut onus grave gravatæ sunt super me. Hinc in Isaia asseritur: Væ qui trahitis iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis, et quasi vinculum plaustri peccatum.
paras.en: [[5:22|His own iniquities catch the wicked|Iniquitates suæ capiunt impium]], that is, they make him subject to the devil and bring him into unhappy captivity, so that he loses the freedom of grace; [[5:22|and he is fast bound with the ropes of his own sins|et funibus peccatorum suorum quisque constringitur]], each one of them, that is, he is hemmed in and tied, so that he cannot reach out to the service of God nor go forth to work meritoriously, since he is spiritually dead and as it were the devil's horse. For sins blind the reason, weaken the powers, and injure the good of nature. Hence the most glorious prince of the Apostles says in his second Canonical Epistle: The wicked are [[2 Pet 2:19|the slaves of corruption|servi corruptionis]]; [[2 Pet 2:19|For by whom a man is overcome, of the same also he is the slave|a quo enim quis superatus est, hujus et servus est]]. The Vessel of election [that is, St Paul] too, speaking of the wicked: [[2 Tim 2:26|they may recover themselves|Resipiscant]], he says, [[2 Tim 2:26|from the snares of the devil by whom they are held captive at his will|a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem]]. The Prophet felt this, who said in penitence: [[Ps 37:5|my iniquities are gone over my head: and as a heavy burden are become heavy upon me|Iniquitates meæ supergressæ sunt caput meum, et sicut onus grave gravatæ sunt super me]] [the margin's Psalm number cannot be read; the verse is Ps 37:5]. Hence it is asserted in Isaias: [[Is 5:18|Woe to you that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as the rope of a cart.|Væ qui trahitis iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis, et quasi vinculum plaustri peccatum]]

paras.t: Ipse iniquus morietur morte æternæ damnationis, quia non habuit disciplinam, id est morum modestiam, et suæ transgressionis castigationem, neque salubrem doctrinam per operis executionem; imo abjecit hæc omnia, juxta illud, Tu vero odisti disciplinam, et projecisti sermones meos retrorsum. Quocontra hortatur Psalmista: Apprehendite disciplinam, nequando irascatur Dominus, et pereatis de via justa. Et in multitudine stultitiæ suæ decipietur, id est, propriis erroribus, ignorantiis, concupiscentiis, vitiisque falletur, non attendendo quæ suam concernunt salutem, sed vana securitate torpendo, et sine timore peccando. Ideo cadet in rete diaboli et lacum inferni. De talibus Baruch ait: Viam disciplinæ non invenerunt, ideo perierunt; et quia non habuerunt sapientiam, interierunt propter suam insipientiam. Unde dicitur: Si non audierint, transibunt per gladium, et consumentur in stultitia.
paras.en: [[5:23|He shall die|Ipse iniquus morietur]] [Denis reads *Ipse iniquus morietur*, "the wicked man himself shall die"] the death of eternal damnation, [[5:23|because he hath not received instruction|quia non habuit disciplinam]], that is, modesty of conduct and the chastisement of his transgression, nor wholesome doctrine carried out in deed; nay, he has cast all these away, according to that: [[Ps 49:17|thou hast hated discipline: and hast cast my words behind thee|Tu vero odisti disciplinam, et projecisti sermones meos retrorsum]]. Against which the Psalmist exhorts: [[Ps 2:12|Embrace discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry, and you perish from the just way.|Apprehendite disciplinam, nequando irascatur Dominus, et pereatis de via justa]] [[5:23|and in the multitude of his folly he shall be deceived|Et in multitudine stultitiæ suæ decipietur]], that is, he will be misled by his own errors, ignorances, desires and vices, not attending to what concerns his salvation, but growing torpid in a vain security and sinning without fear. Therefore he will fall into the devil's net and the pit of hell. Of such Baruch says: [[Bar 3:27|neither did they find the way of knowledge: therefore did they perish|Viam disciplinæ non invenerunt, ideo perierunt]]; [[Bar 3:28|And because they had not wisdom, they perished through their folly.|et quia non habuerunt sapientiam, interierunt propter suam insipientiam]] Whence it is said: [[Job 36:12|if they hear not, they shall pass by the sword, and shall be consumed in folly|Si non audierint, transibunt per gladium, et consumentur in stultitia]].

paras.t: Præterea, per meretricem quidam intelligunt idololatriam: cujus labia sunt favus distillans, quia carnalia oblectamenta admittit; et nitidius oleo guttur ejus, quoniam ejus instructio placet idololatris, et pulchra videtur vanis et imperitis hominibus. Ista expositio non videtur litteralis. Catholici autem, per meretricem spiritualiter intelligunt hæreticam pravitatem, seu hæreticorum collectionem: quæ et ipsa promittit carnalia, et nitore eloquentiæ suæ decipit multos, quos finaliter æternæ acerbitati involvit. Idcirco ab ea cavendum. Atque ad hunc sensum potest littera facillime applicari: quod brevitati studens non prosequor, quia difficultatem non habet.
paras.en: Further, by the harlot some understand idolatry: whose lips are [[5:3|a honeycomb dropping|favus distillans]], because it allows carnal pleasures; [[5:3|and her throat is smoother than oil|et nitidius oleo guttur ejus]], since its teaching pleases idolaters and seems beautiful to vain and unlearned men. This exposition does not seem to be literal. But Catholics understand by the harlot, in the spiritual sense, heretical depravity, or the assembly of heretics: which also promises carnal things, and by the polish of its eloquence deceives many, whom in the end it wraps in eternal bitterness. Therefore it is to be shunned. And the text can very easily be applied to this sense; which, being intent on brevity, I do not pursue, since it holds no difficulty.

paras.t: Porro, per mulierem adolescentiæ, mysticè designatur Ecclesia: quæ est cerva carissima, doctrinam conterens serpentinam, et ad bonum agendum celerrima, atque festinans fluenta sapientiæ et doctrinæ sanctæ potare, cornibus divinæ auctoritatis ac prælaticæ potestatis, eminentiaque virtutum armata, ad resistendum rebellibus. Cujus populus est gratissimus hinnulus spiritualiter renovatus, sua varietate delectabilis et amœnus, agilisque ad bona, et matris suæ sequens vestigia, ad fontem sapientiæ properando. Hujus cervæ ac conjugis uberibus debemus inebriari, id est, utriusque Testamenti scripturis ac consolationibus refici et impleri, ita ut repleamur, juxta Scripturæ doctrinam, omni gaudio, et spe in credendo; sicque abundemus in virtute et gratia Spiritus Sancti. Quæ quum ita sint, cur, o fili, seduceris ab aliena, id est hæreticorum collectione, et vanissimis adinventionibus ac novitatibus credis magis, quam solidissimis Ecclesiæ documentis?
paras.en: Moreover, by [[5:18|the wife of thy youth|mulierem adolescentiæ]] the Church is mystically signified: who is [[5:19|thy dearest hind|cerva carissima]], crushing the doctrine of the serpent [in the bestiaries the deer draws serpents out of their holes and tramples them], most swift to do good, and hastening to drink the streams of wisdom and holy doctrine; armed with the horns of divine authority and of prelatical power, and with the eminence of the virtues, to resist the rebellious. Her people is [[5:19|most agreeable fawn|gratissimus hinnulus]], spiritually renewed, delightful and pleasant in its variety, nimble for good, and following in its mother's footsteps, hastening to the fountain of wisdom. With the breasts of this hind and spouse we ought to be inebriated, that is, to be refreshed and filled with the scriptures and consolations of both Testaments, so that, according to the teaching of Scripture, we may be filled with all joy and with hope in believing[[Rom 15:13||]], and so abound in the power and grace of the Holy Ghost. This being so, why, O son, [[5:20|art thou seduced|seduceris]] [[5:20|by a strange woman|ab aliena]], that is, by the assembly of heretics, and believest the vainest inventions and novelties rather than the most solid teachings of the Church?

6.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI SEXTI : FILI MI, SI SPOPONDERIS PRO AMICO TUO.
6.title_en: Elucidation of the sixth chapter: My son, if thou be surety for thy friend.

paras.t: Tractat hic Salomon de diligentia […] circa fidejussionem, et de negligentia ei contraria, atque de aliis quibusdam vitiis increatæ Sapientiæ odibilibus. Deinde rursus ad sapientiam obedientiamque hortatur, ut sic vitia carnis vitentur.
paras.en: Here Solomon treats of diligence […] in the matter of suretyship, and of the negligence contrary to it, and of certain other vices hateful to the uncreated Wisdom. Then he again exhorts to wisdom and obedience, so that in this way the vices of the flesh may be avoided.

paras.t: Fili mi, si spoponderis pro amico tuo, defixisti apud extraneum manum tuam, id est, manum protendendo promisisti alieno satisfacere ei pro amico tuo, si ipsemet amicus tuus non satisfecerit illi. Illaqueatus es verbis oris tui, id est, propria sponsione velut laqueo es constrictus, ad observandum quod promisisti, et captus, id est obligatus ac tentus, propriis sermonibus : sicque incidisti periculum.
paras.en: [[6:1|My son, if thou be surety for thy friend|Fili mi, si spoponderis pro amico tuo]], [[6:1|thou hast engaged fast thy hand to a stranger|defixisti apud extraneum manum tuam]], that is, by stretching out thy hand thou hast promised a stranger to satisfy him for thy friend, if thy friend himself does not satisfy him. [[6:2|Thou art ensnared with the words of thy mouth|Illaqueatus es verbis oris tui]], that is, by thy own pledge thou art bound as by a snare to keep what thou hast promised, [[6:2|and caught|et captus]], that is, bound and held, [[6:2|with thy own words|propriis sermonibus]]: and so thou hast fallen into danger.

paras.t: Idcirco subinfertur consilium : Fac ergo quod dico tibi, fili mi, quia incidisti in manum proximi tui. Discurre, id est, ratiocinando inquire qualiter agere debeas, et ad loca congrua curre ; festina, quia dilatio in isto casu est periculosa ; suscita amicum tuum, vel a somno corporali, aut a cordis ignavia, facque eum sollicitum, ut personaliter satisfaciat. Ne dederis somnum oculis tuis, nec dormitent palpebræ tuæ eo tempore, quo expedit pro causa hac vigilare. Eruere quasi damula de manu : id est, sicut caprea silvestris seu agrestis, quæ est animal imbecille ac timidum, conatur manum tenentis eam evadere ; sic tu stude periculum tuæ sponsionis effugere ; et quasi avis de insidiis aucupis, id est, sicut avis festinat evolare de laqueo seu retiaculo, quo captor avium eam jam cepit, aut capere cupit.
paras.en: Therefore counsel is added: [[6:3|Do, therefore, my son, what I say|Fac ergo quod dico tibi, fili mi]], [[6:3|because thou art fallen into the hand of thy neighbour|quia incidisti in manum proximi tui]]. [[6:3|Run about|Discurre]], that is, inquire by reasoning how thou oughtest to act, and run to the fitting places; [[6:3|make haste|festina]], because delay in such a case is dangerous; [[6:3|stir up thy friend|suscita amicum tuum]], either from bodily sleep or from sloth of heart, and make him anxious to give satisfaction in person. [[6:4|Give not sleep to thy eyes|Ne dederis somnum oculis tuis]], [[6:4|neither let thy eyelids slumber|nec dormitent palpebræ tuæ]] at a time when it is fitting to keep watch for this cause. [[6:5|Deliver thyself as a doe from the hand|Eruere quasi damula de manu]]: that is, as the wild or field roe [*caprea*], which is a weak and timid animal, strives to escape the hand of him who holds it, so do thou strive to escape the danger of thy pledge; [[6:5|and as a bird from the hand of the fowler|et quasi avis de insidiis aucupis]] [Denis reads *de insidiis aucupis*, "from the snares of the fowler", where the Vulgate has *de manu aucupis*, "from the hand of the fowler"], that is, as a bird hastens to fly out of the snare or net in which the fowler has already caught it, or wishes to catch it.

paras.t: Ecce istud ad litteram est sanum consilium, ne quis incaute pro proximo spondeat ; aut si spoponderit, indesinenter curet ac studeat proximum suum inducere ad satisfaciendum, alioqui ipsemet satisfacere non omittat. Verum quidam sunt adeo negligentes, quod improvide spondent pro aliis : quo facto, nec illos sollicitant, nec ipsimet satisfacere curant ; sicque fidei violationem, juramenti seu promissi transgressionem, et grande incurrunt damnum. Hi igitur istud Salomonis pensent impleantque consilium. Is vero pro quo quis spopondit, omnibus modis satagere debet ut fidejussorem suum servet a damno immunem, sicut in Ecclesiastico legitur : Gratiam fidejussoris tui ne obliviscaris.
paras.en: See, this is, according to the letter, sound counsel: that no one should stand surety for his neighbour without caution; or if he has done so, that he should take care and strive without ceasing to bring his neighbour to give satisfaction, and otherwise should not fail to give satisfaction himself. But some are so negligent that they stand surety for others without foresight, and once that is done they neither urge them nor take care to give satisfaction themselves; and so they incur a breach of faith, the transgression of an oath or a promise, and great loss. Let these, then, weigh and fulfil this counsel of Solomon. And he for whom someone has stood surety ought by every means to take pains to keep his surety free from loss, as we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 29:19|Forget not the kindness of thy surety|Gratiam fidejussoris tui ne obliviscaris]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xxix, 20, the verse's number in the Vulgate; the Douay-Rheims numbers it 19].

paras.t: Spiritualiter vero pro amico spondet, qui prælationem assumendo, alios accipit gubernandos, sicque adstringit se ad reddendum rationem pro ipsis. Ad quod etiam specialiter episcopi in sua consecratione solenni voto se obligant, prout Thomas in secunda secundæ, et in libro de Perfectione status spiritualis, declarat. Prælatus ergo curam assumens animarum, incidit grande periculum, et propriis verbis se obligavit implere debitum sui officii, et præsertim ut se exhibeat exemplarem subditis suis, ac primo impleat quod alios docet, ne ei dicatur : Medice, cura te ipsum ; et illud Apostoli : Qui alium doces, te ipsum non doces ? Nempe cujus conversatio est scandalosa, cujus prædicatio irridenda magis quam reverenda censetur. Et sicut ait Gregorius : Cujus vita despicitur, restat ut ejus prædicatio contemnatur. Hinc et Seneca in suis fatetur Proverbiis : Perturpe est, quod objicitur, in objiciente cognosci. In epistola quoque vicesima : Verba, inquit, rebus proba. Facere docet philosophia, non dicere tantum ; et hoc exigit ad suam legem ut quisque legitime vivat, ne sermo a vita dissentiat. Officium namque et indicium sapientiæ est, ut opera verbis concordent.
paras.en: Spiritually, he stands surety for a friend who, by taking up a prelacy, receives others to govern, and so binds himself to render an account for them. To this bishops in particular bind themselves by a solemn vow at their consecration, as Thomas declares in the Secunda Secundae [the second part of the second part of his Summa] and in the book On the Perfection of the Spiritual State. A prelate, then, in taking up the care of souls, falls into great danger, and has bound himself by his own words to fulfil the duty of his office, and above all to show himself an example to his subjects, and first to fulfil what he teaches others, lest it be said to him: [[Luke 4:23|Physician, heal thyself|Medice, cura te ipsum]]; and that saying of the Apostle: Thou [[Rom 2:21|that teachest another, teachest not thyself|Qui alium doces, te ipsum non doces]]? For when a man's conduct is scandalous, his preaching is thought fit to be laughed at rather than revered. And as Gregory says: When a man's life is despised, it remains that his preaching be contemned. Hence Seneca too declares in his Proverbs: It is most shameful that what is reproached should be found in the one who reproaches. And in his twentieth letter: Prove thy words, he says, by thy deeds. Philosophy teaches us to do, not only to speak; and it requires by its law that each man live by rule, so that his speech be not at odds with his life. For it is the office and the sign of wisdom that works agree with words.

paras.t: Fac ergo quod dico tibi, quia incidisti in manum proximi tui, id est subditi tibi commissi, cujus negligentia esset tua damnatio, nisi circa illum diligens esses. Idcirco discurre, ex caritatis fervore ; festina, quia periculum est in mora ; suscita amicum tuum, exhortando, instruendo, corripiendoque subditum, ut cum metu, timore et tremore suam operetur salutem.
paras.en: [[6:3|Do, therefore|Fac ergo]], [[6:3|what I say|quod dico tibi]], [[6:3|because thou art fallen into the hand of thy neighbour|quia incidisti in manum proximi tui]], that is, of the subject entrusted to thee, whose negligence would be thy damnation unless thou wert diligent about him. Therefore [[6:3|run about|discurre]], out of the fervour of charity; [[6:3|make haste|festina]], because there is danger in delay; [[6:3|stir up thy friend|suscita amicum tuum]], by exhorting, instructing and correcting thy subject, so that he may work out his salvation with fear, dread and trembling[[Phil 2:12||]] [the margin gives Philip. 12, without the chapter].

paras.t: Ne dederis somnum oculis tuis, id est, ne quaquam sis negligens, somnolentus, aut fessus in tui executione officii : sicut de quibusdam in Isaia habetur : Speculatores cæci omnes, nescierunt universi ; canes muti non valentes latrare, videntes vana, dormientes, et amantes somnia. Eruere quasi damula de manu, id est, præfato modo te a damnationis periculo eripe. Damula quoque, quamvis sit imbecillis ac timida, nihilo minus velox est cursu atque acerrima visu : sic et tu agilitate actuum virtuosorum, et perspicacissima consideratione, a præfato periculo te præserva. Et quasi avis de insidiis aucupis fugit volando in altum, sic tu consideratione divini judicii, et contemplatione perpetui ac beatissimi præmii, stude evadere tentamenta diaboli pastoribus præparata, et omnem pigritiam supera. Unde subjungitur :
paras.en: [[6:4|Give not sleep to thy eyes|Ne dederis somnum oculis tuis]], that is, be in no way negligent, drowsy or weary in carrying out thy office; as is said of some in Isaias: His [[Is 56:10|watchmen are all blind, they are all ignorant: dumb dogs not able to bark, seeing vain things, sleeping and loving dreams|Speculatores cæci omnes, nescierunt universi ; canes muti non valentes latrare, videntes vana, dormientes, et amantes somnia]] [the margin gives only Is. lvi]. [[6:5|Deliver thyself as a doe from the hand|Eruere quasi damula de manu]], that is, snatch thyself in the aforesaid manner from the danger of damnation. The doe too, though she is weak and timid, is none the less swift in running and very keen of sight: so do thou also preserve thyself from the aforesaid danger by agility in virtuous acts and by most clear-sighted consideration. [[6:5|and as a bird from the hand of the fowler|Et quasi avis de insidiis aucupis]] flees by flying on high, so do thou, by consideration of the divine judgment and contemplation of the everlasting and most blessed reward, strive to escape the temptations of the devil prepared for pastors, and overcome all sloth. Hence it is added:

paras.t: Vade ad formicam, o piger, ut qui Scripturis non obedis, nec majorum exhortationi obtemperas, saltem irrationabilium exemplo animalium instruaris, et de tua insipientia atque ignavia erubescas. Et considera vias ejus, id est sollicitudinem, agilitatem, providentiamque formicæ, et disce sapientiam. Quæ quum non habeat ducem a quo dirigatur, nec præceptorem a quo impellatur, nec principem cujus jussione inducatur, parat in æstate cibum sibi : quia tunc latibulum suum egreditur, ad quærendum victualia pro se ; et congregat in messe quod comedat : quia in messe colligit grana, et alia quædam quæ in foveam suam deportat, quatenus inde sustentetur in hieme, quando non exit præ frigore, nec tunc taliter inveniret necessaria sibi : et totum hoc agit naturali instinctu ex impressione auctoris naturæ, qui est omnium universalis et summus dux, præceptor et princeps, extra et supra omne genus ac ordinem. Nam, ut Commentator post Aristotelem ait : Opus naturæ est opus intelligentiæ, maxime autem primæ causæ, cujus opus est etiam intelligentiæ opus. Hinc, ut asserit Damascenus, bruta et inanimata animalia in talibus magis aguntur, quam agant.
paras.en: [[6:6|Go to the ant, O sluggard|Vade ad formicam, o piger]], so that thou who dost not obey the Scriptures, nor heed the exhortation of thy elders, mayest at least be instructed by the example of the irrational animals, and blush for thy folly and sloth. [[6:6|and consider her ways|Et considera vias ejus]], that is, the care, the agility and the foresight of the ant, [[6:6|and learn wisdom|et disce sapientiam]]. [[6:7|Which, although she hath no guide|Quæ quum non habeat ducem]] by whom she is directed, [[6:7|nor master|nec præceptorem]] by whom she is driven, [[6:7|nor captain|nec principem]] by whose command she is led, [[6:8|Provideth her meat for herself in the summer|parat in æstate cibum sibi]]: for then she comes out of her hiding-place to seek victuals for herself; [[6:8|and gathereth her food in the harvest|et congregat in messe quod comedat]]: for in the harvest she collects grains and certain other things, which she carries down into her hole, so as to be sustained by them in winter, when she does not go out for the cold, nor could she then find in that way what she needs. And all this she does by natural instinct, from the impression of the author of nature, who is the universal and supreme guide, master and captain of all things, outside and above every genus and order. For, as the Commentator [that is, Averroes] says after Aristotle: The work of nature is the work of an intelligence, and above all of the first cause, whose work is also the work of an intelligence. Hence, as Damascene asserts, brute animals and inanimate things in such matters are acted upon rather than act.

paras.t: Sic ergo et nos, et præsertim qui præsunt, debemus in æstate, in juventute, in sanitate et vigore durante exercere opera bona, et spiritualium alimentorum copiam nobis ipsis ac proximis congregare ; et in messe, id est tempore isto quo mereri et crescere, spiritualiterque ditari valemus, et in quo fervor tentationis, imo et ardor caritatis ac studii currunt, colligere necessaria nostræ saluti, quibus in hieme, hoc est in hora mortis et in die judicii, valeamus refici, adjuvari atque salvari, sicut hortatur Apostolus : Dum tempus habemus, operemur bonum ad omnes ; et rursus, Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis. Contra istud etiam in corporalibus agunt improvidi, qui in juventute sua consumunt et vendunt patrimonia sua, et postea, dum magis indigent, et minus acquirere possunt, patiuntur inopiam.
paras.en: So we too, and especially those who are set over others, ought in the summer, in youth, while health and vigour last, to practise good works, and to gather a store of spiritual food for ourselves and for our neighbours; and in the harvest, that is, in this time in which we can merit and grow and be spiritually enriched, and in which the heat of temptation, and indeed the ardour of charity and of zeal, run their course, to collect what is needful for our salvation, by which in winter, that is, in the hour of death and on the day of judgment, we may be refreshed, helped and saved; as the Apostle exhorts: [[Gal 6:10|whilst we have time, let us work good to all men|Dum tempus habemus, operemur bonum ad omnes]]; and again: [[2 Cor 6:2|Behold, now is the acceptable time: behold, now is the day of salvation|Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis]]. Against this, in bodily things too, the improvident act, who in their youth use up and sell their patrimony, and afterwards, when they are in greater need and can acquire less, suffer want.

paras.t: Usquequo, piger, dormies somno corporali, ad quem pigri sunt inclinati, et item somno negligentiæ et peccati ? De quo ait Apostolus : Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis. Est etiam somnus mortis, de quo dixit Salvator, Lazarus amicus noster dormit ; et somnus contemplationis, de quo accipi solet illud Geneseos, Immisit Dominus soporem in Adam. Porro somnus corporalis immoderatus, non solum animæ, sed corpori quoque est valde nocivus, et gravat naturam, hebetat sensum, malos parit humores, et damna rerum inducit. Insuper obruit intellectum, tempus infructuose expendit, et multorum fomentum est vitiorum. Ideo Cato dixit : Plus vigila semper, nec somno deditus esto : Nam diuturna quies vitiis alimenta ministrat. Hinc sancti viri maxime deplanxerunt jacturam temporis, quod dormiendo expendebant. Verumtamen necessitati naturæ cum discretione est providendum. Quando consurges de somno tuo ? Ironia est, et increpatio justa : quasi dicat, Diutius quam tibi expediat, dormies.
paras.en: [[6:9|How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard|Usquequo, piger, dormies]], with bodily sleep, to which the slothful are inclined, and likewise with the sleep of negligence and of sin? Of which the Apostle says: [[Eph 5:14|Rise, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead|Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis]]. There is also the sleep of death, of which the Saviour said: [[John 11:11|Lazarus our friend sleepeth|Lazarus amicus noster dormit]]; and the sleep of contemplation, of which that verse of Genesis is commonly taken: [[Gen 2:21|the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam|Immisit Dominus soporem in Adam]]. Moreover, immoderate bodily sleep is very harmful not only to the soul but to the body as well: it weighs down nature, dulls the senses, breeds bad humours and brings loss of goods. Besides, it overwhelms the understanding, spends time fruitlessly, and is the tinder of many vices. Therefore Cato said: Watch ever more, and be not given to sleep; for long repose supplies the vices with their food. Hence holy men have most bitterly lamented the loss of the time they spent in sleeping. Nevertheless, the needs of nature must be provided for with discretion. [[6:9|when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?|Quando consurges de somno tuo]] It is irony, and a just rebuke: as if to say, thou wilt sleep longer than is good for thee.

paras.t: Paululum dormies, paululum dormitabis, manendo in vitiis : quia modicum tibi videtur tempus illud, quod ita consumis, et dicere soles, Post aliquantulum tempus pœnitentiam agam. Paululum conseres, id est complicabis, manus tuas, ut dormias : quia consertio manuum solet esse indicium affectionis magnæ ad aliquid. Et veniet tibi quasi viator egestas, id est defectus temporalium et spiritualium bonorum, vel ad minus spiritualium, et pauperies quasi vir armatus, id est, tam fortiter, quod nequibis evadere : quod fit, dum quis in suo perdurans torpore, ante veram pœnitentiam tollitur de hac vita. Propter quod monuit Dominus : Vigilate, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit ; et rursus : Vigilate omni tempore orantes, ut digni habeamini fugere omnia quæ ventura sunt, et stare ante Filium hominis.
paras.en: [[6:10|Thou wilt sleep a little, thou wilt slumber a little|Paululum dormies, paululum dormitabis]], by remaining in vice: because the time thou spendest so seems short to thee, and thou art wont to say: After a little while I will do penance. [[6:10|thou wilt fold|Paululum conseres]], that is, clasp, [[6:10|thy hands a little to sleep|manus tuas, ut dormias]]: for the clasping of the hands is commonly a sign of great affection for something. [[6:11|And want shall come upon thee, as a traveller|Et veniet tibi quasi viator egestas]], that is, the lack of temporal and spiritual goods, or at least of spiritual ones, [[6:11|and poverty as a man armed|et pauperies quasi vir armatus]], that is, so mightily that thou wilt not be able to escape: which happens when someone, persisting in his torpor, is taken from this life before true penance. For this reason the Lord warned: [[Matt 24:42|Watch ye therefore, because you know not what hour your Lord will come|Vigilate, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit]]; and again: [[Luke 21:36|Watch ye, therefore, praying at all times, that you may be accounted worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of man|Vigilate omni tempore orantes, ut digni habeamini fugere omnia quæ ventura sunt, et stare ante Filium hominis]].

paras.t: Quod autem subjungitur : Si vero impiger, id est fervens et agilis, fueris in actibus bonis, veniet ut fons messis tua, id est, copiosus fructus inde proveniet tibi, et retributio gloriosa : sicut alibi scriptum est, Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus. Unde legitur secundo Paralipomenon : Non dissolvantur manus vestræ ; erit enim merces operi vestro. Hinc dixit Apostolus : Qui parce seminat, parce et metet ; et qui seminat in benedictionibus, de benedictionibus et metet vitam æternam. Et egestas longe fugiet a te. Istud in Hebræo (ut dicitur) non habetur.
paras.en: As for what is added: [[6:11|But if thou be diligent|Si vero impiger]], that is, fervent and active, in good works, [[6:11|thy harvest shall come as a fountain|veniet ut fons messis tua]], that is, abundant fruit will come to thee from it, and a glorious recompense: as it is written elsewhere: [[Wis 3:15|the fruit of good labours is glorious|Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus]]. Hence we read in the second book of Paralipomenon: [[2 Par 15:7|let not your hands be weakened: for there shall be a reward for your work|Non dissolvantur manus vestræ ; erit enim merces operi vestro]]. Hence the Apostle said: [[2 Cor 9:6|He who soweth sparingly shall also reap sparingly: and he who soweth in blessings shall also reap blessings|Qui parce seminat, parce et metet ; et qui seminat in benedictionibus, de benedictionibus et metet]]: [[Gal 6:8|life everlasting|vitam æternam]]. [[6:11|and want shall flee far from thee|Et egestas longe fugiet a te]]. This, it is said, is not found in the Hebrew.

paras.t: Ex his docemur, in Dei obsequio omnem pigritiam, somnolentiam, accediamque vitare, atque viriliter aggredi opera bona. Et certe pigris valde est ponderandum ac formidandum, quod in Apocalypsi ait Altissimus : Utinam calidus esses aut frigidus ; sed nunc quia tepidus es, incipiam te evomere ex ore meo. Denique pigri in divinis, in præsenti et in futuro sustinent detrimentum, quia id ipsum boni quod agunt, faciunt cum labore et tædio, sine consolatione et gustu : propter quod aut parum, aut nihil merentur. Ferventes vero et agiles, serviunt Deo cum gaudio, et delectabile est eis exercere divina. Ideoque in præmio crescunt præcipue, et sunt Deo cari et complacentes. Pigritia ex caritatis defectu, et inconsideratione divinæ majestatis ac novissimorum procedit. Ideo ait Bernardus : Pigri si diu in suo torpore permanserint, aut opprimuntur sub onere et succumbunt ; aut quodammodo in inferno sunt, ut nunquam ad plenum respirent in lucem miserationum Domini, nec in libertatem spiritus, quæ solum facit jugum suave et onus leve. Inde autem tam perniciosa emanat tepiditas, quia voluntas eorum nondum purgata est, nec sic volunt ac diligunt bonum, sicut noverunt, a propria concupiscentia abstracti et illecti. Amant enim in carne sua terrenas consolatiunculas, sive in verbo, sive in signo, sive in facto. Et si hæc aliquando interrumpunt, non tamen penitus rumpunt. Inde est quod raro dirigunt affectiones suas in Deum, et compunctio eorum non continua, sed horaria est.
paras.en: From these things we are taught to avoid, in the service of God, all sloth, drowsiness and acedia [that is, spiritual sloth, a weariness in the things of God], and to set about good works manfully. And certainly the slothful should greatly weigh and dread what the Most High says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:15|I would thou wert cold or hot|Utinam calidus esses aut frigidus]] [Denis has "hot or cold"]; [[Apoc 3:16|But because thou art lukewarm|sed nunc quia tepidus es]], [[Apoc 3:16|I will begin to vomit thee out of my mouth|incipiam te evomere ex ore meo]]. In short, the slothful in divine things suffer loss both now and hereafter, because the very good that they do, they do with toil and weariness, without consolation or relish; and for this reason they merit little or nothing. But the fervent and active serve God with joy, and it is delightful to them to practise divine things. And so they grow above all in reward, and are dear and pleasing to God. Sloth proceeds from a lack of charity, and from failing to consider the divine majesty and the last things. Therefore Bernard says: The slothful, if they remain long in their torpor, are either crushed under the burden and give way, or are in a manner in hell, so that they never fully breathe again in the light of the Lord's mercies, nor in the liberty of the spirit, which alone makes the yoke sweet and the burden light[[Matt 11:30||]]. And so pernicious a lukewarmness springs from this, that their will is not yet purged, and they do not will and love the good as much as they know it, being drawn away and enticed by their own concupiscence. For they love in their flesh little earthly consolations, whether in word, or in sign, or in deed. And if they sometimes interrupt these, they do not break them off altogether. Hence they seldom direct their affections to God, and their compunction is not continual but by the hour.

paras.t: Homo apostata, id est recedens a fide, vel a religione, sive a Deo per mentis aversionem, vir inutilis sibi et aliis, imo nocivus et scandalizans, ut refuga legis ; graditur ore perverso, id est vitiosa proferens verba, ut alios suis involvat erroribus ; annuit oculis, id est, vanos nutus per visum ostendit ; terit pede, id est, lascive, seu composito gressu ex elatione procedit ; digito loquitur, id est, loquendo digitum petulanter extendit et agitat : quod malum esse, patet ex eo, quod scriptum est Isaiæ quinquagesimo octavo, Si desieris digitum extendere, et loqui quod tibi non expedit. Aliquando tamen sapientes loquendo digitum extendunt et manum, ad excitandam audientium attentionem. Nam et sacratissimus Joannes digitum extendendo Christum monstravit : Ecce, inquiens, Agnus Dei. Et in Actis fertur : Paulus extenta manu cœpit rationem reddere.
paras.en: [[6:12|A man that is an apostate|Homo apostata]], that is, one who falls away from the faith, or from religious life, or from God by turning his mind away from Him, [[6:12|an unprofitable man|vir inutilis]] to himself and to others, nay, harmful and a cause of scandal, as a deserter of the law, [[6:12|walketh with a perverse mouth|graditur ore perverso]], that is, uttering wicked words, so as to entangle others in his errors; [[6:13|He winketh with the eyes|annuit oculis]], that is, makes vain signs with his look; [[6:13|presseth with the foot|terit pede]], that is, walks wantonly, or with a studied gait, out of pride; [[6:13|speaketh with the finger|digito loquitur]], that is, in speaking he stretches out his finger and waves it insolently. That this is evil is plain from what is written in the fifty-eighth chapter of Isaias: If thou wilt [[Is 58:9|cease to stretch out the finger, and to speak that which profiteth not|desieris digitum extendere, et loqui quod tibi non expedit]]. Yet sometimes wise men in speaking stretch out the finger and the hand to rouse the attention of their hearers. For the most holy John too pointed out Christ by stretching out his finger: [[John 1:36|Behold|Ecce]], he said, [[John 1:36|the Lamb of God|Agnus Dei]][[John 1:29||]]. And in the Acts it is related that Paul, [[Acts 26:1|stretching forth his hand, began to make his answer|extenta manu cœpit rationem reddere]].

paras.t: Pravo corde machinatur malum, id est, ex proposito cogitat qualiter aliis possit nocere, et omni tempore jurgia seminat, id est lites atque discordias inter proximos : quod est peccatum gravissimum, caritati et paci omnino contrarium.
paras.en: [[6:14|With a wicked heart he deviseth evil|Pravo corde machinatur malum]], that is, he thinks deliberately how he can harm others, [[6:14|and at all times he soweth discord|et omni tempore jurgia seminat]], that is, quarrels and dissensions among neighbours: which is a most grievous sin, wholly contrary to charity and peace.

paras.t: Huic extemplo, id est statim ac subito, veniet perditio sua, id est damnatio : imo hæc faciendo, perdit continuo semetipsum. Et subito conteretur morte improvisa, nec habebit ultra medicinam, id est pœnitentiam salutarem, præsertim post mortem. Tales quoque raro ac difficulter pœnitent in hac vita, quum sint vehementer malitiosi. Verumtamen auxiliante pietate infinita ac omnipotente Medici supercœlestis, possunt converti. Idcirco quamdiu hic vivunt, non est desperandum de eis. His demum verbis consonat quod legitur in Isaia : Pro eo quod elevatæ sunt filiæ Sion, et ambulaverunt collo extento, et nutibus oculorum ibant, et composito gradu incedebant ; decalvabit Dominus verticem filiarum Sion.
paras.en: [[6:15|To such a one|Huic]] [[6:15|presently|extemplo]], that is, at once and suddenly, [[6:15|his destruction|perditio sua]] shall come, that is, damnation: nay, in doing these things he straightway destroys himself. [[6:15|and he shall suddenly be destroyed|Et subito conteretur]] by an unforeseen death, [[6:15|and shall no longer have any remedy|nec habebit ultra medicinam]], that is, saving penance, above all after death. Such men, too, seldom and with difficulty repent in this life, since they are exceedingly malicious. Yet with the help of the infinite and almighty goodness of the heavenly Physician they can be converted. Therefore, as long as they live here, we must not despair of them. Finally, with these words agrees what we read in Isaias: [[Is 3:16|Because the daughters of Sion are haughty, and have walked with stretched out necks, and wanton glances of their eyes|Pro eo quod elevatæ sunt filiæ Sion, et ambulaverunt collo extento, et nutibus oculorum ibant]], [[Is 3:16|and moved in a set pace|et composito gradu incedebant]]; [[Is 3:17|The Lord will make bald the crown of the head of the daughters of Sion|decalvabit Dominus verticem filiarum Sion]].

paras.t: Sex sunt quæ odit Dominus tanquam enormia crimina, et septimum tanquam gravissimum, detestatur anima ejus, id est mens ejus : non quod Deus in sua natura habeat animam, sed Scriptura more humano loquitur de Deo : sicut Amos ait, Juravit Dominus Deus in anima sua, etc., Detestor ego superbiam; et Isaias, Solennitates vestras odivit anima mea.
paras.en: [[6:16|Six things there are, which the Lord hateth|Sex sunt quæ odit Dominus]] as monstrous crimes, [[6:16|and the seventh|et septimum]] as the gravest of all [[6:16|his soul detesteth|detestatur anima ejus]], that is, his mind: not that God has a soul in his nature, but Scripture speaks of God in human fashion, as Amos says: [[Amos 6:8|The Lord God hath sworn by his own soul|Juravit Dominus Deus in anima sua]], etc., [[Amos 6:8|I detest the pride|Detestor ego superbiam]]; and Isaias: [[Is 1:14|My soul hateth your new moons, and your solemnities|Solennitates vestras odivit anima mea]].

paras.t: Oculos sublimes, id est corda superba, quæ animose efferunt semetipsa. Unde scriptum est: Oculi sublimis hominis humiliati sunt. Linguam mendacem, id est mendacia perniciosa loquentem. Quemadmodum scriptum est : Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium. Quum enim Deus adorandus et benedictus, sit essentialiter veritas ipsa, valde displicet illi tale mendacium, quod est directe recessus a summa veritate.
paras.en: [[6:17|Haughty eyes|Oculos sublimes]], that is, proud hearts, which boldly lift themselves up. Hence it is written: [[Is 2:11|The lofty eyes of man are humbled|Oculi sublimis hominis humiliati sunt]]. [[6:17|a lying tongue|Linguam mendacem]], that is, one that speaks pernicious lies [that is, lies that do real harm, as distinct from officious or jesting ones]. As it is written: [[Ps 5:7|thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie|Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium]]. For since God, adorable and blessed, is in his essence truth itself, such a lie, which is a direct turning away from the supreme truth, greatly displeases him.

paras.t: Manus effundentes innoxium sanguinem, lædendo, mutilando aut occidendo ; cor machinans cogitationes pessimas, id est, intra se excogitans, qualiter mala intenta impleat. Ideo apud Jeremiam loquitur Dominus : Usquequo morabuntur in te cogitationes noxiæ? Et Michæas ait : Væ qui cogitatis inutile. Pedes veloces ad currendum in malum : qui scilicet ex ferventi desiderio et habitu vitioso festinant in opera mala procedere.
paras.en: [[6:17|hands that shed innocent blood|Manus effundentes innoxium sanguinem]], by wounding, maiming or killing; [[6:18|A heart that deviseth wicked plots|cor machinans cogitationes pessimas]], that is, one that thinks out within itself how to carry out the evils it intends. Therefore the Lord says in Jeremias: [[Jer 4:14|how long shall hurtful thoughts abide in thee?|Usquequo morabuntur in te cogitationes noxiæ?]] And Micheas says: [[Mich 2:1|Woe to you that devise that which is unprofitable|Væ qui cogitatis inutile]]. [[6:18|feet that are swift to run into mischief|Pedes veloces ad currendum in malum]]: those, namely, who out of fervent desire and vicious habit hasten to go forth into evil works.

paras.t: Proferentem mendacia testem fallacem : qui fraudulenter et mendose testimonium contra proximum profert, præsertim in foro judicii : propter quod tenetur ei restituere famam, et damnum recompensare. Et eum qui seminat inter fratres, id est proximos, cujuscumque sint sexus, discordias veræ et virtuosæ paci contrarias.
paras.en: [[6:19|A deceitful witness that uttereth lies|Proferentem mendacia testem fallacem]]: he who deceitfully and falsely bears witness against his neighbour, above all in a court of justice; for which he is bound to restore his good name to him and make good the damage. [[6:19|and him that soweth|Et eum qui seminat]] [[6:19|among brethren|inter fratres]], that is, among neighbours, of whichever sex they may be, [[6:19|discord|discordias]] contrary to true and virtuous peace.

paras.t: Circa hæc ait Glossa : Enumeravit sex capitalia crimina, quæ tamen comparatione seminationis discordiæ, quasi minora deprompsit : quoniam majus est facinus illud, quo dissipatur unitas atque fraternitas, quæ per Spiritus Sancti gratiam est connexa. Attamen, sicut Thomas in secunda secundæ, et in Summa contra gentiles declarat, inter omnia peccata quæ fiunt in proximum, homicidium exstat gravissimum. Tamen, quantum ad aliquid, potest seminatio discordiæ gravior reputari, quia directe aufert vitam, caritatem et pacem ; homicidium vero, vitam naturæ. Hinc constat, quam vehementissime debeamus seminationem discordiæ abhorrere ac evitare. Verumtamen quidam inter se habent pravam concordiam, pacem carnalem, vitiosum amorem : quorum concordiam dissipare est bonum, quemadmodum inter Pharisæos et Sadducæos in persecutione B. Pauli concordes, ipse gloriosus Apostolus seminavit discordiam, ut patet in Actibus. Denique congregatio fidelium est exercitus Dei, ad quem pertinet contra invisibiles hostes, contra aciem vitiorum, contra adversarios Dei salutisque propriæ, unanimiter præliari. In exercitu autem optimum est concordia, qua se invicem juvant ; pessimum autem discordia, qua sibi invicem adversantur. Qui igitur inter fideles discordiam seminat, est omnino inimicus Dei, cooperator et adjutor diaboli, proditor proximorum, traditor exercitus Spiritus Sancti, demolitor castri divini. Idcirco est summe nocivus, et penitus detestandus.
paras.en: On these things the Gloss says: He has listed six capital crimes, which he has nevertheless set out as lesser, as it were, in comparison with the sowing of discord; for that crime is greater by which unity and brotherhood, which are bound together by the grace of the Holy Ghost, are torn apart. And yet, as Thomas declares in the Secunda Secundae [the second part of the second part of his Summa theologiae] and in the Summa contra Gentiles, among all the sins committed against one's neighbour homicide is the gravest. Yet in a certain respect the sowing of discord can be reckoned graver, because it directly takes away life, charity and peace [that is, the life of the soul, which is charity], whereas homicide takes away the life of nature. Hence it is clear how very vehemently we ought to abhor and shun the sowing of discord. Some, however, have among themselves a wicked concord, a carnal peace, a vicious love: and to break up their concord is good, as the glorious Apostle himself sowed discord between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, who were agreed in persecuting blessed Paul, as is plain in the Acts[[Acts 23:6||]][[Acts 23:7||]]. Lastly, the congregation of the faithful is the army of God, whose part it is to fight with one mind against invisible enemies, against the battle-line of the vices, against the adversaries of God and of their own salvation. Now in an army the best thing is concord, by which its men help one another; and the worst is discord, by which they oppose one another. He, then, who sows discord among the faithful is altogether an enemy of God, a fellow worker and helper of the devil, a betrayer of his neighbours, a traitor to the army of the Holy Ghost, a destroyer of the camp of God. He is therefore supremely harmful, and utterly to be detested.

paras.t: Conserva, fili mi, præcepta patris tui cœlestis : cui jugiter dicimus, Pater noster qui es in cœlis; qui jure creationis, conservationis, gubernationis, provisionis, liberationis et glorificationis, merito dicitur Pater noster. Cui etiam Isaias dicit : Tu, Domine, Pater noster, Redemptor noster. Et ne dimittas legem matris tuæ sanctæ Ecclesiæ. Liga eam in corde tuo jugiter vinculo caritatis, et assiduitate recordationis. Vinculum autem caritatis est actualis dilectio, quæ dicitur quasi duorum ligatio, id est connexio ; et necessarium est ad salutem ex caritate legem Dei corde tenus conservare. Et circumda gutturi tuo, id est, paratus sis loqui de ea. Istud superius habitum, pleniusque expositum est, capitulo tertio.
paras.en: [[6:20|My son, keep the commandments of thy father|Conserva, fili mi, præcepta patris tui]], thy heavenly Father, to whom we say continually: [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven|Pater noster qui es in cœlis]]; who by right of creation, preservation, governance, providence, deliverance and glorification is deservedly called our Father. To him Isaias also says: [[Is 63:16|thou, O Lord, art our father, our redeemer|Tu, Domine, Pater noster, Redemptor noster]]. [[6:20|and forsake not the law of thy mother|Et ne dimittas legem matris tuæ]], holy Church. [[6:21|Bind them in thy heart continually|Liga eam in corde tuo jugiter]] [Denis has *eam*, "it", that is, the law] with the bond of charity and by constant remembrance. Now the bond of charity is actual love [*dilectio*, which Denis explains as *duorum ligatio*, "a binding of two"], which is so called as being, as it were, a binding of two, that is, a joining together; and it is necessary for salvation to keep the law of God in the heart out of charity. [[6:21|and put them about thy neck|Et circumda gutturi tuo]], that is, be ready to speak of it. This came above, and was more fully expounded, in the third chapter[[Prov 3:3||]].

paras.t: Quum ambulaveris, gradiantur tecum, id est, cordi tuo per actualem considerationem inhæreant. Quum dormieris in lecto vel in morte, custodiant te, ut in eorum meditatione obdormias, et merito adimpletionis eorum desuper custodiaris a culpa et illusionibus somniorum, et a condemnatione æterna ; et evigilans, post somnum corporalem, vel in resurrectione futura, loquere cum eis, id est, ea mox ad memoriam revoces, ac mercedem pro eorum custodia præstoleris. Juxta hunc modum in Deuteronomio scriptum est : Erunt verba Domini in corde tuo ; et narrabis ea filiis tuis, et meditaberis sedens in domo tua, et ambulans in itinere, et dormiens atque consurgens ; et ligabis ea quasi signum in manu tua, eruntque et movebuntur inter oculos tuos, scribesque ea in limine et in ostiis domus tuæ.
paras.en: [[6:22|When thou walkest, let them go with thee|Quum ambulaveris, gradiantur tecum]], that is, let them cleave to thy heart by actual consideration. [[6:22|when thou sleepest|Quum dormieris]], in bed or in death, [[6:22|let them keep thee|custodiant te]]: so that thou mayest fall asleep meditating on them, and by the merit of having fulfilled them be guarded from on high from sin and from the illusions of dreams, and from eternal condemnation; [[6:22|and when thou awakest|et evigilans]], after bodily sleep or in the resurrection to come, [[6:22|talk with them|loquere cum eis]], that is, recall them to memory at once, and await the reward for keeping them. In this manner it is written in Deuteronomy: The words of the Lord [[Deut 6:6|shall be in thy heart|Erunt verba Domini in corde tuo]]. [[Deut 6:7|And thou shalt tell them to thy children, and thou shalt meditate upon them sitting in thy house, and walking on thy journey, sleeping and rising|et narrabis ea filiis tuis, et meditaberis sedens in domo tua, et ambulans in itinere, et dormiens atque consurgens]]. [[Deut 6:8|And thou shalt bind them as a sign on thy hand, and they shall be and shall move between thy eyes|et ligabis ea quasi signum in manu tua, eruntque et movebuntur inter oculos tuos]]. [[Deut 6:9|And thou shalt write them in the entry, and on the doors of thy house|scribesque ea in limine et in ostiis domus tuæ]].

paras.t: Ex quibus elicitur, cum quam summa diligentia et frequentia recolenda sint et implenda divina præcepta, tum præcipientis intuitu et amore, tum propter enormitatem transgressionis eorum vitandam, tum propter ineffabile præmium observationis ipsorum, tum propter intolerabilia supplicia prævaricantium ea. Etenim maledicti qui declinant a mandatis Dei. Qui et in ignem dejicientur tartareum, et in miseriis non subsistent. De quibus satis terribiliter atque verissime ait Psalmista ad Dominum : Pones eos ut clibanum ignis in tempore vultus tui. Dominus in ira sua conturbabit eos, et devorabit eos ignis.
paras.en: From this is drawn out with what supreme diligence and frequency the divine precepts are to be recalled and fulfilled: out of regard for him who commands them and love of him, so as to avoid the enormity of transgressing them, for the unspeakable reward of observing them, and for the unbearable torments of those who transgress them. For [[Ps 118:21|they are cursed who decline from thy commandments|maledicti qui declinant a mandatis Dei]] [Denis has "from the commandments of God"]. They shall also be cast down into the fire of hell, and [[Ps 139:11|in miseries they shall not be able to stand|in miseriis non subsistent]]. Of them the Psalmist says to the Lord, terribly enough and most truly: [[Ps 20:10|Thou shalt make them as an oven of fire, in the time of thy anger: the Lord shall trouble them in his wrath, and fire shall devour them|Pones eos ut clibanum ignis in tempore vultus tui. Dominus in ira sua conturbabit eos, et devorabit eos ignis]].

paras.t: Quia mandatum lucerna est, et lex lux. Lucerna per testam, et minus clare illuminat ; lux per semetipsam, et clarius. Mandatum ergo dicitur lucerna imperfectioribus, qui nondum clare divina intelligunt ; lex vero dicitur lux perfectioribus, quibus lex Dei clarius fulget, et qui limpide contemplantur quæ Dei sunt. Sic communiter exponitur istud. Nihilo minus utrumque ad eosdem potest referri, præsertim quum dicat Propheta : Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, Domine, et lumen semitis meis. Mandatum ergo lucernæ comparatur, quia illustrat ac dirigit ad bene vivendum ; et lex, quoniam intus illuminat mentem, similiter luci.
paras.en: [[6:23|Because the commandment is a lamp, and the law a light|Quia mandatum lucerna est, et lex lux]]. A lamp gives light through its earthen vessel [*testa*, the clay body of an oil lamp], and less clearly; light gives it of itself, and more clearly.
